Choosing a train / validation / test split for temporal graph learning on the U.S. Congress (108-118): evidence, interpretation and recommendation

CS224W project · Congress.gov / GovInfo data, Congresses 108–118 · generated 2026-11-07 from notebooks/split_analysis.ipynb outputs
Bottom line

Use rolling-origin, by-Congress folds with an expanding training window and graphs built strictly as of each bill's prediction time. The window is recency-weighted: validated for Task 1, and a tuned choice still to be checked for Task 2. Develop and compare models on test Congresses 112-117 (train 108..c-2, validate c-1, refit 108..c-1, test c), score Congress 118 once as the locked final test, and check on 119 prospectively.

Full recommendation, protocol and justification ↓

Executive summary

The question. Both tasks predict the future from the past. Task 1 asks which legislators will cosponsor a new bill within 30 days (temporal link prediction, scored with Recall@K and NDCG). Task 2 asks whether a law-capable bill will be reported out of committee within 180 days (node classification, scored with AUROC and average precision). The split decides whether the reported numbers say anything about a future Congress. The notebook split_analysis.ipynb tested this in four steps. Section A asked whether labels and features drift between Congresses. Section B asked whether the graph seen at test time matches the one seen in training. Section C asked whether Congress boundaries are clean cut points and whether information leaks from the future. Section D trained and scored simple baselines (not GNNs) under nine candidate splits. A final section combined 100 de-duplicated checks into explicit decision rules.

What the evidence says. (1) Random and within-Congress splits are invalid. A random bill split inflates Task-1 Recall@20 by +0.075 over a temporal split on the same bills (D7), and 45.2% of its evaluation bills have a later twin bill in training (C20). The within-Congress split loses 80.8% of its Task-2 test bills to censoring (C6b). (2) One test Congress is too imprecise to compare models. For a real +0.020 AUROC Task-2 difference, a single test Congress fails to confirm the direction in 3 of 7 Congresses (43%; very imprecise with n = 7, and it never reverses the sign) (D9). For Task 1 a single Congress passes the formal check (worst Task-1 miss 1 of 7), so the Task-1 case for several folds is about precision and representativeness, not validity. (3) Letting the model see the evaluation Congress's own edges dated up to the prediction time (+stream) is leakage-free and raises Task-1 Recall@20 from 0.259 to 0.296, higher in 7 of 7 folds (D13). (4) On plain (non-streaming) rolling folds, validation on the previous Congress picks near-best Task-1 models and predicts the Task-1 score level (D11, D21, D23, D1, D14). For Task 2 it reliably separates models that are far apart (D6) but barely ranks near-ties (hit rate 14-29%), and it does not predict the AUROC level, which moves between Congresses by more than sampling noise (D2b, D4).

What stays uncertain. All evidence comes from count and rate baselines, not GNNs. Model selection was never tested under streaming, and the full recommended recipe (expanding window + streaming + recency weighting) was never run as a whole. Both must be checked on the development folds before GNN work. For Task 2, neither the notebook's streaming variant (which feeds back the labels of same-Congress bills whose 180-day window had already closed: +0.008 AUROC on 7 folds, driven by one fold) nor expanding vs sliding windows (-0.009, also driven by one fold) is resolved. Six dependent folds detect only fairly large differences: with 80% power, about 0.012-0.015 for a single Task-1 comparison and about 0.017-0.036 AUROC for Task 2 (and more for highly heterogeneous pairs), because Task-2 differences vary more between Congresses. Holm correction across several candidates raises these further. Comparisons are therefore decided by a t(5) test on the six per-fold differences (Holm-adjusted when several candidates compete), and differences it does not resolve are ties. Congress 118 has already been looked at during this baseline analysis.

Recommendation: use rolling-origin, by-Congress folds with a recency-weighted expanding window: for each test Congress c = 112..117, train on 108..c-2, tune on c-1, refit on 108..c-1 and test on c; then score Congress 118 once as a locked final test and use 119 as a prospective check. Build every graph strictly as of each bill's prediction time: Task 1 also sees the current Congress's earlier cosponsorships (+stream), while Task 2's primary result uses only earlier Congresses plus the bill's own edges (plain S3).

Key findings

  1. A random bill split is leaky and optimistic. It inflates Task-1 Recall@20 by +0.0745 (about 29% of the temporal level of 0.259), and 45.2% of its evaluation bills have a later twin bill in training. It is usable only as a labelled upper bound.

    D7 D-c124-txt C20 C-c106-txt decision-c147-txt

  2. Splitting inside a Congress (S4) is invalid for Task 2 and fails the Task-1 censoring check. Its test slice at the end of each Congress loses 80.8% of Task-2 test bills to the 180-day window. Its higher Task-1 score (0.311) comes from a small, late, censored slice (about 777 bills per fold). No break inside a Congress justifies cutting there: the only located break (House original-cosponsor share, January 2021) falls exactly at the start of Congress 117.

    C5 C6b C-c82-txt D8 C23 C-c80-txt

  3. One test Congress cannot settle Task-2 comparisons, and is imprecise for Task 1. For the deployable Task-2 pair (eb_rate_t0safe minus chamber_maj, mean +0.020 AUROC, twice the MDE), 3 of 7 single test Congresses fail to confirm the direction (exact 95% binomial CI roughly 10-82%; it is never reversed). The D9 FAIL for single-Congress splits comes only from Task-2 pairs. On Task-1 pairs the worst single-Congress miss is 1 of 7 (sh_hl1 vs sh_none+caucus, which also flips sign once), under the 0.20 bar.

    D9 D-c128-txt D-c128-o1

  4. Averaging over folds sharpens the average effect but not the next-Congress effect. These are different quantities: the single-Congress miss share is empirical and includes Congress-by-model heterogeneity, while the k-fold miss is a power calculation for the mean. The 95% prediction interval for one new Congress's paired difference is 2.4x the MDE for stream vs plain, 3.1x for eb_rate_t0safe vs chamber_maj, and up to 15x overall (D9b), whatever k is. Per-fold results must therefore be reported next to the mean.

    D9 D9b D-c128-txt

  5. The notebook's 6-fold miss risk (0.115, D27) relies on a normal approximation that treats fold differences as independent with known spread. Recomputing from the per-fold differences on 112-117 with a t distribution on 5 degrees of freedom (noncentral t), the worst relevant pair (eb_m20_t0s vs eb_nomaj_m20_t0s) misses with probability about 0.28, and sh_hl1 vs sh_none+caucus moves from 0.08 to about 0.24. Both are above the 0.20 bar, but for different reasons. The eb_m20 pair is a large effect (mean about +0.08 AUROC) whose size and even direction vary strongly between Congresses (between-Congress sd about 0.06). The problem is heterogeneity, not a small effect. The sh_hl1 pair is a small effect near the detection limit. More generally, the smallest difference six folds detect with 80% power depends on the pair's between-Congress spread. It is about 0.0115-0.0145 for typical Task-1 pairs (sd 0.008-0.010) and about 0.017-0.036 AUROC for Task-2 pairs (sd 0.012-0.025, D-c128-txt). With Holm correction over 3-5 comparisons (for example each candidate against the incumbent) it rises to about 0.015-0.021 (Task 1) and 0.022-0.054 (Task 2). Holm's m counts comparisons, not candidates: comparing 5 candidates all-pairwise means m = 10, a first-step critical t of about 4.8, and larger detectable differences still. These detectable differences are our Monte Carlo computations, not notebook outputs.

    D27 D-c140-txt D-c140-o1 D-c128-txt

  6. For Task 1, validation on the previous Congress picks near-best models within each family and predicts the test level (all on plain S3). Mean regret is 0.0028 Recall@20 for sponsor_hist, 0.0002 for rw2hop and 0.0007 for the learned SVD, all under the 0.005 tolerance. Kendall tau between validation and test orderings is 0.86-0.94, and the mean |val-test| gap is 0.61x the test CI half-width.

    D11 D21 D23 D1 D14 D-c119-txt D-c140-txt decision-c147-txt

  7. For Task 2, validation separates models that are far apart (main baselines keep their order in 7 of 7 folds, D6) but does not rank near-ties: hit rate 14-29%, Kendall tau 0.24-0.33. Regret is small only because the candidates nearly tie. Single-validation regret exceeds MDE/2 for the policy-area family (0.0078 on 7 folds) and for the at-introduction family on the development folds (0.0053). Both pass only because the regret is significant in fewer than 2 folds. Selecting on the mean of the last three validation Congresses brings Task-2 regret to at most 0.0019 (D17, 7 folds). Validation also does not predict the AUROC level: fold means fall from 0.655 (112-115) to 0.583 (116-118), the gap is 1.28x the CI half-width, and a precise level would need about 13 test Congresses.

    D6 D12 D12b D17 D2b D4 D15 D-c119-txt D-c124-txt D-c140-txt D-c115-txt

  8. Streaming the evaluation Congress's own edges dated up to introduction + t0 is legitimate and strongly helps Task 1: +0.037 Recall@20 (+0.026 to +0.053 per fold, 7/7 positive; +0.034 on 112-117). It cuts the share of positives from legislators unseen in training from about 20% to at most 0.7%. For Task 2 the notebook's streaming variant is a different mechanism: it adds the labels of same-Congress bills whose 180-day window had closed by the scored bill's introduction, not same-Congress edges. Its gain (+0.0077 on 7 folds, +0.0114 on 112-117) is positive in only 4 of 7 folds and comes mostly from c = 112 (+0.051; without it the remaining six folds average about +0.001). For the day-30 eb_rate reference the same label feedback gives only +0.0010 AUROC (every fold between -0.002 and +0.004, D13), so the eb_rate_t0safe gain is mostly the c = 112 fold. The notebook's rules pick plain S3 for Task 2. Streaming same-Congress edges into Task 2 was never tested.

  9. For Task 1, old Congresses hurt only unweighted models. Unweighted, the expanding window loses 0.0124 Recall@20 to a 3-Congress sliding window (sliding significantly better in 6 of 7 folds). With a one-Congress recency half-life the difference is -0.0008, and for the learned SVD -0.0003. The recency-weighted comparison was run for Task 1 only. D10 also ran an unweighted Task-2 series (eb_rate, the day-30 policy-area reference): there the expanding window is ahead by +0.0027 AUROC (better in 5 of 7 folds, sliding significantly better in none), whereas for eb_rate_t0safe S3 minus S2 is -0.009 / -0.011. The Task-2 window sign therefore depends on the variant, consistent with it being unresolved. No recency-weighted Task-2 window comparison was run, although recency weighting itself helps Task 2 (+0.0096, better in 2 folds, worse in 0; D26).

    D10 D-c130-txt D26 D-c132-txt R5 decision-c151-txt

  10. Refitting on train + validation before testing helps the baselines. Under the recommended streaming protocol it adds about +0.025 Recall@20 (7/7 folds). Without streaming it adds about +0.06, mostly because refitting adds the most recent Congress's counts. It does not hurt Task 2 (+0.005). For a GNN, refitting with a transferred epoch budget and no early-stopping signal is untested.

    D19 D-c138-txt

  11. Graphs must be time-masked at evaluation, and the target bill's own future edges must be excluded in training. About 52% of an evaluation Congress's final cosponsor graph does not exist yet at t0 (B10). Training with the target bill's own future edges costs a simple ranker 1.8 Recall@20 points (95% CI -3.1 to -0.3). Training on the final graph minus those edges shows no measurable harm (+0.007, CI -0.005 to +0.017), so full as-of-t0 training snapshots are recommended for consistency but not shown to be necessary. This test is small (2 folds, 3,000 training bills, a logistic count ranker). 42.7% of related-bill links point to later bills, and non-referral committee edges encode the Task-2 label (0 of 92,423 bills without one advanced).

    B10 B-c65-txt B12 B-c67-txt B6b B-c57-txt B7 B-c59-txt

  12. Recent Congresses are off-distribution in task-specific ways. The Task-2 label weakens in 116-117 (58-61% of chamber-passed bills have no committee report within 180 days). Task-1 positive density drops in 118 (about 40-47% below the training mean), and late cosponsors arrive later there (median lag 92 vs 62-75 days). The share of cosponsors who are original (day 0) breaks upward in 117-118 (0.460 and 0.466 vs 0.330-0.394 in 108-115, A4 FAIL). That leaves less to predict after day 0, which matters most for Task 1 at t0 = 0. These are drifts to report and remedy. They do not invalidate the forward split.

    A1b A2 A3 A4 A8 A13 A-c13-txt A-c17-txt C3 C-c77-txt decision-c151-txt

  13. Congress 118 is not untouched. Every backtest number used to choose the protocol includes 118. On folds 112-117 alone the Task-1 conclusions hold, while the Task-2 streaming and window differences cross the 0.01 MDE, but they remain unresolved under the t(5) interval because they are driven by c = 112. For sponsor_hist, 118 falls outside the development prediction interval. The other three models' 118 levels, and 8 of 9 relevant paired differences, fall inside it.

The question and the tasks

Goal: decide how to split the Congress data (Congresses 108–118) for the two tasks in the proposal:

  1. Cosponsor prediction (temporal link prediction): for a bill at time t (day 0 or day 7 after introduction), rank the eligible legislators who will cosponsor it in (t, t+30].
  2. Bill advancement (node classification): will a law-capable bill (HR, S, HJRES, SJRES) be reported out of committee within 180 days of introduction?

The default idea is a by-Congress temporal split (train on earlier Congresses, validate on the next, test on the last). That split is only trustworthy if a set of conditions hold: similar label rates, similar feature distributions, enough node overlap for the graph model, no leakage, fully observed labels, and stable baseline scores across folds. Each section below tests a group of those conditions and records a check (pass / fail / info). The last section collects every check and compares the candidate splits.

Run it: JupyterLab, kernel with pandas, pyarrow, numpy, scipy (see notebooks/requirements.txt). Charts use D3 v7, vendored at notebooks/vendor/d3.v7.min.js (no internet needed). Run the cells top to bottom; charts appear as interactive SVGs (hover for values).

A. Label / target and covariate stationarity

116, 117 and 118 differ from 108-115, but each in different ways: Task 2 (base rate, label validity) breaks in 116-117 and partly reverts in 118, while Task 1 (positive density) breaks only in 118. So the two candidate test Congresses (117 for S1a, 118 for S1b) are off-distribution for different tasks. Section A therefore argues for a forward split that is evaluated per task and per Congress, with base-rate- and density-aware metrics. It does not single out one val/test pair as clean.

Section A asks whether what a model learns from (labels, features, and the label-feature relationship) stays stable from the training Congresses (108-115) to the candidate validation/test Congresses (116, 117, 118). Each candidate is judged against a 95% t prediction interval: the range one new Congress should fall in if nothing changed. The interval is built from only 6-8 reference Congresses (8 for most checks, 7 for A18, 6 for the forward-chained A12/A13/A18b), so it is wide, about +/-2.5 to 2.8 times the between-Congress SD. A check fails only if a test survives a Holm multiple-comparison correction. Holm-surviving failures are strong evidence, but their p-values are approximate. Some failures rest only on the joint test, which compares the mean of the three candidates with the reference Congresses and treats 116, 117 and 118 as independent draws. They are consecutive and probably autocorrelated, so those joint p-values are anti-conservative. In the other direction, a pass often means not detectable with n = 6-8, not stable.

Which Congress shifts in what (Holm survivors; "joint only" = no single cell survives): - 116: label validity (A1b, cell), House Task-2 rate (A2, joint only), bill volume (A8), Task-2 AUROC (A13: t0-safe part by cell, full part joint only). Task-1 density and original share are normal. - 117: everything 116 has, plus original-cosponsor share (A4). It has the lowest Task-2 rate in the series (2.81%; raw failure of A1, not Holm-surviving). Task-1 density is low but inside the interval (t = -2.0). - 118: Task-1 density (A3, cells at t0 = 0 and 7), original share (A4), volume (A8), Task-2 AUROC (A13, joint only). Its Task-2 rate (4.41%), label-miss share (0.473) and House rate are back inside the train spread.

Only volume and A13 fail in all three. The cluster test A17 rejects chance for each candidate (p = 0.005, <0.001 and 0.044).

What the shifts look like. Task-2 rate: pooled 6.5% in train against 4.14% / 2.81% / 4.41%. In 116 and 118 most of the drop comes from a bigger denominator (law-capable volume 1.32x and 1.54x the mean train Congress), not from fewer reported bills. The exception is 117, where fewer reports dominate. In 116-117, 58-61% of chamber-passed bills have no committee report within 180 days, against 35-53% in train, so the label captures less of real advancement. Task-1 density in 118 is 0.47% at t0 = 0, about 40% below the train mean (about 0.80%). The number of new day-1-30 cosponsorships in 118 is normal, so this looks mainly like a normal number of joiners spread over many more bills.

What held. The bill-feature mix is no more shifted than train Congresses are from each other (A7, A9, A11). For Task 1, a simple pair model (5 features, t0 = 7 only) fitted on earlier Congresses discriminates at or above its train level on 116-118, with calibration slope near 1 (A18b). This is pair-level AUROC, not per-bill Recall@K/NDCG. The majority-sponsor effect differs strongly by controlling party within train (A5c). Regime explains part of its 116-117 dip, but all three House candidates still sit below their own regime's reference.

Inference for the split. All of these are differences between history and the period the model will be used in. Forward splits measure them (S1a and S1a+stream fail 6 of 20 judged checks, the others 7, because they also evaluate 118). The random split S5 cannot see them. Section A barely discriminates between forward splits on counts. Its main message for the val/test choice is that S1a tests Task 2 on its most anomalous Congress (117), while S1b validates Task 2 on 117 and tests Task 1 on its most anomalous Congress (118). Results should therefore be reported per task and per Congress, and any tuning or recalibration on a single val Congress should be checked out of sample.

Implications for the split

  • Use a forward, by-Congress split, and treat S5 (random) only as a leakage reference. The shifts found here (volume and Task-2 AUROC in all candidates, Task-2 rate and label validity in 116-117, Task-1 density in 118) are differences between history and the deployment period that only a forward split measures. Section A's failure counts barely discriminate between forward splits (6 vs 7 of 20).

  • The val/test choice is task-specific. 116-117 are the Task-2 break Congresses (label-miss share 60.5% / 58.1%, House rate t = -2.4 / -3.6), and 118 partly reverts on Task 2 but breaks on Task-1 density. S1a (val 116, test 117) tests Task 2 on its most anomalous Congress (A14 rate gap 0.786). S1b (val 117, test 118) validates Task 2 on that same Congress and tests Task 1 on the density outlier (gap 0.591). 118 is only marginally closer to 119 (domain AUROC 0.548 vs 0.559). Neither single pair is clean, so report each task per Congress (116, 117, 118). Prefer rolling-origin evaluation across 116-118 to a single test Congress, letting no one Congress's anomaly dominate the conclusion.

  • Task 2 calibration: forward OE is 0.47-0.73 on candidates, but train folds also swing (0.70-1.46). Recalibrating the intercept on the val Congress alone is not supported by section A. In S1b, carrying over 117's level (2.8%, OE 0.47) to 118 (4.4%, OE 0.73) would under-predict by roughly 1.5x. Treat recalibration as a choice to test out of sample (section D's backtest), or base it on pooled recent Congresses. Select models with base-rate-insensitive metrics (AUROC). Report AP together with each test Congress's prevalence (or AP / prevalence), and report House and Senate separately.

  • Task 2 label: report the alternative label (reported OR passed origin chamber within 180 days) as a sensitivity analysis. In 116-117, 58-61% of chamber-passed bills have no committee report within 180 days (35-53% in train; 47% in 118), so in those Congresses the main label penalises correctly ranked bills that advanced by other routes.

  • Task 1: compare Recall@K/NDCG against per-Congress baselines (random, popularity, same-party heuristics), stratify by number of positives, and report t0 = 0 and t0 = 7 separately. 118's density is about 40% below the train mean (0.47% vs about 0.80% at t0 = 0), apparently because a normal number of joiners (23,736) is spread over 1.54x more bills. So raw score drops on 118 partly reflect task difficulty, not model failure. A simple pair model's pooled-pair AUROC (t0 = 7) does not degrade, but that does not guarantee stable per-bill ranking scores.

  • Model design: add chamber-control (regime) features and a sponsor-majority x controlling-party interaction. Within train, the House majority OR is 4.78 under R vs 2.38 under D (z = -4.17). Regime alone does not close the gap: all three House candidates sit below their regime reference (z = -1.2 to -1.7). Do not select or weight training Congresses by regime on bill-feature similarity, because A15b finds no regime effect once party-encoding features are removed.

  • Consider recency weighting or a shorter window as a tuned option, not a default. Recent pools are modestly closer to their test Congress (S2 closer in 18/28 comparisons; 113-118 form a tight topic-mix block). Let section D's backtest decide, given the smaller sample. Include bill-volume-sensitive and t0-dependent features such as original-cosponsor count, whose distribution is shifting upward (A4, A7 n_original).

Detailed results

What this tests (from the notebook)

Every forward split (train on earlier data, evaluate on later data: S1a/S1b/S2/S3 by Congress, and S4 within the last Congresses) evaluates Congresses that come after its training data. The model will also be deployed on a later Congress (119). So any shift found here is a difference between history and the deployment target, not a defect of a forward split: the forward split is the protocol that measures it honestly, and the random split S5 is the one that hides it. A drift FAIL below therefore selects a remedy (recency-weighted training, recalibration on the val Congress, density-normalised metrics, per-Congress reporting), not a different split. All A checks are recorded as kind='drift'; every forward split, including S4 (whose test units are the late parts of 116-118), gets the same verdict from the candidate Congresses it evaluates, and S5 is left unjudged (None), which is not the same as passing. Four kinds of shift are tested:

  • Label shift: the positive rate P(y) changes (e.g. fewer bills get reported). Threshold-based metrics, calibration and AUPRC all move with the base rate even when the model is unchanged.
  • Label-definition drift: the label stops measuring the same thing (e.g. bills advance without a committee report more often), so a base-rate change is partly an artifact.
  • Concept shift: the relationship P(y | x) changes. This is the shift that makes a trained model wrong. It can be regime-conditional (it depends on which party controls the chamber), in which case a regime feature fixes it.
  • Covariate shift: the inputs P(x) change, marginally or jointly.

Train pool and candidates. The reference pool is split S1a's train set (108-115, REL_REF). The candidate val/test Congresses are 116, 117 and 118 (S1a: val 116, test 117; S1b: val 117, test 118).

Verdict rule (shared rel_to_train). A candidate fails a check part when it falls outside the 95% t prediction interval for one new Congress built from the 8 reference Congresses (mean +/- t(7, 0.975) * sd * sqrt(1 + 1/8), about 2.5 SD; log scale for rates and counts; one-sided for distances such as PSI or AUROC, where a reference Congress's value is its leave-one-out distance to the other 7). Three extra readings guard against over-calling shift:

  • Multiplicity. Each check has several parts (features, chambers, t0 values) times 3 candidates. A check is recorded as FAIL only if at least one test survives a Holm correction within that check. The family holds one test per (part x candidate) cell plus one joint test per part that asks whether the 3 candidates as a group sit off the reference mean (two-sample t of the candidate mean vs the 8 reference Congresses; it catches a drop that recurs in every candidate but is too small to survive in any single cell). The raw per-part t-PI failures are still printed and kept in detail, next to the family-wise nested-LOO false-alarm rate. by_split: a split fails if a candidate Congress it evaluates has a Holm-surviving cell, or a raw cell failure confirmed by a Holm-surviving joint test (same direction).
  • Trend vs break. Each failing level quantity gets one of three labels: break (also outside the prediction interval of a linear trend fitted on 108-115), consistent with trend (inside the trend interval AND the 108-115 slope is itself significant), or undetermined (inside the trend interval but no significant slope: with n = 8 and 1-3 Congresses of extrapolation, the trend test simply has too little power to separate trend from level shift). Only the first two map to a remedy.
  • Deployment proxy (A15). The in-progress 119th Congress is where the model would be used; A15 checks which Congresses look most like it, and A15b whether similarity follows recency or party regime (same House / Senate majorities), with and without the sponsor-party features that encode party control by construction.

Fixed bands (e.g. 0.8-1.25x) are kept as a secondary column. Congress 119 is excluded from every split.

Interpretation

Setup for section A. The reference pool is 108-115 and the candidates are 116, 117 and 118. There are 110,802 uncensored advancement labels (censored = not yet followed for the full 180 days), and 47 bill-level features over 128,791 law-capable bills. Both chambers of the 119th are Republican-controlled, which matters for the regime comparisons in A15. A handful of bills (at most 11, in 117) have a sponsor with no caucus/party assignment.

Caveats.

These 11 bills in 117 later drive the top domain-classifier coefficient for 117 (sponsor_caucus=(missing), +3.10 log-odds) in A11. With so few bills this is plausibly a data-coding effect rather than substantive drift.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A1. Advancement base rate (Task 2) per Congress, and what drives its change

Why it matters: if the share of bills reported within 180 days differs a lot between train and the held-out Congress, a model trained on 108-115 is mis-calibrated there, and AUPRC / F1 on the test Congress cannot be compared with validation scores. How to read it: rate per Congress; ratio = rate / pooled-train rate, h = Cohen's h and p = chi-square p (train rows: vs the other train Congresses). With about 10k bills almost every gap is "significant", so the verdict uses the t prediction interval of the train Congresses (t = standardised distance, tr = residual vs the 108-115 trend). The decomposition splits each candidate's log rate change into a volume part (more bills introduced) and a count part (fewer bills reported), both relative to the mean train Congress.

Interpretation

The Task-2 positive rate per Congress is 4.3-8.7% in train (pooled 6.5%), against 4.14% (116), 2.81% (117) and 4.41% (118). Only 117 falls outside the prediction interval [3.29%, 12.19%] (t = -2.9). The joint test that all three sit low is nominally significant (t = -3.0, p = 0.02), but nothing survives Holm, so A1 is recorded as PASS. The decomposition is the informative part. Reported-bill counts in 116 and 118 are normal (491 and 611 vs a train range of 414-839; A1d PASS), and bill volume is 1.32-1.54x the mean train Congress. Volume explains 61% of the log drop in 116 and all of it in 118. In 117, fewer reports explain the larger share (count part -0.476 vs volume part -0.362, volume share 0.43). So 118 is near the train spread (t = -1.3), and 117 is the real Task-2 base-rate outlier.

Caveats.

PASS here is a power statement. With 8 reference Congresses the interval spans almost a factor of 4 in rate, and the candidates are three of the four lowest values (only 112, at 4.32%, is below 118). Chi-square p-values are uninformative at about 10k bills per Congress. Rates are computed on uncensored bills only, and candidates have higher censored shares (15.0-17.3% vs 9.6-15.2% in train). If late-introduced bills differ systematically in their reporting odds, the candidate rates carry a selection effect that the notebook does not quantify.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A1b-A1c. Does the Task-2 label measure the same thing in every Congress?

Why it matters: "reported out of committee within 180 days" misses bills that advance without a committee report: suspension of the rules in the House, unanimous consent in the Senate. If that route grows in later Congresses, part of the base-rate drop is a label-definition artifact, and a model would be penalised for correctly ranking bills that did advance. How to read it: among uncensored bills that passed their chamber of origin within 180 days, the share not reported within 180 days (unrep_share; never_rep = no Reported action at all). A1c recomputes the base rate with an alternative label (reported or passed the origin chamber within 180 days) and checks whether the candidates' drop shrinks under it.

Interpretation

A1b measures how much real advancement the label misses. Among bills that passed their chamber of origin within 180 days, the share without a committee report within 180 days is 60.5% in 116 and 58.1% in 117, against 34.7-52.6% in train. 116 survives Holm on its own, and so does the joint test (t = +3.0, p = 0.0095). Both are labelled breaks. 118 is back at 47.3% (t = +0.7), inside the train spread. So the label-validity problem is specific to 116-117, not a growing trend. In those two Congresses the label captures a smaller fraction of bills that actually advance, plausibly via suspension of the rules or unanimous consent, though the notebook does not test those routes directly. Under the alternative label (reported OR passed origin chamber), the 116 and 117 drops shrink (log ratio -0.451 to -0.272 and -0.838 to -0.558), but in 118 the drop grows slightly (-0.387 to -0.469).

Caveats.

The joint test pools 116-118 as independent draws. 116 and 117 are consecutive and share a House-D majority, so its p-value is optimistic. The 116 cell result does not depend on that assumption. The alternative label still trends down (joint t = -2.6, p = 0.038, not Holm-surviving), so part of the base-rate drop is a label artifact, but not all of it. Passed-bill counts are small (353-787 per Congress), so unrep_share is noisy, and the chamber splits rest on even fewer bills.

How to read it: the chart shows the rate per chamber, the pooled rate and the pooled rate under A1c's alternative label; the check applies the t prediction-interval rule within each chamber.

A3. Cosponsor-task labels (Task 1) at t0 = 0 and t0 = 7

How to read it: per Congress and t0: share of bills with at least one positive, mean positives per bill, positives / eligible (density) and censored share. The eligible pool is the point-in-time roster (members in office, delegates included, in the month of introduction + t0), the same pool section D ranks; density_legacy uses the full-Congress roster for comparison. A3 checks density, A3b the share of bills with any positive.

For Task 1, the eligible pool is the point-in-time roster of legislators in office (delegates included). The share of bills gaining at least one new cosponsor in (t0, t0+30] stays inside train (0.320-0.384 at t0 = 0; A3b PASS). Both cells survive Holm and are labelled breaks (A3 FAIL). 117 is low but inside the interval (t = -2.0 and -2.2), and 116 is normal (t = +0.6 and +0.1). Caveats.

Censoring is small (2.2-3.9% in candidates) and similar in 117 and 118, so it does not explain the 118 drop. The legacy full-Congress denominator gives nearly identical densities, so the pool definition is not the cause either. For the mechanism, see A4 and A6: the evidence points more to dilution by bill volume than to a smaller pool of joiners.

Caveats.

Ranking metrics such as Recall@K and NDCG depend on how many positives each bill has. A lower density makes 118 harder for any model, so a raw score drop on 118 cannot be attributed to the model without a density-matched baseline (e.g. random and popularity rankers scored on the same Congress).

What this tests (from the notebook)

A5. Concept stability: majority vs minority sponsor advancement, overall and by regime

Why it matters: majority-party sponsorship is one of the strongest Task-2 signals. If its effect (odds ratio, OR) changes between train and the held-out Congress, the learned relationship is wrong there. The effect may depend on which party controls the chamber. If candidates match train Congresses with the same controlling party, the remedy is a regime feature or interaction, not a different split. How to read it: A5 compares the pooled-chamber OR per Congress with train Congresses. A5b compares each candidate chamber-Congress with the train chamber-Congresses that have the same chamber and controlling party (random-effects z: sampling variance plus the between-Congress variance seen in train). A5c tests in train whether D-control and R-control ORs differ. Majority from majority_party(); sponsors are assigned to their caucus.

Interpretation

The pooled-chamber odds ratio (OR) for a majority-party sponsor's bill being reported is 1.96-3.72 in train, against 1.72 (116), 1.44 (117) and 2.48 (118). Only 117 is outside the interval (t = -2.8), and nothing survives Holm (A5 PASS). Conditioning on regime (which party controls the chamber) explains part of the dip. Between-Congress variance of the log OR is about 4x smaller within regime (tau^2 = 0.023) than within chamber with regime ignored (0.088), and no candidate cell differs significantly from same-regime train Congresses (A5b PASS, largest |z| = 1.70). All three House candidates still fall below their own regime reference (z = -1.70 for 116 House-D, -1.54 for 117 House-D, -1.23 for 118 House-R). That same-direction pattern suggests a residual House decline that this per-cell test cannot confirm. Within train, the majority effect is larger under R control than under D control, in the House (4.78 vs 2.38, z = -4.17) and in the Senate (2.38 vs 1.61, z = -2.40; A5c INFO).

Caveats.

A5b tests each cell alone against a reference with n = 2 for House-D (110, 111), so it has very little power. Its pass is weak evidence of a match. Party control is also partly confounded with era (both D-House train Congresses are 110-111).

A-c21-o1
Interpretation

In the per-chamber ORs coloured by controlling party, R-controlled train Houses (108, 109, 112-115) cluster high (3.67-7.32) and D-controlled train Houses (110, 111) lower (2.87, 1.97). The candidate D-Houses 116 and 117 (1.64, 1.69) sit below both D-controlled train Houses. 118's R-controlled House (3.45) is higher than 116-117 but is the lowest R-controlled House in the series. The Senate is lower and flatter (1.16-3.19). So the regime pattern is real, but it does not account for the whole candidate decline. The concept looks regime-dependent, with a possible additional downward drift in the House that n = 2-6 reference Congresses per regime cannot resolve.

Caveats.

Several Senate confidence intervals include or approach 1 (e.g. 112 Senate 0.85-2.00, 117 Senate 0.83-1.62). Single-Congress Senate ORs are noisy.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A6. Concept stability: partisanship of new cosponsors (P(y | x) for Task 1)

Why it matters: a link-prediction model will learn "same party as the sponsor" as a strong prior. If the share of new cosponsors from the sponsor's party drifts (polarisation), the learned prior is off in the held-out Congress. How to read it: among cosponsors joining in days 1-30 of law-capable bills with a D/R sponsor, the share from the same party and from the other major party.

This is a marginal share. It does not show whether which cross-party members cosponsor changed, which A18 addresses partly. The count row is descriptive (no interval is computed for it), and it covers bills with a D/R sponsor only.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A7-A8. Marginal covariate drift (PSI) and bill volume

Why it matters: even with stable labels, a held-out Congress with a different mix of policy areas, bill types, chambers, sponsor status, original-cosponsor counts or introduction timing tests the model on a differently weighted population. How to read it: PSI of each candidate vs pooled 108-115 bills; a train Congress's value is its PSI vs the other 7 train Congresses. The t prediction-interval rule decides, on the log scale (PSI is bounded at 0 and right-skewed, so a raw-scale interval has a negative lower bound and over-calls large values; section B judges PSI the same way) (the usual 0.1 / 0.25 PSI bands are shown in the chart subtitle only). The chart shows PSI divided by the largest train LOO PSI, so bars above 1 mean "more drift than any train Congress". policy_area_harm folds categories absent from some Congress (taxonomy changes) into one bucket (PA_UNSTABLE).

Interpretation

Population stability index (PSI) measures how much one feature's distribution moved. Against pooled 108-115, no bill feature shows Holm-surviving drift (A7 PASS). Harmonised policy area has PSI 0.238-0.288 for candidates, against 0.035-0.272 for train Congresses left out one at a time (leave-one-out, LOO). Chamber, bill type and sponsor status are essentially unchanged (PSI at most 0.002). The only consistent signal is n_original (original-cosponsor count, PSI 0.079-0.114, joint p = 0.034, not Holm-surviving), which echoes A4. Without harmonisation, policy-area PSI is 0.357-0.436, inflated by taxonomy changes, and folding 4 unstable categories removes that. Law-capable bill volume is 14,340 / 15,242 / 16,565 against 8,621-11,414 in train. All three cells and the joint test (t = +5.9) survive Holm (A8 FAIL), so this is the one shift present in every candidate. 118 is labelled a break, and 116-117 are undetermined because the 108-115 slope is not significant.

Caveats.

The A7 reference spread is wide because 109 and 112 are themselves far from later Congresses (see the JSD heatmap), so a moderate policy-area shift would pass. The family-wise LOO false-alarm rate of 25% over 6 parts shows the raw per-part rule is noisy, which is why Holm is applied. Volume growth affects graph size (bill nodes per Congress) and dilutes both the Task-2 rate and Task-1 density.

A-c25-o1
Interpretation

The chart divides each candidate's PSI by the largest train LOO PSI, so a bar above 1 means the candidate drifts more than any train Congress does from the others. Only n_original exceeds 1 in all three candidates (1.09, 1.14, 1.58, rising with time), and policy area just exceeds it in 118 (1.06). All other features sit far below 1.

Caveats.

A ratio just above 1, measured against the maximum of 8 values, is weak evidence on its own. Its weight comes from agreeing with A4.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A9-A10. Congress x Congress drift matrix (policy-area mix)

Why it matters: the heatmap shows which Congresses look alike. If distance grows with the time gap, drift is gradual: the most recent Congresses are the best training data and an expanding window dilutes them. How to read it: JSD (base 2, 0 = identical) of the harmonised policy-area distribution. A9 compares each candidate's mean JSD to the train Congresses with each train Congress's mean JSD to the other train Congresses (same rule as PSI, so A7 and A9 agree in method).

Interpretation

Each candidate's mean Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) of the policy-area mix to the train Congresses is 0.049-0.057. That sits inside the train LOO interval [0.024, 0.070] (A9 PASS). The Spearman correlation between Congress gap and JSD is 0.68 (A10 INFO, above the 0.5 threshold). Topic-mix drift is gradual, with nearby Congresses more alike than distant ones.

Caveats.

A10's correlation runs over all pairs of one matrix, so pairs are not independent. 0.68 describes the pattern; it is not a significance test.

A-c27-o0
Interpretation

The heatmap has a clear block structure. Congresses 113-118 are nearly identical in policy-area mix (pairwise JSD 0.002-0.023). 108-111 are moderately distant from them (about 0.035-0.067), and 109 and 112 are far from 113-118 (0.089-0.113). They are close to their own neighbours, though (109 vs 110 0.013, 109 vs 111 0.029, 112 vs 111 0.022). So the real structure is a boundary between 112 and 113, not two isolated outliers. For the candidates, the nearest training Congresses are 113-115, not the full 108-115 pool.

Caveats.

Hypothesis, not tested here: the sharp 112 to 113 boundary may reflect a change in how policy areas were coded or harmonised rather than a change in agenda. Either way, the pre-113 Congresses widen the reference spread used by A7/A9/A11 and make those checks more lenient.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A11. Joint covariate shift: can a classifier tell a candidate's bills from train bills?

Why it matters: each marginal PSI can look fine while the joint distribution shifts (e.g. the same policy areas, but sponsored by a different party). A domain classifier (logistic regression on the bill features: chamber, type, sponsor caucus and majority status, harmonised policy area, introduction-day bin, log original cosponsors) is trained to separate train-pool bills from one Congress's bills; its 2-fold cross-validated AUROC is 0.5 when the two are indistinguishable. Policy area is not known at t0 for most fresh bills (PA_MISS_T0), so a second part drops it (the t0-safe feature set). How to read it: candidates are compared with train Congresses classified against the other 7 (LOO). The top coefficients say which features drive the separation.

A domain classifier (logistic regression on bill features, 2-fold cross-validated) separates each candidate's bills from the 108-115 pool with AUROC 0.629 / 0.630 / 0.646. Train Congresses separate from the other seven with AUROC 0.586-0.669, so the candidates are not unusual (A11 PASS). Without policy area (the t0-safe set), candidate AUROCs are 0.584-0.591 against 0.542-0.668. No joint covariate shift beyond normal between-Congress variation is detectable. The top separating coefficients are an (unstable/missing) policy-area bucket, Foreign Trade and International Finance (about -1.8 to -2.2 log-odds in all three), and, in 117, the 11 caucus-less sponsors (+3.10). The first and last are plausibly bookkeeping effects. Whether the Foreign Trade coefficient is a coding change or a real topic shift is a hypothesis the notebook does not test.

Caveats.

An AUROC of 0.6-0.65 for every Congress, train included, means Congresses are always somewhat distinguishable. The test shows the candidates are no more distinct than usual, not that they are identical to train. A linear classifier cannot detect nonlinear or graph-structural shift. Section B covers graph structure.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A12-A13. Calibration and concept stability of a fitted Task-2 model

Why it matters: marginal ORs are a partial view. A logistic model using the same bill features as A11 is fitted on earlier Congresses and scored on a later one. The main comparison is forward-chained (one step ahead, like split S3): Congress c is scored by a model fitted on 108..c-1, for c = 110-115 (train reference) and 116-118 (candidates). A leave-one-out variant (train Congress scored by a model fitted on the other 7, which is interpolation and so easier) is shown for context. How to read it: OE = observed / mean predicted rate (calibration-in-the-large; this mostly tracks A1's base rate). slope = calibration slope: 1 means relative risks transfer, < 1 means the model is over-confident (the feature effects weakened). coef_shift = majority-status log-odds effect refitted on Congress c alone, minus the effect in the fitted model. A12 checks slope and coefficient shift; A13 checks AUROC with and without policy area (auroc_noPA = t0-safe features only, since policy area is mostly missing at t0).

Interpretation

In a forward-chained logistic Task-2 model (Congress c scored by a model fitted on 108..c-1), calibration-in-the-large (OE, observed / predicted rate) is 0.62, 0.47 and 0.73 on the candidates, so the model over-predicts, as A1 implies. Train forward folds also swing widely (OE 0.70-1.46), so base-rate miscalibration from one Congress to the next is normal, not new. The calibration slope is 0.675 / 0.791 / 0.621 (over-confident), inside the wide 6-Congress interval [0.613, 1.176] (A12 PASS; joint p = 0.039, not Holm). Discrimination drops. Forward AUROC is 0.666 / 0.674 / 0.664 against 0.712-0.781 for train folds. With t0-safe features only, it is 0.562 / 0.558 / 0.599 against 0.620-0.681 (A13 FAIL). Evidence strength differs by part. auroc_noPA has Holm-surviving cells for 116 and 117. The full auroc and the 118 noPA value fail only through joint tests (t = -4.6 and -5.0). Whether the majority-coefficient shift drives this cannot be resolved here: the coef_shift interval [-1.527, 0.819] is wider than 2 log-odds, and the majority OR did fall in 116-117 (A5: 1.72, 1.44), which plausibly explains part of their AUROC loss. 118's normal majority OR (2.48) next to a low AUROC suggests the majority effect is not the whole story.

Caveats.

The joint tests treat 116-118 as independent, so their p-values are optimistic. The consistency of the drop (all six candidate values below the train minimum) is still hard to attribute to chance. The reference is 6 forward folds, each fitted on fewer Congresses than the candidates' models, which if anything favours the candidates. The leave-one-out columns show the same drop (0.661-0.678), so it is not an artifact of the forward protocol. This is a linear model with bill features only, and a GNN using cosponsor-graph signals may degrade differently. Inference, not tested: the AUROC drop together with volume growth fits an influx of low-probability bills that look ordinary on these features.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A18. Concept stability for Task 1: do pair-feature effects on cosponsoring stay the same?

Why it matters: A6 looks at one marginal share; A12/A13 test P(y | x) only for Task 2. A link predictor for Task 1 learns how much each (bill, legislator) pair feature raises the chance of cosponsoring: past cosponsoring of this sponsor's bills, reciprocity (the sponsor cosponsored the legislator's bills), the legislator's general activity, same caucus, same state. If those effects moved, model selection on the val Congress can still work (ranking survives) while calibrated scores and the learned weights drift. How to read it: for each Congress, a logistic model on sampled (bill, eligible legislator) pairs at t0 = 7 (point-in-time pool incl. delegates; history counted in the 730 days before introduction + 7 d). A18 judges each coefficient of 116-118 against 109-115 (108 is dropped from the reference because its look-back window starts before the data). A18b scores each Congress with a model fitted on all earlier Congresses (forward-chained, like A13): AUROC over pairs and the calibration slope.

Interpretation

Per-Congress logistic fits on sampled (bill, legislator) pairs at t0 = 7 give coefficients for five pair features: sponsor-to-legislator cosponsor history, reciprocity, legislator activity, same caucus and same state. Two raw failures appear, both breaks: history in 116 (0.416 vs 0.507-0.723) and same_state in 117 (0.370 vs 0.521-0.897). Neither survives Holm over 15 cells plus 5 joint tests (A18 PASS; 7 reference Congresses, 109-115). The only directional hint is same_caucus, higher in 116-118 (1.19-1.36 vs 0.67-1.15; joint p = 0.039, not Holm), which agrees with A6. A forward-chained pair model gets pooled-pair AUROC 0.718 / 0.730 / 0.751 on 116-118. 116 is inside the train-fold range (0.703-0.724), and 117-118 are above it. Calibration slope is 0.98-1.14 (A18b PASS). So the pair-level discrimination of a simple model does not degrade at t0 = 7. 118's t = +4.3 is a distribution change in its own right, even though its direction is favourable.

Caveats.

The family-wise LOO false-alarm rate of the coefficient checks is 43% over 5 parts, so single-coefficient deviations are expected and the two raw breaks should not be over-read. A18b is a pooled-pair AUROC with negatives subsampled to 10%, from a 5-feature model at t0 = 7 only. It is not per-bill Recall@K/NDCG, and t0 = 0 is not tested. 118's higher AUROC coincides with the density drop (A3) and a higher same_caucus coefficient. It may reflect a change in the composition of positives (fewer, more predictable joiners) rather than a stable relationship, and per-bill ranking scores can still fall on 118.

Interpretation

The coefficient trajectories are mostly noisy flat bands. History stays around 0.4-0.7. Reciprocity fluctuates around zero (-0.199 to +0.124) and changes sign across Congresses. Activity is mostly 0-0.2, with sign flips in 108 (-0.093) and 112 (-0.015) and a high of 0.444 in 109. Same_caucus drifts up from about 0.7-1.15 in train to 1.19-1.36 in 116-118. Same_state is 0.52-0.90 apart from 117's dip (0.37). The near-zero features changing sign is expected noise, not a concept reversal. The features with clearly non-zero effects (history, same_caucus, same_state) keep their sign throughout.

Caveats.

The coefficients are per unit on different scales (log1p counts vs binary indicators), so their raw sizes are not an importance ranking. 108 is shown but excluded from the reference because its 730-day look-back starts before the data.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A14. Which candidate split's training pool is closest to the Congress it evaluates?

Why it matters: this compares the shared candidate splits (SPLIT_DEFS: S1a/S1b expanding, S2 sliding k=SLIDE_K, S3 rolling-origin expanding) on the distribution distance between each evaluation unit's training Congresses and its evaluated Congress. A smaller distance means the evaluated Congress is better represented by that split's training data. How to read it: mean distance per split and role over its evaluation units (iter_eval_units). The chart shows domain-classifier AUROC per test fold for S2 and S3 (S1a/S1b units are a subset of S3's units). This is a proxy: closer distributions do not guarantee better scores (section D's backtest decides), and sliding pools have fewer examples.

Interpretation

A14 measures, for each split and role, how far each evaluation unit's training pool is from the Congress it evaluates. It uses four distances: domain AUROC, |log| advancement-rate ratio (adv_logratio), |log| cosponsor-density ratio (dens_logratio) and topic JSD. The S1 rows matter most for the val/test choice, and they show a task-specific mismatch. S1a validates on 116, whose Task-1 density is almost identical to its pool (0.012), and tests on 117, which has the largest Task-2 rate gap of any unit (0.786). S1b validates on 117 (the same 0.786 Task-2 gap) and tests on 118, which has the largest Task-1 density gap (0.591) but a small Task-2 gap (0.259). So in S1a, Task-2 model selection happens on a near-normal Congress and is scored on the outlier. In S1b, Task-2 selection and any recalibration happen on the outlier, and Task 1 is scored on its outlier. For S2 vs S3 test units, sliding window S2 (k = 3) has lower mean domain AUROC (0.622 vs 0.631), density gap (0.182 vs 0.214) and topic JSD (0.024 vs 0.040), and a slightly larger rate gap (0.385 vs 0.354). It is closer in 18 of 28 fold x metric comparisons (A14 INFO 0.6429).

Caveats.

This is a distribution proxy, not performance. A 3-Congress pool has far fewer examples, and section D's backtest decides the trade-off. S2/S3 mean differences are small (about 0.01 in domain AUROC), and the 28 comparisons are not independent. Each S1 row is a single Congress, so its distances describe that Congress, not a typical one.

A-c35-o1
Interpretation

Per test fold, the sliding pool is less distinguishable from its test Congress in 115, 117 and 118 (e.g. 0.561 vs 0.611 in 117, 0.574 vs 0.624 in 118). The expanding pool is closer in 112-114 and 116. On domain AUROC alone, sliding wins only 3 of 7 folds, but its advantage is largest in the most recent folds.

Caveats.

Fold-level domain AUROCs carry 2-fold cross-validation noise. Differences of a few hundredths in one fold are within the train LOO spread seen in A11.

What this tests (from the notebook)

A15. Does the test Congress look like the deployment target (the in-progress 119th)?

Why it matters: a test score is only a good forecast of deployed performance if the test Congress resembles the Congress the model will be used on. 119 is in progress (excluded from every split), but its bills introduced so far can be compared with earlier Congresses. How to read it: to make the comparison fair, every Congress is restricted to bills introduced by the same day of its Congress as the latest 119th bill. The domain classifier uses t0-safe features only (no policy area, which young 119th bills mostly lack). The primary feature set also drops sponsor caucus and majority status: the share of bills sponsored by each party moves with the majority (table below), so those features make same-majority Congresses look alike by construction. The with party column keeps them for comparison. 119 vs c = AUROC separating 119's bills from Congress c's (lower = more alike); c vs c-1 shows how far consecutive Congresses usually are. PSIs per feature compare 119 with 116-118 and with 108-117. INFO only: it tells you which candidate test Congress (117 for S1a, 118 for S1b) is the better deployment proxy.

The with-party line equals the no-party line for Congresses that share 119's RH/RS regime (108, 109, 114, 115). It is raised for every Congress with a different regime, most strongly for 110-113 and 116 (0.643-0.713, including the R-House/D-Senate Congresses 112 and 113), and less for 117-118 (0.600, 0.561). What this tests (from the notebook)

A15b. Does similarity to 119 follow recency or party regime, once party-encoding features are removed?

Why it matters: if Congresses with the same House / Senate majorities look alike in substance, regime is a useful feature; if similarity follows recency, recent data matter most. A classifier that sees sponsor caucus and majority status will find same-regime Congresses alike by construction (the sponsor-party mix moves with the majority), so the test is run three times: no party (chamber, bill type, day bin, original cosponsors), majority only (adds the caucus-agnostic 'sponsor in majority' flag) and with party (adds sponsor caucus; the earlier version). How to read it: every pair of Congresses (108-119, same day window) gets a domain AUROC (heatmap = no party). A regression over pairs, AUROC ~ gap + [gap = 1] + same_regime, separates time distance (the dummy absorbs the consecutive pairs, several of which share a regime; the count is printed) from sharing the regime; its one-sided p-value comes from permuting the regime labels across Congresses. Regimes = shared REGIME from majority_party(). Whatever the result, section D's D26 is the outcome-based test of regime weighting; this is a bill-feature proxy.

Interpretation

A regression over all 66 Congress pairs (AUROC ~ gap + [gap = 1] + same_regime, with permutation p-values) separates time distance from shared party control. With party-encoding features removed, sharing a regime has essentially no effect (b = -0.0035, p_perm = 0.30). Time gap has a small positive effect at the edge of significance (b = 0.0034 per Congress, p = 0.056). Adding the majority flag gives b_same = -0.013 (p = 0.098). Only when sponsor caucus is included does regime become strongly significant (b = -0.062, p = 0.002), which is the by-construction effect. In bill-feature space, the evidence favours weak recency over regime. 115 is the closest Congress to 119 under every feature set.

Caveats.

This proxy uses bill composition only. A5/A5c show that regime does matter for the outcome relationship (majority-sponsor OR), which this test cannot see. Regime belongs in the model as a feature or interaction, but these data give no basis for selecting or weighting training Congresses by regime. Section D's D26 is the outcome-based test. With 12 Congresses and 4/11 consecutive pairs sharing a regime, power is limited.

The pairwise no-party heatmap shows that 113-119 form a tight cluster (most pairwise AUROCs about 0.53-0.56). 109 and especially 112 are distinct from everyone (often 0.60-0.64), and 108-111 are moderately separated from the recent block. Labels with the same House/Senate majority do not visibly cluster once party features are removed, which agrees with the null regime coefficient in A15b.

Caveats.

Pairwise AUROCs share Congresses, so cells are strongly dependent. Visual clusters should not be read as independent confirmations.

What this tests (from the notebook)

Section A summary: multiplicity, trend vs break, and what survives

Why it matters: section A runs dozens of check parts per candidate. At a 5% level, about one part in twenty fails by chance even if nothing changed, and the parts are correlated. Every check above is already decided by its Holm survivors (cells plus joint candidate tests). A17 then asks whether a candidate fails more than chance predicts. Because several checks track the same underlying quantity (A1 / A1c / A1d / A2 all see the Task-2 rate drop), A17 counts clusters of checks (one per underlying quantity family), each with a false-alarm rate of 1 - 0.95^m for m member checks, and compares the count with a Poisson-binomial null. A drift FAIL here means "the later Congresses, and so the deployment target, differ from history; the forward split measures it; apply the remedy", not "this split is invalid". The trend-vs-break table labels every failing level part and the remedy each implies. The heatmap shows the standardised distance t of every check part.

Interpretation

Section summary: 13 pass, 6 fail, 5 info. Holm survivors, with the evidence type: 116: A1b (cell + joint), A2 House (joint only), A8 (cell + joint), A13 auroc (joint only), A13 auroc_noPA (cell + joint). 117: the same plus A4 (cell + joint). 118: A3 at both t0 (cells), A4 (cell + joint), A8 (cell + joint), A13 auroc and auroc_noPA (joint only, confirming raw cell failures). So the Task-2 base-rate and label-validity clusters fail for 116-117 but not 118, and the Task-1 label cluster fails for 117 (A4) and 118 (A3, A4). Candidates fail 4/6, 5/6 and 3/6 clusters against 0.89 expected (Poisson-binomial p = 0.005, <0.001, 0.044), so A17 FAILs. Two thirds of the failing level parts are labelled breaks (A16 metric 0.667). The rest are undetermined because the train slope is not significant, and none is a predictable trend. S1a and S1a+stream fail 6 of 20 judged checks and the other forward splits 7, the difference being A3 (118 only). S5 is judged on 0 checks.

Caveats.

Three layers of approximation: (1) joint tests treat 116-118 as independent although they are consecutive and partly share regimes; (2) the cluster false-alarm model 1 - 0.95^m assumes roughly independent clusters, although A1b and A2 House are linked; (3) trend-vs-break labels come from a linear fit on 8 points extrapolated 1-3 steps, so 'break' does not rule out a nonlinear trend. 118's A17 result (p = 0.044) is borderline, and its Task-2 concept cluster rests on joint tests only. Near-identical failure counts across forward splits mean the counts do not discriminate between forward splits. The per-Congress pattern does.

A-c41-o1
Interpretation

The heatmap of t (candidate vs train, in prediction-interval-scaled units) shows the per-Congress pattern. Task-2 rows (A1, A2 House, A1b) are most extreme in 116-117 and much milder in 118 (e.g. A1b +2.7 / +2.4 / +0.7; A2 House -2.4 / -3.6 / -1.6). The Task-1 density rows are extreme only in 118 (-5.2, -4.9; 116 at +0.6). Original share is high in 117-118 (+3.8, +4.0). Covariate rows (PSI, JSD, domain AUROC) are mostly near zero, as are A3b and A6. A1c and A5 are moderately negative across candidates without individual failures.

Caveats.

For one-sided distance checks such as PSI, a large negative t (e.g. A7 ch 117 at -4.5) means less drift than train, not a failure. The colour scale treats both directions symmetrically.

Open questions

  • Is the 116-118 drop in Task-2 discriminability (forward AUROC 0.664-0.674 vs 0.712-0.781) a property of the bills (e.g. more low-probability bills inflating volume), of the majority effect weakening in 116-117, or of the simple feature set? Section A cannot tell whether a graph model using cosponsor-network signals would recover it.

  • Will 119 resemble 116-117 (Task-2 label/rate break) or 118 (Task-1 density break and Task-2 reversion)? Its outcomes are still censored. 116-117 overlap COVID-era procedural changes, and 118 is a single Congress, so neither pattern can yet be called lasting.

  • Several passes (A1, A1c, A5, A12 slope, A7 n_original, A18 same_caucus) show same-direction deviations across candidates with nominal joint p < 0.05 that do not survive Holm. With 6-8 reference Congresses and autocorrelated candidates, these may be real but small shifts or chance.

  • Is the sharp 112 to 113 boundary in policy-area mix a coding or harmonisation artifact? If so, the reference spreads for A7/A9/A11 are inflated and the covariate-stability passes are more lenient than they appear.

B. Graph and node conditions

On the graph side, every by-Congress split whose training window ends right before the evaluated Congress (S1a, S1b, S2, S3) shows no detectable drift beyond train-to-train noise (a low-power test), while S1pool's test design (train 108-116, test 118) is the one split-level failure: under the base protocol it fails sponsor overlap and has about 1.7x the cold start, and even under the streaming protocol it keeps stale cross-Congress history (58% new sponsor-cosponsor pairs vs about 39%) because it skips 117 without a refit. The larger dangers are graph-construction leaks (future edges, label-bearing committee edges, a bill's own target edges in training), which must be fixed under any split.

This section asks whether a graph model sees the same kind of graph in train and test. In particular: are the test nodes known, are degree structure and homophily (the tendency to cosponsor within one's own party) stable, are the committee and subject vocabularies stable, and does any edge carry information from after the prediction time t0? The answer separates cleanly into split conditions, which can favour one split over another, and construction requirements, which every split must meet.

Split conditions. Cold start is an election-driven level, not a drift. For units evaluating 116-118 with a window that ends right before the evaluated Congress, 12.7%-18.4% of test positives come from legislators unseen in train; across all evaluated Congresses 109-118 the share ranges from about 8% to 20%. Allowing the evaluated Congress's own history up to intro + t0 (the +stream protocol) cuts this to at most 0.7% with no edge and at most 1.5% with fewer than 5 edges. For the distribution checks (bill degree, scale-normalised legislator degree, density, mean degree, homophily), no split shows a detectable excess of failures over chance. That is weaker evidence than it sounds: the binomial excess test has little power (S1a/S1b need 2 failures of 4 in B3 and 3 of 12 in B8 to reject), the per-split counts pool older folds, and folds evaluating 111-115 are tested against a noise reference (108-115) that contains those same Congresses. The units that matter, those evaluating 116-118, show real near-misses: - P10 (S1a val, 116) fails scale-free legislator degree (leg_rel 0.135 > 0.127), and P11 is just below it (0.123). - P12 (S1a test / S1b val, 117) fails House same-party share (t = +2.4). - The House drop in cosponsors per bill in 118 hits S1b's test unit (P14: density / mean degree t = -2.2 / -2.3) almost as hard as S1pool's (P15: -2.3 / -2.4*). The S1pool B8 'failure' is therefore not meaningfully different from S1b. A sliding pool centred on recent Congresses shows smaller shifts (P16: -1.6 / -1.7).

Only two movements were checked against a trend: House cosponsors per bill in 118 (trend_z -1.0) and House homophily in 117 (trend_z +1.3) are classed as consistent with a linear trend over 108-115, which, with 8 points, means "not a detectable break" rather than an established trend. Legislator degree was not trend-tested: it shows a step increase at 116 (mean 301 in 115 to 396 in 116, PSI vs previous Congress 0.217) that mostly disappears after per-Congress normalisation (leg_rel 0.010-0.031 for 117-118). Committee codes and the post-111 subject vocabulary leave virtually no unseen nodes (<= 0.2% of referral edges, <= 0.04% of subject links). The one split-level FAIL is S1pool's test design (evaluate 118 from 108-116): 21.7% of bills have a sponsor with no train history (bound 14.4%). Under the base protocol it also has 31.5% cold positives (vs 18.1%-18.4% for adjacent 118 windows). Under streaming those node and sponsor penalties mostly vanish, but 58.3% of positives are new sponsor-cosponsor pairs (vs 38.8%-39.4%), because train-period history is one Congress stale.

Construction requirements (apply to every split, including random): only about 48% of a Congress's final cosponsor graph exists at intro + t0, so the graph must be time-masked for both evaluation and training examples. Training with a bill's own target edges in the graph costs a simple ranker 1.8 points of Recall@20 (95% CI -3.1 to -0.3). The absence of any non-referral committee edge fully determines the Task-2 negative class (0 of 92,423 advanced). 42.7% of related-bill links point to later-introduced bills. Subjects are essentially absent at t0 (about 1% of young bills), and policy area is present for only 14.3% of bills aged 0-7 days (n = 56).

What is inferred, not shown. The noise bands come from 7-8 overlapping Congresses, so the tests have modest power and only approximate independence. Degree statistics use final snapshots. The at-t0 coverage figures are proxies from the in-progress 119th Congress. The cost of inconsistent training is measured with a 3-feature linear ranker, not a GNN.

Implications for the split

  • Use a by-Congress split whose training window ends immediately before the evaluated Congress, and refit on train + val before testing (S1a/S1b, or rolling S3/S2 folds). Avoid S1pool's test design (test 118 from 108-116). Under the base protocol it fails sponsor overlap (21.7% vs bound 14.4%) and has about 1.7x the cold start of adjacent 118 windows (31.5% vs 18.1%-18.4%). Under the streaming protocol those node and sponsor penalties mostly vanish (cold_lt5 1.4%, sponsor cold 0.0%), but its cross-Congress history is one Congress stale: 58.3% new sponsor-cosponsor pairs vs 38.8%-39.4% (about 1.5x), because 117 is skipped without a refit.

  • Adopt the streaming protocol: let the model use evaluated-Congress edges dated <= intro + t0. This removes over 90% of legislator cold start (no-edge share at most 0.7%, fewer than 5 edges at most 1.5%), and in-Congress history is worth about 3.9 Recall@20 points to a simple ranker.

  • Make the GNN inductive, or at least not ID-dependent: give legislator nodes features (party, chamber, tenure, in-Congress degree and pair counts as of t0) so the 12.7%-18.4% of 116-118 positives from legislators unseen in train are not scored by untrained embeddings. Reset or make chamber-specific the state of chamber switchers (<= 1% of positives, low priority).

  • Build every training and evaluation example from an as-of-(intro + t0) snapshot, with the target bill's own future cosponsor edges excluded from message passing. Final-graph training measurably hurts (-1.8 R@20 points pooled, 95% CI -3.1 to -0.3).

  • Graph schema: keep only referral committee edges dated <= t0 (lacking any other committee edge means 0 of 92,423 bills advanced), and keep related-bill links only to bills introduced <= intro + t0 (or drop the relation). Exclude legislative subjects as t0 features (about 1% available at t0; B5b requirement). Treat policy area more cautiously: it is present for 14.3% of bills aged 0-7 days (n = 56), so drop it unless its assignment can be timestamped at or before t0, in which case use it with a missing indicator.

  • Normalise degree-type features per Congress, or use mean aggregation. Legislator degree stepped up at 116 (mean 301 in 115, 372-396 in 116-118; scale-free PSI still fails for P10, 0.135 > 0.127) and House cosponsors per bill fell to 12.88 in 118 (S1b's test unit P14 at t = -2.3), so raw-count scales differ between train and test even for the recommended splits.

  • The graph evidence does not separate sliding (S2) from expanding (S3) windows, and small differences point both ways: S2 has 2/16 raw B3 failures vs 0/16 for S3 and a B9 max gap (0.144) closer to the 0.168 bound, but it shows smaller 118 House shifts in B8 (P16 -1.6/-1.7 vs P14 -2.2/-2.3) and no extra sponsor loss (13.3% vs 13.2%). Drift (rising homophily, the 116 degree step, the pre-113 high zero-cosponsor regime) mildly favours windows that emphasise recent Congresses, i.e. S2 or recency weighting of an expanding window. The final choice should rest on section D's backtest performance.

Detailed results

What this tests (from the notebook)

A GNN does not only see a table of bills: it sees nodes (legislators, bills, committees, subjects, policy areas) and edges (cosponsorship, sponsorship, committee referral, subject tags, related-bill links). A by-Congress split is only trustworthy for a graph model if (1) the nodes the model must score at test time are known, either from training or from history inside the test Congress that is available before the prediction time t0 (otherwise learned node embeddings are useless and the model must be inductive), (2) the graph's degree structure and density look the same across Congresses (message passing aggregates over neighbours, so a shift in degree changes every representation), (3) the relation schema and vocabularies (committee codes, subject terms, policy areas) are stable, so a "committee" or "subject" node means the same thing in train and test, and (4) no edge carries information from after t0 (related-bill links to later bills, committee edges that record the label, cosponsor edges dated after t0).

Evaluation pools. Every pool here comes from the shared SPLIT_DEFS / iter_eval_units() (the same units section D backtests): S1a (train 108-115, val 116, test 117), S1b (train 108-116, val 117, test 118), S2 (sliding, k = SLIDE_K) and S3 (rolling, expanding) folds, plus the S1pool variant (val 116, test 117 + 118). Many units share the same (train Congresses, evaluated Congress) pair, so metrics are computed once per distinct pool (ids P01, P02, ...; the mapping to units is printed once below, later tables are keyed by pool id). Tables show the pools that evaluate 116-118; the per-split lines summarise all folds. The +stream variants (eval-Congress events dated <= intro + t0 allowed) and S4 (within-Congress: prior Congresses + events before the cut date) are evaluated where the protocol changes the answer (cold start, sponsor history). S5 (random) ignores time and is not evaluated. Congress 108 is the first in the data, so "never seen before" is left-censored there.

Noise rule (no pool-size bias). "Differs from train" verdicts use ONE fixed reference: the leave-one-out spread of the S1a train Congresses 108-115 (REL_REF, shared rel_to_train), whatever pool is evaluated. A short S2 pool is not judged against its own 3 Congresses (the max of 3 values is exceeded by chance about 1/(3+1) = 25% of the time). Because a split has many evaluation units, a split is judged on the excess of failures over the number expected by chance (binomial test: observed failures vs alpha x tests), not on "any unit fails".

Sets the scale of the graph checks: 6,083 member-Congress rows (1,369 distinct legislators), 1,920,006 active cosponsorships, and 294,865 Task-1 positive edges at t0 = 0 (232,856 at t0 = 7; fewer because cosponsors who joined in the first week are already known at t0 = 7 and do not count as targets). The 35 evaluation units of S1a, S1b, S2, S3 and S1pool reduce to 16 distinct (train Congresses, evaluated Congress) pools, P01-P16. Several splits reuse the same pool (for example P12, train 108-116 evaluated on 117, is S1a test, S1b val, an S3 fold and S1pool test), so per-split verdicts below are not independent pieces of evidence.

Caveats.

Because pools overlap, a single unusual Congress (for example 118) can drive the verdict for several splits at once.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B1. Legislator node overlap with train (transductive view)

Why it matters. Task 1 ranks legislators for a bill. A transductive model (a learned embedding per legislator, e.g. an embedding table or a GNN with ID features) can only score legislators it saw in training. A brand-new member falls back to an untrained vector. This is a model and protocol requirement, not a split-ranking criterion: every election replaces a sizeable share of members (first table), so every by-Congress split has a similar cold-start share (see the per-split line). Whether it hurts depends on whether the model may use history inside the evaluated Congress, which B1b measures. How to read it. The first table is per Congress against all earlier Congresses. The second table evaluates the candidate pools. "New to chamber" counts legislators who served before, but only in the other chamber.

Interpretation

Every election brings in new legislators: 9.5%-19.6% of members in 109-118 had never served in any earlier Congress in the data, with peaks in 112 (19.6%, after the 2010 election) and 116 (18.2%, after 2018). For the candidate pools that evaluate 116-118, legislators unseen in train account for 12.7%-18.4% of Task-1 positive edges when the train window ends right before the evaluated Congress (P10-P14, P16). The exception is P15 (train 108-116, evaluated on 118, used only by S1pool), at 31.5%, because 117 is skipped and two elections' worth of newcomers pile up. Across all units, the per-split maxima are S1a 18.0%, S1b 18.1%, S2 20.5%, S3 20.4% (the last two from folds evaluating 112). Moving between chambers is rare (0.5%-1.4% of members).

Caveats.

Recorded as INFO, not a split criterion: a learned per-legislator embedding (an ID embedding) cannot score about one in six test positives under any by-Congress split, so the cure is the protocol and the model (B1b/B1c), not the choice of split. 109 is understated because 108 is the first Congress in the data (left-censoring).

B-c45-o1
Interpretation

The four series track each other closely. The shares of new members, of new active cosponsors and of positive edges involving a new legislator all rise and fall with elections (lowest in 109, 8.3% of positive edges; highest in 112, 20.4%; again about 18% in 116 and 118). So newcomers cosponsor at roughly the same rate as everyone else from their first Congress on. The new-to-chamber line stays near 1% throughout. Nothing here trends upward: cold start is a recurring, election-driven level of about 8%-20% of positives across 109-118, not a drift that gets worse in the test Congresses.

Caveats.

Shares are computed from the final snapshot of each Congress. At prediction time a newcomer has even less history (see B1b).

B-c45-o2
Interpretation

Member overlap decays steadily with distance between Congresses. Among members of Congress c, 79%-90% also served in c-1 (116: 81.3%, 117: 85.1%, 118: 83.4%), 65%-79% in c-2 (118 seen in 116: 70.2%), and 55%-66% in c-3. Only 15.3% of the 118th Congress also served in the 108th. A train window that skips a Congress therefore loses about 13 points of node coverage for 118 (83.4% to 70.2%), which is the mechanism behind the P15/S1pool results in B1, B2 and B9. A window far in the past covers mostly retired legislators.

Caveats.

Overlap is membership in the window, not activity. A legislator can be a member of a train Congress and still have few edges there.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B1b / B1c. Within-Congress warm-up before t0 (streaming view of cold start) and neighbourhood depth

Why it matters. In the realistic streaming setup the model may use every edge of the evaluated Congress dated on or before the prediction time (bill introduction + t0): earlier cosponsorships and sponsorships by the same legislator. A new member who already cosponsored other bills before t0 is no longer an empty node. But one or two edges are not a neighbourhood: message passing over a node with 1-2 neighbours gives a representation dominated by those few bills. B1b counts a positive as warm after >= 1 in-Congress edge; B1c asks for >= 5 (the low end of typical GraphSAGE-style neighbour-sampling fan-outs) and also shows >= 10. The verdicts are per protocol: base splits forbid eval-Congress history (their cold share is B1's train-cold share), +stream variants allow it up to intro + t0, S4 allows events of the Congress dated before its cut date. How to read it. One row per (pool, t0). cold_train = positives whose cosponsor has no edge in the train Congresses; cold_lt1/5/10 = of all positives, cold in train AND fewer than 1 / 5 / 10 in-Congress edges by intro + t0 (cold_lt1 is B1b's streaming-cold share); new_ge1/5/10 = of the train-cold positives, share with >= 1 / 5 / 10 in-Congress edges by t0; all_ge5 = of ALL positives, share whose cosponsor has >= 5 in-Congress edges by t0; spon_cold = evaluated bills whose sponsor has no train edge and no other in-Congress edge by t0.
