Interpretation

Once the model may use edges of the evaluated Congress dated on or before intro + t0 (the +stream protocol), cold start nearly disappears. Positives whose cosponsor has no edge at all fall from 12.7%-31.5% (no train edge) to 0.2%-0.7% (cold_lt1). Positives whose cosponsor has fewer than 5 edges fall to 0.6%-1.5% (cold_lt5). Of the positives involving a train-cold cosponsor, 92%-95.5% have a cosponsor with at least 5 in-Congress edges by t0 = 0 (91.2% at minimum in S4 units), and at least 95% do by t0 = 7. Both checks pass every unit: B1b, worst unit 0.71% < 2%; B1c, worst unit 1.45% < 2%. Sponsors are almost never fully cold (spon_cold at most 0.1%). S4 (within-Congress cut) behaves the same, with max cold_lt5 0.66%.

Caveats.

new_ge5 is a share of positives (edges), not of legislators. Positives are weighted toward active newcomers, so the share of cold legislators with a usable neighbourhood is likely lower. Most positives also come from bills introduced well into a Congress, when newcomers have already been active; bills from the first weeks of a Congress will be much colder than these averages, and the analysis does not split results by bill date. The >= 5-edge bar is a heuristic tied to typical neighbour-sampling fan-outs, not a measured threshold for embedding quality.

B-c47-o1
Interpretation

For each pool evaluating 116-118, the chart shows three levels of history. With no history from the evaluated Congress (base split), 13%-31% of positives are cold. With the evaluated Congress's history up to t0, under 1.5% have fewer than 5 edges and under 0.75% have none. The gap between the bars is the case for the streaming protocol: in-Congress history up to t0 removes over 90% of the cold-start problem, whatever the train window. P15's extra cold start (31.5%) vanishes under streaming (1.4% below 5 edges, the same as P10's 1.4%), and its spon_cold is 0.0%. So under streaming, what remains of the S1pool penalty is staleness of train-period history, mainly sponsor-cosponsor pair history (B9: 58.3% new pairs vs 38.8%-39.4% for adjacent 118 windows).

What this tests (from the notebook)

B2. Sponsor overlap

Why it matters. The sponsor is the strongest single signal for who cosponsors (sponsor-cosponsor ties repeat across bills). Bills whose sponsor is new to the train period have no sponsor history, so the model sees a cold-start bill neighbourhood. New sponsors are mostly freshmen, who sponsor fewer bills, so the bill-level share is usually smaller than the member-level share. Unlike B1, this depends on the train window: a short sliding window (S2) forgets sponsors who were absent in its few Congresses. How to read it. Share of law-capable bills (and of Task-1 positives) in the evaluated Congress whose sponsor was not a member during the train Congresses, and the stricter version, "never sponsored a law-capable bill in the train Congresses" (fail = above the noise bound). The bound is not a fixed band: it is the 95% upper t prediction interval of the one-step-ahead share (train 108..c-1, evaluate c) over the reference Congresses 109-115, i.e. how many new sponsors an ordinary election brings. As elsewhere, only units evaluating 116-118 decide a split. The streaming version is in B1b.

[FAIL] B2: Few val/test bills have a sponsor with no sponsorship history in train, relative to train-to-train noise | metric=0.2172 (threshold <= 0.144 (outside 95% t prediction interval of ref 109-115 (upper tail; n=7); one-step-ahead share)) [fails for: S1pool]
Interpretation

In 116-118, when train ends right before the evaluated Congress, 9.1%-13.3% of law-capable bills (11.5%-14.8% of positive edges) have a sponsor who never sponsored a law-capable bill in the train Congresses (8.8%-13.2% have a sponsor who was not even a member in train). These shares sit inside the band an ordinary election produces (one-step-ahead shares 5.1%-12.6% over 109-115, 95% upper prediction bound 14.4%). The only failure is P15 (S1pool's 118 test with 117 skipped): 21.7% of bills and 25.0% of positives have a history-less sponsor, well above the bound. S2 (3-Congress window) is barely worse than S3 (13.3% vs 13.2%), so a short window does not measurably forget sponsors.

Caveats.

The bound comes from 7 reference Congresses (a t prediction interval with 6 degrees of freedom). It is coarse, but P15's 21.7% exceeds it by a wide margin, so the verdict is robust for the base protocol. Under the streaming protocol sponsors are essentially never fully cold (B1b spon_cold <= 0.1%, 0.0% for P15), so this FAIL matters mainly for models that lean on sponsor history from the train Congresses, not on in-Congress history.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B3. Degree distribution stationarity

Why it matters. GNN layers aggregate over neighbours. If bills get many more cosponsors, or a few legislators dominate cosponsoring in later Congresses, the scale of aggregated messages and the base rate of positives per bill both move. A model trained on old degree regimes is then miscalibrated at test time. How to read it. First table: per Congress, per-bill cosponsor counts (law-capable bills) and per-legislator cosponsorship counts, KS / PSI against the previous Congress (KS p-values are tiny at this sample size, so read the statistic), Gini and top-10% share (tail concentration). Second table: PSI of each pool's evaluated Congress against that pool's train Congresses. The noise reference is fixed for every pool: the one-vs-rest PSI of each Congress in 108-115 against the other seven, with a 95% upper t prediction interval on the log scale (rel_to_train). * marks a PSI above that bound. The split table compares observed failures with the number expected by chance (5% per test). Degrees count all active cosponsorships (final snapshot), a proxy for what is seen at prediction time.

[PASS] B3: Val/test bill and legislator degree distributions are no further from the train pool than train Congresses are from each other | metric=2 (threshold per split: failures (PSI > fixed 108-115 95% upper t-PI) not in excess of chance (binomial p >= 0.05))
Interpretation

Bill degree (cosponsors per bill) is stable. The mean is 10.2-13.9 in every Congress, and PSI (population stability index, a binned measure of distribution shift) against train pools is 0.003-0.066, far below the fixed 0.191 noise bound. Legislator degree shows an untested step: mean cosponsorships per legislator were 240-357 in 108-115 and 372-396 in 116-118, with the jump at 116 (301 to 396, PSI vs 115 = 0.217). One pool exceeds the raw bound (P11, 113-115 to 116: 0.423 > 0.390), and P10 is at 0.353. After dividing degree by the Congress mean (leg_rel), P10 (S1a val, 116) still fails (0.135 > 0.127) and P11 is just below it (0.123), while 117-118 are tiny (0.010-0.031). Per split, no excess of failures is detectable (raw: S2 2 of 16, p = 0.19, all others 0; scale-free: 0-1 per split, all p >= 0.185).

Caveats.

The per-split verdict is weak evidence. The binomial test has little power: with 4 tests (S1a, S1b) it needs 2 failures to reject, so a single failing unit, like P10's, cannot flag a split. The per-split lines pool all folds, so older folds dilute 116-118. Folds evaluating 111-115 are compared against a noise reference (108-115) that includes those Congresses, which widens the reference and biases toward PASS. Degrees use final snapshots (a proxy for as-of-t0 graphs). A pass means "not detectably different", not "identical"; the 116 step is real and argues for per-Congress normalised degree features.

B-c51-o1
Interpretation

Concentration measures move slowly. Bill-degree Gini (inequality of cosponsor counts across bills) drifts down from about 0.80 (109, 112) to 0.74 (118). The share of bills with no cosponsor falls from 28%-38% in 108-112 to 19%-20% in 115-118, and the drop is concentrated around 113. Legislator Gini rises in 115-116 (0.31-0.33, up from 0.24-0.25 in 112-114), and the top-10% share stays between 0.20 and 0.23. The recent Congresses (115-118) look alike, while 108-112 look different. So a long expanding window mixes in an older regime with more zero-cosponsor bills.

Caveats.

These are descriptive trends with no test attached. The zero-cosponsor share matters for Task 1, because bills with no positives contribute nothing to Recall@K and should be handled consistently in train and test.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B4. Committee schema stability

Why it matters. Bill-committee referral edges are a natural relation for both tasks (the committee is the gatekeeper for advancement). Committees are renamed, merged, and subcommittees are reshuffled across Congresses. A committee node that exists only in test has no learned embedding, and a renamed committee splits one concept into two nodes. How to read it. Per Congress: share of committee codes and of referral edges (activity "Referred to") whose code never appeared in an earlier Congress, split into full committees vs subcommittees. Codes in this data appear to be normalised to current codes (e.g. 108 rows use today's subcommittee names). That helps stability but means historical renames are hidden, not absent.

Interpretation

No referral edge to a full committee ever points to a code unseen in earlier Congresses (new_edges_full = 0.000 in all of 109-118). Unseen subcommittee referrals are 0%-3.8% after 109 and at most 0.9% in 116-118. Per pool, unseen referral edges are 0.05%-0.19%, and the check passes every by-Congress unit (worst 1.28% < 5%). The Jaccard overlap of committee code sets is lower for expanding pools (0.50-0.62) than for sliding pools (0.72-0.91), because old pools carry codes that no longer receive referrals. This dilutes the vocabulary but does not cause unseen nodes.

Caveats.

As the notebook notes, codes appear to be normalised to current names, so renames are hidden rather than absent. A committee whose jurisdiction changed under the same code would pass this check but still shift in meaning. The subcommittee share of referrals also falls in 118 (19.1% vs 22%-34% earlier), which may reflect data latency for the latest Congress.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B5. Subject and policy-area vocabulary stability and coverage

Why it matters. Legislative subjects (CRS index terms) and policy areas are candidate bill features or bill-subject edges. Two failure modes break a temporal split: (a) the vocabulary changes (a thesaurus revision makes old and new subject nodes disjoint), and (b) coverage lag: CRS assigns subjects after introduction, sometimes much later, so recent Congresses have fewer tagged bills. Coverage lag means test bills look different from train bills purely because of data latency. It is also a leakage risk (tags are not timestamped, so they may encode later events). How to read it. Per Congress: vocabulary size, share of subject terms / bill-subject links not seen in any earlier Congress, Jaccard vs previous Congress, and share of law-capable bills with at least one subject and with a policy area (final snapshot). The last line estimates policy-area availability at t0 from the youngest bills of the in-progress Congress 119. Because subjects are essentially absent at t0, B5b is recorded as a feature-exclusion requirement (every split), not as a split condition.

[PASS] B5a: Val/test bill-subject links use subject terms seen in train (every by-Congress unit) | metric=0.0161 (threshold < 0.05)
[INFO/REQ] B5b: Requirement: do not use legislative subjects as node / edge features at t0 (not available at prediction time; coverage lags in 117-118) | metric=0.0096 (threshold info: feature-exclusion requirement (all splits))
Interpretation

Two different problems show up. (a) Vocabulary break: the subject thesaurus changed at 111 (vocabulary 4,247 to 957 terms, Jaccard with 110 = 0.194). After 111 the vocabulary is stable (Jaccard 0.89-0.95, new links <= 0.7%), so unseen subject links in 116-118 pools are 0.00%-0.04% and B5a passes. (b) Coverage lag: the share of law-capable bills with at least one subject falls from 96%-98% (114-116) to 61.8% in 117 and 37.2% in 118, even in the final snapshot. At prediction time it is about 1.0% (bills aged 0-30 days in the 119th, n = 732). So subjects are a post-introduction feature, and B5b records excluding them at t0 as a requirement for every split. Policy area is a separate, weaker case: near-complete in the final snapshot (99%+), but present for only 14.3% of bills aged 0-7 days (n = 56).

Caveats.

Whether subject tags also correlate with the label (for example, being tagged faster when a bill moves) is a hypothesis this section does not test; the case for exclusion rests on availability alone. The at-t0 figures come from the in-progress 119th Congress, not from timestamps on historical tags, and assuming CRS (Congressional Research Service) tagging latency was similar in earlier Congresses is an untested inference. The policy-area estimate rests on 56 bills, so excluding policy area is a softer recommendation than excluding subjects; an alternative is to use policy area with a missing indicator, but only if its assignment date can be shown to be at or before t0. Expanding pools show low Jaccard (0.20-0.22) only because they include the pre-111 thesaurus.

B-c55-o1
Interpretation

The chart shows the 111 thesaurus break as a single dip in Jaccard (to 0.19), with continuity of about 0.9 elsewhere. It also shows subject coverage collapsing from 98% (116) to 62% (117), 37% (118) and 24% (119), while policy-area coverage stays flat at about 99%. The coverage collapse coincides exactly with the test Congresses. A model given subject features would see fully tagged training bills and mostly untagged test bills, a pipeline artefact that would make every temporal split look worse and every random split look better.

Caveats.

Final-snapshot policy-area coverage says nothing about availability at t0. See the 14.3% at-t0 proxy in the text output.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B6. Cross-split edges: related-bill links and within-Congress future links

Why it matters. bill_related connects bills. In a temporal split, an edge from a train bill to a bill in a later Congress (or a later-introduced bill in the same Congress) lets the model see the future when building train representations. Edges that cross the val/test boundary leak test structure into training. Links to earlier Congresses are legitimate context. How to read it. For each source Congress: number of links to earlier / same / later Congresses. Second table: among same-Congress links, the share pointing to a bill introduced after the source bill (these must be dropped or time-filtered when building a snapshot at t0). Caveat: the source stores almost only same-Congress links, so the cross-Congress count says little about cross-Congress leakage.

Interpretation

Related-bill links are stored almost only within a Congress. Across 108-117 there are zero links to earlier or later Congresses, and in 118 only 36 earlier and 20 later, so cross-split leakage through this relation is negligible (B6a, 0.014%). Within a Congress, however, 39%-44% of related links point to a bill introduced after the source bill (42.7% overall, B6b FAIL). 30%-38% point more than 7 days ahead and 21%-32% more than 30 days ahead. In a snapshot at intro + t0, these links connect a bill to bills that do not yet exist.

Caveats.

Links carry no creation timestamp. Even links whose target was introduced before t0 may have been added later, for example when CRS records identical bills, so filtering by target introduction date is necessary but may not be sufficient. The "no cross-Congress links" result reflects how the source stores the data, not proof that no such relation exists.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B7. Committee edges that encode the advancement label

Why it matters. bill_committees mixes the referral edge (known on day 0-7) with later activity edges such as "Reported by", "Markup by", "Discharged from", "Hearings by". "Reported by" is the Task 2 label, and markup / hearings are strong post-introduction signals. If the graph builder keeps all rows as bill-committee edges, every split (temporal or random) leaks the label. How to read it. Activity mix per Congress, the share of referral edges that occur more than 7 days after introduction (late referrals are not in a t0=7 snapshot), and how strongly having a non-referral edge predicts the advancement label.

[INFO/REQ] B7: Graph builder must keep only referral committee edges known by t0 (label leakage) | metric=1 (threshold info: must filter)
Interpretation

Committee rows mix the referral (78%-86% of rows) with post-introduction activity: markup, hearing or discharge (10%-14%) and "reported" (3.8%-7.5%). Not having any non-referral committee edge fully determines the negative class: 0 of 92,423 such bills advanced. Having one raises the rate to 33.5% (n = 18,379), since such an edge is a necessary condition for advancement. A graph that keeps these edges hands Task 2 a near-label under any split, temporal or random. Also, 12.6%-27.1% of referral edges occur after day 7, a share that falls over time (27% in 108, about 13% in 116-118). So the t0 = 7 snapshot keeps slightly more of the referral information in recent Congresses than in old ones.

Caveats.

The 0.000 rate is partly by definition, since "reported" is one of the non-referral activities, but markup and hearings are also strong post-t0 signals. The falling share of late referrals is a small structural drift between old train Congresses and test Congresses that time-masking reproduces faithfully but does not remove.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B8. Network structure stability per Congress

Why it matters. Structural summaries of the bill-legislator cosponsor graph (density, mean degree) and of homophily (share of cosponsorships within the sponsor's party) describe what a GNN learns to exploit. Rising polarisation changes how much "same party as sponsor" explains, so a model trained in a bipartisan era over-predicts cross-party cosponsors in a polarised one. How to read it. Per Congress and chamber: density = edges / (bills x members), mean cosponsors per bill, same-party share (cosponsor party == sponsor party, D/R only). Pool test: the evaluated value is compared with the mean of that pool's train Congresses, scaled by ONE fixed noise SD (the spread of the same metric over 108-115): t = (value - pool mean) / (SD_ref x sqrt(1 + 1/k)), fail if |t| exceeds the 95% t quantile (df = 7). The pool sets the centre (a recent sliding pool is centred near the present), the fixed reference sets the width, so S2 is not penalised for having 3 Congresses. Last table: for 116-118, the fixed-reference verdict and the trend residual (trend_z), which separates a steady trend (large t, small trend_z) from a break (large trend_z).

Interpretation

Per chamber, density (edges / (bills x members)), mean cosponsors per bill and same-party share of cosponsorships mostly stay within train-to-train noise. Of the pool-centred t statistics for pools evaluating 116-118, 2 exceed |t| = 2.36: P12 (S1a test / S1b val, 117) has House same-party share at t = +2.4, and P15 (S1pool, 118 with 117 skipped) has House mean cosponsors at t = -2.4. Several others are near-misses: P14 (S1b test, 118) has House density / mean degree at t = -2.2 / -2.3, barely different from P15's -2.3 / -2.4, so the 118 House drop affects S1b's test as much as S1pool's, and P15's 'failure' is not evidence against S1pool relative to S1b. The sliding pool for 118 (P16) shows smaller shifts (-1.6 / -1.7). No split shows an excess of failures (S1a 1/12, S1b 1/12, S2 0/48, S3 1/48, S1pool 2/18; all p >= 0.23). Against the fixed 108-115 reference, the trend check classes House cosponsors per bill in 118 (12.88, t = -2.4, trend_z = -1.0) and House homophily in 117 (0.849, t = +2.6, trend_z = +1.3) as consistent with a linear trend rather than breaks.

Caveats.

The binomial test needs 3 failures of 12 to reject for S1a/S1b, so it can barely flag a split; S2 and S3 counts are diluted by folds evaluating 111-115, which are partly in-sample for the 108-115 reference. The reference SD comes from 8 Congresses that share members, so the 2.36 cut-off is approximate. The six metrics per pool are positively correlated (density and mean degree within a chamber are nearly redundant). Correlated tests overdisperse the failure count, so the binomial p-values for excess are too small (anti-conservative): a PASS is not weakened by this, but correlated failures effectively count about once, not twice, which lowers power further. The trend_z check fits a line to 8 points, so 'on trend' means 'no detectable break', not an established trend.

B-c61-o1
Interpretation

Party homophily rises over the period: the House goes from 72% same-party cosponsorships (108-109) to 80%-85% (116-118), and the Senate from 63%-65% to 74%-77%. The rise is mostly a step around 110-112 plus a further step in the House at 116-117, not a continuous ramp. A model trained mostly on 108-110 would over-predict cross-party cosponsors in 116-118, which favours windows that include recent Congresses or a party-match feature whose weight can be refit on the latest data.

Caveats.

The shares are restricted to D/R sponsor-cosponsor pairs, with independents assigned by data-derived caucus. Homophily also depends on which bills get cosponsors (composition), not only on legislator behaviour.

B-c61-o2
Interpretation

Senate density is higher than House density (about 0.05 vs 0.03-0.04) and broadly flat. House density declines in the last two Congresses (0.0367 in 116, 0.0329 in 117, 0.0286 in 118, the lowest of the period). For a GNN this means fewer neighbours per House bill in the test Congress than in train. Normalised degree features or degree-robust aggregation (mean rather than sum) protect against the scale change.

Caveats.

Density is computed on final snapshots. 118 is complete, but late-arriving cosponsorships recorded after the snapshot could depress it slightly.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B9. Dyadic (sponsor-cosponsor pair) novelty: val vs its own test

Why it matters. Link-prediction models often succeed by memorising recurring pairs: "X always cosponsors Y's bills". If most test positives are pairs already seen in train, a pair-memorising baseline will look strong; if most are new pairs, the model must generalise. Each split's val unit should have a share similar to its own test unit, or model selection on val may not transfer. Consecutive Congresses differ through elections, so some val-test gap is unavoidable. The gap is therefore judged against the year-to-year swing among train Congresses: |new_pair(c) - new_pair(c-1)| for c in 110-115 with expanding pools (fixed reference, 95% upper t-PI). How to read it. First table: per pool, share of positives whose (cosponsor, sponsor) pair never occurred in the train Congresses, and the share where both legislators were seen (warm nodes, new pair). Second: per split, val-test gaps vs the noise bound and failures vs chance. Per-fold gaps are kept in B_PAIR_GAPS so the decision section can relate them to D's Task-1 val-test gap.

[PASS] B9: Each split's val unit has a new-pair share similar to its own test unit (relative to train year-to-year swing) | metric=0.1439 (threshold per split: gaps above the 110-115 swing bound (0.168, 95% upper t-PI) not in excess of chance)
Interpretation

For windows ending right before the evaluated Congress, 33%-42% of Task-1 positives in 116-118 are a (cosponsor, sponsor) pair never seen in the train Congresses. Only 11%-13% are new pairs between two legislators who were both seen; the rest involve a cold node. So pair memorisation can explain at most 58%-67% of positives depending on the Congress (57.7% for P11, 67.0% for P12), and real generalisation is needed. Skipping 117 (P15) raises the new-pair share to 58.3%, against 38.8%-39.4% for the adjacent 118 windows (about 1.5x). The check itself asks whether each split's validation Congress resembles its own test Congress. The val-test gaps (S1a 0.083, S1b 0.057, S2 max 0.144, S3 max 0.135, S1pool 0.028) all fall below the 0.168 year-to-year swing bound, so B9 passes for every split.

Caveats.

The bound's nested leave-one-out check gave 1 false alarm in 6, so it is not loose. S2's worst gap (0.144) is close to it. S1pool's small gap (0.028) compares val 116 with pooled test 117+118 and hides that its 118 part has a much higher new-pair share.

B-c63-o1
Interpretation

The new-pair share swings between 30% and 44% from Congress to Congress (for example 29.7% in 111, 43.2% in 112, 41.3% in 116, 33.0% in 117), in step with election turnover. Sliding 3-Congress windows give a new-pair share consistently about 1 point higher than expanding windows (for example 44.0% vs 43.2% in 112, 42.3% vs 41.3% in 116), so a short window raises novelty only slightly. Any by-Congress split inherits the election-driven swing, which is a plausible contributor to val-test score gaps even under a well-built split (that link is tested in section D).

What this tests (from the notebook)

B10. As-of-t0 graph completeness

Why it matters. A full-graph GNN trained and evaluated on the final snapshot of a Congress sees every cosponsor edge of that Congress, including the evaluated bill's own future cosponsors (the Task 1 labels) and the later activity of its neighbours. At prediction time (introduction + t0), only part of that graph exists. This is the graph-level version of the leakage in B6b / B7: it applies to every split, so it is a construction requirement (snapshot or temporal-edge masking), not a split preference. Its size also shows how different the as-of-t0 graph is from the final one. How to read it. For each eval bill (law-capable, uncensored): visible = share of its Congress's final cosponsor edges dated <= introduction + t0. nbr_deg_after = share of the final degree of the bill's legislator neighbours known at t0 (sponsor + cosponsors by t0) that accrues after t0. hop1_vis = (sponsor + cosponsors by t0) / (sponsor + all cosponsors): share of the bill's final 1-hop neighbourhood that exists at t0; hop2_vis = edges of the as-of 1-hop legislators dated <= t0 / final edges of the final 1-hop legislators (2-hop edge mass). Means over bills. The train Congresses (108-115) matter as much as the eval ones: training examples must be built the same way (B12).

[INFO/REQ] B10: Share of the eval Congress's final cosponsor graph that is NOT available at t0 (full-graph GNN leakage) | metric=0.5197 (threshold info: must time-mask edges)
Interpretation

At prediction time, only about half of a Congress's final cosponsor graph exists. For eval bills in 116-118 at t0 = 0, 52.0% of the Congress's final edges are dated after intro + t0, and about 50%-52% of the final degree of the bill's known legislator neighbours accrues later. Only 70%-75% of a bill's final 1-hop neighbourhood and 33%-40% of its 2-hop edge mass are visible at t0 = 0, rising only slightly at t0 = 7 (hop1 72%-78%, hop2 36%-43%). These shares are nearly the same in train (108-115) and eval Congresses, so masking does not create a train-test shift by itself. Skipping it, though, gives the model a mostly-future graph and, by construction, all of the bill's own Task-1 labels.

Caveats.

The visible share mostly reflects where the bill falls in the Congress's calendar (90th percentile 0.85-0.93), so it is a property of the event stream, not of individual bills. hop1_vis is inflated by bills with no cosponsors, which count as fully visible. Recorded as a requirement for every split, not a split criterion.

B-c65-o1
Interpretation

The lines are flat across 108-118. About 46%-51% of final edges are visible at t0 = 0 (47%-52% at t0 = 7), and 48%-53% of neighbour degree accrues after t0. The temporal structure of the event stream is stationary, which supports a single time-masked snapshot procedure for every Congress. Globally, the two t0 settings see nearly the same graph (about 1 point more visible at t0 = 7). Locally they do not: the bill's own 1-hop visibility rises 3-5 points (for example 0.700 to 0.742 in 116), and Task-1 positives drop by 21% (294,865 to 232,856) because first-week cosponsors become inputs rather than targets. That bill-local difference is what matters for the ranking task.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B12. Train / eval input consistency for a temporal GNN

Why it matters. B10 shows the eval graph must be the as-of-(intro + t0) snapshot. If the model is nevertheless trained on final graphs of the train Congresses (with each training bill's own target edges still in the message-passing graph), its inputs in training are complete and partly label-bearing, while at val/test time they are partial and label-free. The model learns weights for features that look different at test time (a covariate shift created by the pipeline, not by the data), and the val score understates what a consistent pipeline would reach. This affects every split equally, so it is a construction requirement; its size tells how strictly the training pipeline must replay time. How it is measured. A count-feature logistic ranker (log1p of: the candidate's pair count with the sponsor in the 3 previous Congresses, its in-Congress pair count with the sponsor, its in-Congress degree) is trained on sampled bills of the train Congresses of the S2 pools evaluating 116 and 117, with in-Congress features taken (a) from the final graph including the bill's own edges, (b) from the final graph minus the bill's own edges, (c) from the as-of-intro snapshot (t0 = 0). All are evaluated on val bills with snapshot features (the only inputs available at prediction time). R20_* = mean per-bill share of positives in the top 20 of the point-in-time same-chamber pool (sponsor and cosponsors at t0 excluded); d_* = R@20 minus the snapshot-trained model's, with a paired bootstrap 95% CI over val bills. hist_only drops the in-Congress features (reference: what in-Congress history adds at all). Proxy: a 3-feature linear model, not a GNN; a GNN aggregates the same in-Congress structure.

[FAIL/REQ] B12: Training inputs match eval inputs: train examples from as-of-(intro + t0) snapshots, target edges excluded from message passing | metric=-0.0198 (threshold FAIL (= the rule is binding) if training on final-graph features lowers val Recall@20 vs snapshot training (paired 95% CI < 0) in any fold or pooled)
Interpretation

A 3-feature logistic ranker shows what inconsistent training inputs cost. All variants are evaluated on snapshot features. Training on final graphs that include each training bill's own target edges lowers val Recall@20 by 1.6 points (P11 to 116) and 2.0 points (P13 to 117), against 29.9%-31.0% for snapshot training. The pooled loss is 1.8 points (95% CI -3.1 to -0.3), which triggers the FAIL. The learned weights show why: the in-Congress pair count gets weight +1.54 when the target edges are present, and train positives' pair count is 3.92 in the final graph vs 1.24 in snapshots. The model learns a label-bearing feature that is much weaker at test time. Removing only the target edges from the final graph is statistically indistinguishable from snapshot training (pooled +0.7, CI -0.5 to +1.7). Dropping in-Congress features entirely costs 3.9 points (CI -5.0 to -2.8), so in-Congress history is worth keeping when it is built correctly.

Caveats.

This is a linear proxy with 3 count features, 3,000 training bills and 1,000 val bills per fold, on two folds. A GNN can exploit label-bearing edges more flexibly, so the true cost could be larger. P13's per-fold CI touches 0 (upper bound +0.000). The FAIL means the construction rule is binding, not that any split is invalid.

B-c67-o1
Interpretation

Of the three bars per fold, only "final graph incl. own edges" is consistently negative (-0.016 and -0.020). "Final graph, own edges removed" is mixed (+0.015 and -0.001), and "no in-Congress features" is clearly negative (-0.037 and -0.041). In practice, the essential rule is to keep a training bill's own target edges out of message passing. Full snapshot replay is the safest way to guarantee that and costs nothing measurable.

Caveats.

Each bar is a point estimate from one fold. See the text output for the confidence intervals.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B11. Node identity across Congresses: chamber and party switchers

Why it matters. A legislator keeps one node id across Congresses. When a House member moves to the Senate, or a member changes party, that node's training neighbourhood comes from the other chamber (whose bills they can no longer cosponsor in the same way) or from the other party's coalition, while Task 1 ranks only same-chamber legislators and party homophily is strong (B8). A learned embedding (or sponsor-history feature) then describes the wrong role. If such nodes carry a visible share of test positives and are ranked much worse, the model needs chamber-specific node features (or a chamber-switch reset) and the split's test score depends on how many switchers that Congress happens to have. How to read it. Per pool, Task-1 positives (t0 = 0) are classed by their cosponsor's status in their most recent train Congress: cold (never a member in train), chamber_switch (served only in the other chamber then), party_switch (same chamber, different party_code_asof), stable. other_ch_edges = for chamber switchers, share of their train cosponsorships on bills of the other chamber. R@20 = share of positives of each class that a sponsor_hist ranker (train counts of cosponsoring this sponsor, popularity tie-break, point-in-time same-chamber pool incl. delegates, sponsor and t0 cosponsors excluded; section D's baseline, re-implemented per positive) places in the top 20. Computed on the S3 folds and all pools evaluating 116-118. Impact = switcher share x (R@20 stable - R@20 switcher) = the Recall@20 lost overall.

Interpretation

Chamber switchers (served only in the other chamber in their latest train Congress) are 0.3%-1.0% of positives in 116-118, and party switchers are 0%-0.5%. The S3 folds show the same: 0.37%-0.99% per Congress. Switchers are ranked poorly by a sponsor-history baseline (Recall@20 3.3%-7.8%, against 22.5%-26.1% for stable legislators), but they are so few that the overall recall lost is 0.1-0.2 points per pool, below the 0.5-point tolerance, and B11 passes. Caveats.

Cold legislators have Recall@20 of exactly 0 under this baseline by construction, since they have no train counts. That says nothing about a model with in-Congress features. The party-switch recall of 65.2% for eval 111-115 rests on only 69 positives and is not meaningful. The n of 166 for 116-118 is also small.

B-c69-o1
Interpretation

Stable legislators are ranked consistently across periods (sponsor_hist Recall@20 23.1% for eval 111-115 and 23.5% for 116-118), which is reassuring evidence that the baseline's mechanism does not degrade in the test Congresses. Chamber switchers are much worse (8.0% and 5.9%), and cold legislators get 0%. The party-switch bar jumps from 65% to 8%, but both bars rest on small samples (n = 69 and 166). The practical message: a chamber-specific node state, or resetting a switcher's history, would help a sliver of positives, while cold start (14,743 positives in 116-118) is the slice that actually matters.

What this tests (from the notebook)

B summary

All graph and node checks recorded in this section. FAIL does not always mean "do not split by Congress": read the detail column for the remedy (allow within-Congress history up to t0, refit on val, inductive features, filter edges by time, restrict subjects to a stable vocabulary, normalise degree features). Checks tagged with a shared quantity are deduplicated in the decision section. Every split-dependent check carries a by_split verdict (base splits, +stream variants, S1pool and, where meaningful, S4). Distribution checks (B3, B8, B9) judge each split on failures in excess of chance against one fixed 108-115 noise reference, so short sliding pools are not penalised for their size. Every check keys every split in ALL_SPLITS; splits a check does not judge get None with a stated reason (e.g. S5 random, or base splits in B1b / B1c, whose cold share is B1's INFO and is a protocol choice, not a failure of the split). B11 and section D's D25 share the node_identity_switch key, so the decision section sees one row and a conflict flag if they disagree. B5b, B6b, B7, B10 and B12 are recorded as requirements (requirement=True): graph-construction rules every split must follow (no subject features at t0, time-filter related links, referral-only committee edges, time-masked cosponsor graph for eval AND training examples, target edges out of message passing). Each leakage path has its own quantity key, so none is hidden behind another section's check; count split failures from checks_summary(requirements=False).

Interpretation

Section summary. Of the split conditions, 8 pass, 1 fails and 2 are INFO; 5 are construction requirements, and 2 of those need filtering (related links, B6b; training-input consistency, B12). The one split-level failure, B2 (sponsor overlap), fails only for S1pool; the worst values of B1 (31.5%) and B9's new-pair share (58.3%) also come from S1pool's 118 test, for the same reason: it evaluates 118 with a model trained on 108-116. The distribution checks (B3, B8, B9) show no detectable excess of failures for any split under the fixed 108-115 noise reference, though with low power and with unit-level near-misses on 116-118 for S1a and S1b. The requirements (B5b, B6b, B7, B10, B12) apply equally to every split, including the random split S5, so they say how to build the graph, not which split to choose.

Caveats.

"PASS" in a distribution check means no detectable excess over train-to-train noise, judged on 7-8 dependent reference Congresses. It is not a guarantee of equivalence.

Open questions

  • Committee codes appear normalised to current names, so historical renames and jurisdiction changes are hidden. True committee schema drift is unknown.

  • Related-bill links have no creation timestamp, so links between bills both introduced before t0 may still have been created after t0. How much residual leakage remains after date filtering cannot be measured from this data.

  • The cost of inconsistent training inputs was measured with a 3-feature linear ranker on two folds. How much a GNN would exploit label-bearing or future edges, likely more, is untested.

  • Cold-start averages are dominated by bills introduced later in a Congress. The analysis does not show how cold the graph is for bills in the first weeks of a new Congress, when freshmen have little history even under streaming.

C. Temporal structure, regime changes, censoring, leakage

Congress boundaries are adequate cut points (no location-identified break falls inside a Congress; the Senate original share changes significantly beyond trend but cannot be located, which fits a gradual bend), temporal splits leak no future twins, and C24 finds no evidence of missing labels in 118; on this section's evidence S5 leaks future twins, S4 loses most task-2 test bills to censoring and S2 misses chamber majorities, so S1b and S3 remain (S1a and S1pool are weaker on C23b), with Congress 118 reported separately as a shifted test set whose later cosponsor timing is most likely real rather than data latency.

This section asks whether each Congress is a comparable draw of one process, and whether what the model sees at prediction time t0 was really known then. Mostly, yes. The calendar of bill introductions passes both tests (C1, C2). Censoring is small for task 1 (at most 3.9% of bills, C5) and within train-to-train noise for task 2 (C6). Every evaluation Congress's House and Senate majority appears in training for S1a, S1b and S3 (C8). The one significant break whose location is identified, a jump in the House original-cosponsor share, sits at the start of Congress 117 (2021-01, month 1). That is a Congress boundary, so a by-Congress cut does not straddle it. The Senate original share also changes significantly beyond its trend (p < 0.001), but the two fits place the change nine years apart (2008 vs 2017). That fits a gradual bend rather than a step. It is not a cut-point problem, but it is a non-stationarity inside the training window. A House cosponsor-timing break at 2024-01 (month 13 of Congress 118, p = 0.038, not significant after Bonferroni correction) hints that 118's slower late cosponsors may start inside 118 rather than at its boundary. C23 therefore passes, with these two qualifications.

Some drifts pass the tests but sit at the edge of the training range. The share of bills introduced in the last 90 days is 0.058-0.061 in all three evaluation Congresses, above every training value (max 0.056). It passes C2 only because an interval built from n=8 Congresses is wide. Bill volume was never tested: 116-118 have 14.3k-16.6k law-capable bills, 26-45% more than the largest training Congress (11.4k). Volume is a candidate explanation for 118's lower positive density (more bills competing for a fixed pool of legislators).

The main warning is Congress 118. Its non-original cosponsors arrive later: median lag 92 days vs 62-75 in 108-115, and a KS distance of 0.093 vs at most 0.039 among training Congresses (C3 FAIL for every split that tests on 118). Its task-1 positive density at t0=7 is 0.0035, 47% below the 108-115 mean (C4). C24 finds no evidence of missing labels: snapshot counts match the event tables exactly, and the end-of-Congress tails show no deficit. The tail test is weak, though. Late introductions rise in 116-118, which inflates late-event tails and could mask a small deficit. It also cannot see events missing from both the counts and the event tables. And 118 records are still being maintained: the withdrawn-row share is 0.34% vs 0.04-0.12% earlier, 29.2% of records were edited in the past year, and bills with cosponsor rows were edited more often (31.7% vs 18.6%). So 118's shift is most likely real (behavioural or procedural; the data cannot say which) rather than data latency, but not proven. A test on 118 measures performance under drift, roughly what deploying on 119 would face. It should be reported as such, not averaged away.

The section rules out three candidates on its own evidence: - S5 (random split) puts a later twin bill in training for at least 25% and up to 45% of evaluation bills (C20: 20% same-Congress plus 25% later-Congress; the two can overlap). That is direct future leakage. - S4 (within-Congress) tests on the end of a Congress. It loses up to 86% of its task-2 test bills to censoring (C6b) and 16.8% of task-1 bills (C5). - S2 (3-Congress sliding window) leaves some evaluation folds without their chamber majority in training (C8: only 57% of units fully covered).

S1pool fails C23b because both its test Congresses (117 and 118) come after the 2021 break, which its fit set (108-116) never saw (2/2, binomial p = 0.01). That fail depends on the assumed deployment break rate (0.10, one break in ten transitions). Under section A's broader break list it would pass. S1a passes only because a single test unit cannot fail (its one unit, 117, is post-break). More generally, with 1-7 test units per split, the C23b passes for S1a, S1b, S2 and S3 are weak evidence.

Finally, the section sets several construction rules that apply to every split: - Rebuild all count and outcome fields as of t0. Snapshot values differ from the t0 values for 48.5% of bills for n_cosponsors (C11). - Use the as-of-Congress party label (C10). - Use a point-in-time candidate pool that includes delegates (C17, C22). - Never use CRS summaries or legislative subjects (C13, C15a). - Mask the policy area at t0 <= 7 days. It is missing for 85.7% of bills aged 0-7 days in Congress 119 (C18). - Fix task 2's prediction time explicitly (C25).

Caveats: - Each "within noise" verdict uses a 95% prediction interval built from only 8 reference Congresses. Consecutive Congresses are not independent (they share members and trends), so these passes are low-power. - About 10 of the checks are statistical tests (prediction-interval or permutation), each at roughly 5%. The rest are thresholds, requirements or INFO. The tests are correlated (they reuse the same Congresses), so no simple expected count of false verdicts applies, but a single borderline verdict should not be over-read. - The policy-area latency figures rest on a small proxy: n=56 bills aged 0-7 days in Congress 119, at today's CRS speed.

Implications for the split

  • Cut at Congress boundaries. No location-identified break lies inside a Congress: the one located break (House original share, 2021-01) sits exactly at the start of 117. The Senate original share changes significantly beyond trend, but its location cannot be pinned down (2008 vs 2017), which fits a gradual bend. Within-Congress splits buy nothing, and S4 is also ruled out by censoring (up to 86% of task-2 test bills lost, C6b).

  • Do not use the random split S5 even as a reference baseline unless it is labelled leaky. At least 25%, and up to 45%, of its evaluation bills have a later twin in training (C20: 20% same-Congress plus 25% later-Congress; the two can overlap). This comes on top of the snapshot-field leakage in C11.

  • Prefer expanding-window designs (S1b, or S3 rolling origin) over the 3-Congress sliding window S2. Short windows miss the previous time a party held a chamber (C8: S2 covers both majorities for only 57% of units). The final model for deployment on 119 should be refit on 108-118 so its fit set contains the post-2021 regime (C23b).

  • Treat Congress 118 as a shifted test set and report it separately. Its cosponsor timing differs beyond training noise (C3, KS 0.093), and its task-1 density is 47% below the training mean (C4). C24 finds no evidence of missing labels, so the shift is most likely real rather than latency. Still, the tail test is weak and 118 records are still being edited, so treat 118 labels as provisional. Report per-Congress scores and gains over simple baselines (popularity, sponsor history), not only a pooled average.

  • Check whether the 118 timing shift begins inside 118. The House timing break at 2024-01 (p = 0.038, nominal only) suggests comparing 118 session-1 vs session-2 lags. If late-118 behaviour persists, 119 will resemble late 118 more than the 108-115 average, which favours recency weighting or including 118 in the final fit.

  • For the GNN graph, include the evaluation Congress's own events up to t0 (the '+stream' variants). About 36% of evaluation bills have a same-Congress twin known by t0 (C21), plus earlier cosponsorships and sponsor activity in the same Congress, and a frozen by-Congress graph throws that away. Every edge and node feature must be timestamp-filtered to no later than introduced_date + t0. Bill volume (26-45% above the training maximum in 116-118) argues for per-Congress normalised features (e.g. counts relative to Congress size) rather than raw counts.

  • Feature construction rules for every split: - Rebuild counts and outcomes as of t0 (C11). - Use party_code_asof (C10). - Use the point-in-time pool including delegates (C17, C22). - Use referral as a t0 feature (C12). - Exclude CRS summaries and subjects (C13, C15a). - Mask policy area at t0 <= 7, ideally with an explicit 'not yet assigned' state applied identically in training (C18). - Fix task 2's prediction time before modelling: t0 = 7 spends at most 4.6% of positives but needs policy area masked; t0 = 30 makes policy area available (96.9%) but spends 11.8-24.7% of positives and requires dropping already-reported bills from evaluation (C25).

Detailed results

What this tests (from the notebook)

A by-Congress split assumes that each Congress is a comparable "draw" of the same process, and that whatever we feed the model at prediction time (day 0 or day 7 after introduction) was really known at that time. This section tests the time-related conditions behind that assumption:

  1. Within-Congress dynamics: are bills introduced on the same calendar rhythm in every Congress?
  2. Cosponsorship timing: is the 30-day prediction window equally hard in every Congress?
  3. Procedural breakpoints: does the original-cosponsor share jump on a date inside a Congress, and does each split's fit set contain the post-break regime it is evaluated on?
  4. Censoring: how many bills lose their label because the window runs past the end of the Congress?
  5. Regime changes: is each chamber's controlling party in every validation/test Congress represented in training, and does the joint House x Senate regime matter at all?
  6. Snapshot leakage: which bill fields describe the bill after introduction and must never be features?
  7. Data latency and label completeness: is the most recent Congress (118) less complete than older ones, and are its labels (cosponsor events, committee reports) fully loaded, or only its annotations?
  8. Member turnover / point-in-time pool: how much does the full-Congress roster distort task-1 densities and Recall@20 compared with members in office at t0?
  9. Feature availability and companion bills: is the policy area known at t0, and do companion / reintroduced bills connect evaluation bills to the training portion of each candidate split?
  10. Task-2 prediction time: which t0 makes which features legitimate, and how much label is spent by waiting?

"Differs from train" verdicts use the shared rel_to_train() rule (95% t prediction interval of the 108-115 reference, with nested leave-one-out false-alarm rates). Pool-dependent checks iterate over the shared evaluation units iter_eval_units() (plus the S1pool variant) and record a by_split verdict per candidate split, so the decision section can score splits without parsing text. Quantities owned by another section (label rates -> A) are shown here only as cross-references (INFO). Congress 119 is still in session and is used only as context.

law-capable bills 108-119: 145,738; train pool 108-115, evaluation candidates [116, 117, 118]
What this tests (from the notebook)

C1-C2. When are bills introduced inside a Congress?

Why it matters. Bills introduced in the first weeks of a Congress (reintroductions, leadership priorities) and bills dropped in the final months (messaging bills, the end-of-Congress rush) behave differently: early bills have two years to gather cosponsors, late bills are mostly censored. If the introduction-time profile differs between train and test Congresses, a model learns a mix that the test set does not have. It also tells us whether a test set must be a full Congress: a partial window (for example session 1 only, as in S4) has a very different bill mix from a full Congress.

How to read it. The heatmap shows the share of each Congress's bills introduced in each quarter of the Congress (Q1 = first three months). The table gives the session-1 share, the share introduced in the last 90 days, and the KS distance of day_of_congress versus the 108-115 pool (KS is an effect size here: with ~10k bills every p-value is tiny, so we threshold the statistic, not the p-value).

Interpretation

Introduction timing is broadly stable across Congresses. The session-1 share is 0.56-0.69 everywhere. The KS distance of introduction day against the pool of the other training Congresses is 0.030-0.123 in training and 0.051-0.062 for 116-118. The largest evaluation KS (0.062, Congress 116) is within train-to-train noise (C1 PASS), and so are the session-1 and last-90-day shares (C2 PASS, max |t| = 1.96). Two drifts deserve separate mention. (a) The last-90-day share is 0.058-0.061 in all three evaluation Congresses, above every training value (0.012-0.056). It passes C2 only because an n=8 interval is wide. (b) Bill volume is not tested by C1 or C2 and lies far outside the training range: 14.3k-16.6k bills in 116-118 vs 8.6k-11.4k in training, i.e. 26-45% more than the largest training Congress. More bills competing for a fixed pool of legislators is a plausible contributor to the C4 drop in positives per eligible legislator. Within the training pool, session-2 bills have a lower task-1 positive rate at t0=7 (0.0051 vs 0.0074), and fewer have any positive (24% vs 33%). So a bill's position inside the Congress matters, and a test slice made only of late bills (S4) is not representative.

Caveats.

KS is used as an effect size here because with ~10k bills every p-value is tiny. The threshold is a prediction interval built from n=8 training Congresses, which is wide, so a pass is weak evidence of equality. The volume-density link is a hypothesis; the notebook does not test it. The session contrast is descriptive and does not adjust for bill type or chamber.

C-c75-o1
Interpretation

The heatmap shows the same rhythm in every Congress. There is a large first quarter (about 20-29% of bills), a second-quarter bump, a quieter middle and a small last quarter (1-6%). The outliers are second-year spikes in Q6: 26.6% in Congress 112 and 16.8% in 109, against roughly 9-13% in most others. Congress 112 is also the training Congress with the highest KS (0.123). The evaluation Congresses 116-118 have typical Q1 shares (22-23%), but their Q8 shares (5.8-6.3%) are at or above the training maximum (5.6%, Congress 115). That matches the rising last-90-day share in the table. A model trained on full Congresses sees nearly the same timing mix it is tested on, provided the test unit is also a full Congress. The recent Congresses carry slightly more late, mostly censored bills.

Caveats.

Shares are of law-capable bills in the snapshot. Quarter boundaries are calendar-based and ignore recesses.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C3-C4. Cosponsorship timing and task difficulty

Why it matters. Task 1 predicts cosponsors who join in (t0, t0+30]. Beyond how many cosponsors a bill gets (label rate, owned by section A: A3/A4), what matters for the window is when the later cosponsors arrive: if in some Congresses non-original cosponsors trickle in over months while in others they join in the first weeks, the same 30-day window captures a different slice of the cosponsor list.

How to read it. The line chart shows, per Congress, the cumulative share of cosponsorships that are original (lag 0) and that arrive within 7, 30 and 37 days (37 = end of the t0=7 window). C3 tests the timing of non-original cosponsorships (lag > 0) with a KS distance against the 108-115 pool, and judges it against the leave-one-out spread among the train Congresses themselves (a FAIL means "more different than train-to-train noise", not just "different"). C4 (INFO) is a cross-reference to section A's label rate.

The original share (cosponsors who sign on at introduction) is 0.33-0.39 in 108-116, then jumps to 0.460 in 117 and 0.466 in 118. For non-original cosponsors, 118 is clearly different. Their median lag is 92 days vs 62-75 in training. Only 19.6% of non-original cosponsorships (lag > 0) fall in days 8-37 (the t0=7 window), vs 22.8-26.9% in training. C3 fails for every split whose evaluation includes 118 (S1b, S2, S3, S4, the stream variants and S1pool), but not for S1a: 117's KS of 0.041 is just above the training maximum, yet inside the prediction interval. In plain terms, 118 cosponsorship is more front-loaded with originals, while later joiners arrive more slowly. Both shrink the slice of joiners a 30-day window after t0=7 can catch.

Caveats.

The upper-tail interval assumes the training Congresses are exchangeable. The median lag drifts upward within training (63 -> 75 by 114-115), so part of 118's deviation may continue a trend rather than be a jump. Why it happened (procedural or behavioural) is not identifiable from these data.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C23. Procedural breakpoints inside a Congress (original-cosponsor share and timing)

Why it matters. The jump in the original-cosponsor share in 117-118 (table above) may come from a procedural change (for example electronic cosponsor submission and remote operations in the House in 2020-2021) rather than from gradual drift. A procedural change is a break: it happens on a date, not at a Congress boundary. If the break falls inside a Congress, that Congress is a mix of two regimes, a validation Congress can straddle it, and a fit set that ends before it has never seen the new regime. That decides whether a by-Congress cut is enough or whether a within-Congress cut (or dropping pre-break data) is needed.

How to read it. Monthly series by introduction month (law-capable bills, uncensored at t0 = 0): share of 30-day cosponsors that are original, and the median lag of non-original cosponsors joining within 180 days (bills with a full 180-day window). Each series is de-seasonalised by its month-of-Congress mean (to remove the start/end-of-Congress cycle). A constant-mean CUSUM ("raw") would call any steady trend a break, because block permutation destroys trends; the verdict therefore uses the largest level shift BEYOND a linear trend (trend and step fitted jointly, segments >= 6 months; null = linear trend + 2,000 permutations of 6-month residual blocks, approximate). C23b then asks whether a split has more test folds on a never-seen post-break regime than deployment itself would. The chart shows the raw monthly series with Congress boundaries and the trend-adjusted break.

Interpretation

Four de-seasonalised monthly series were tested for a step beyond a linear trend (Bonferroni alpha 0.0125). (1) The House original-cosponsor share has a significant, location-identified break at 2021-01 (raw and trend-adjusted fits agree): 0.620 -> 0.713, +1.2 SD. It falls in month 1 of Congress 117, on a Congress boundary, so it does not count as inside a Congress. (2) The Senate original share changes significantly beyond trend (p < 0.001, |shift| 1.5 SD), but the location is not identified: the raw fit puts it at 2017-04, the trend-adjusted fit at 2008-01 (month 13 of 110). The trend-adjusted step is negative (-1.55 SD) even though the raw means rise (0.736 -> 0.782). With a rising trend (+0.008/yr) fitted jointly, a negative step means the series rose faster early and then flattened. That is a bend, not a step, and it is a real non-stationarity inside the training window that no Congress cut can isolate. (3) The House cosponsor-timing break sits at 2024-01, month 13 of Congress 118 (inside a Congress). Raw and trend-adjusted fits agree (raw p = 0.032, trend-adjusted p = 0.038), and the median lag rises from 42 to 49 days (+1.6 SD). That is nominally significant but not after Bonferroni correction. It points the same way as C3's 118 failure and suggests 118's slower late cosponsors may begin in its second session rather than at the Congress boundary. (4) The Senate timing break (2017-11, month 11 of 115, both fits agree, p = 0.023, +1.0 SD) is also nominal only. Hence C23 PASS: no location-identified, Bonferroni-significant break lies inside a Congress. C23b then asks whether a split puts more test units on a regime unseen in training than deployment would (1 break in 10 transitions, rate 0.10). Only S1pool fails (2/2 test units post-break, binomial p = 0.01). S1a has 1/1 but cannot fail with a single unit (minimum p = 0.10). Under section A's broader break list (116-118), every S1 and S4 test unit and 3 of 7 S2/S3 units are post-break. That is the normal deployment case, not a defect of any one split.

Caveats.

The permutation null (2,000 shuffles of 6-month blocks) is approximate, and a single-break model cannot represent several breaks or gradual bends. The timing series (median lag of non-original cosponsors within 180 days, bills with a full 180-day window) is not the same measure as C3's untruncated median lag (92 days), so the two sets of numbers are not comparable. The 2024-01 House break is at the end of the series (108-118 only). Its post-break segment covers only the 118 months with a full 180-day window, so it is short and edge effects are possible. A check of 118 session 1 vs session 2 lags would settle it. C23b has almost no power: with 1-7 test units per split it can only flag extreme cases. The 2021-01 timing is consistent with House remote and electronic cosponsor submission, but the data cannot establish that cause.

C-c80-o1
Interpretation

The monthly original-cosponsor share (House and Senate, with Congress boundaries) is noisy month to month (single months reach 0.38-1.00), but the House level visibly rises from January 2021. The Senate series sits higher than the House and drifts upward over the whole period, which is why its single-break location is not identified. The dashed line at 2021 coincides with a Congress boundary, which is the key fact for the split: a by-Congress cut never puts both regimes in one evaluation unit.

Caveats.

The chart shows raw (not de-seasonalised) series. The House break label reads p=0.001 while the table prints 0.0000; both are at the resolution floor of 2,000 permutations. Months with few bills create the extreme points.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C5-C6. Label censoring at the end of each Congress

Why it matters. Unpassed bills die when a Congress adjourns, so a bill introduced 20 days before the end has no full 30-day window (task 1) and one introduced 100 days before the end has no full 180-day window (task 2). These bills are excluded. If the excluded share differs by Congress, or if the excluded bills are systematically different (the end-of-Congress rush), the evaluation population differs from the training population. Note that 119 is censored much more because it is in progress.

How to read it. The chart shows the censored share per Congress for task 1 (t0=0, t0=7) and task 2. The table adds the share of evaluation bills each candidate split loses (from iter_eval_units()); S4's test slice is the end of the Congress, so it is hit hardest.

Task-1 censoring (the 30-day window runs past the end of the Congress) is small: at most 3.9% of bills at t0=7 in any Congress 108-118 (C5 PASS for full-Congress splits). Task-2 censoring (180-day window) is much larger: 9.6-15.2% in training and 15.0-17.3% in 116-118. That costs 2,289-2,721 bills per evaluation Congress, but stays within train-to-train noise (C6 PASS). By split, every full-Congress design loses 2.6-3.9% (task 1) and 14-17% (task 2) of evaluation bills. S4 is the exception: its test slice is the last 20% of introductions, so it loses 16.8% for task 1 and up to 85.8% for task 2 (C6b FAIL, mean 0.81). S4's task-2 test set would be tiny, made only of the earliest of the late-introduced bills (those at least 180 days before adjournment).

Censored bills are excluded, not modeled. Because they are the end-of-Congress bills, which have lower positive rates (C2 table), the evaluated population is shifted the same way in every Congress. It is comparable across splits but not the full population. Congress 119's 0.000 task-1 and 0.119 task-2 shares reflect the snapshot cut-off, not adjournment.

The two task-1 lines (t0=0 and t0=7) almost coincide: the extra 7 days of waiting costs under one percentage point of bills.

Share of law-capable bills. Not split-specific; see the table for per-split losses.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C7-C10. Party-control regimes and party labels

Why it matters. Cosponsorship and committee action depend on who holds the gavel. A model trained only on Republican-House Congresses may not transfer to a Democratic House. A by-Congress split works best if each chamber's controlling party in the validation and test Congresses also appears in training (and, only if it measurably matters, the joint House x Senate regime). If not, the test measures extrapolation to a new regime, and we should at least report per-regime results.

How to read it. The strip shows the majority party per chamber per Congress from the shared majority_party() (point-in-time at mid-Congress, party as of the Congress, independents counted with their caucus, Senate ties broken by the Vice President's party and cross-checked against the data). Diamonds mark a control flip versus the previous Congress. C8 checks, for every evaluation unit of the candidate splits, that each chamber's controlling party appears in training (task 2 depends on the bill's own chamber). C8b asks whether the joint regime (divided vs unified government) changes anything measurable beyond the chamber majority; only then does joint-regime coverage become a requirement. C9 shows how narrow the margins are and how C8 would change if a tie went the other way; C10 checks that per-Congress party labels are used (a time leak otherwise).

What this tests (from the notebook)

C11-C14. Snapshot leakage: which fields are known at t0?

Why it matters. The parquet tables are a snapshot taken years after each Congress ended. Many bill-level fields summarize the bill's whole life (latest action, became law, number of actions, cosponsors, text versions, summaries). Using any of them as a feature at t0 leaks the future, and a random split (S5) or even a temporal split would look far better than reality. Fields with a timestamp can be rebuilt "as of t0"; fields without one (policy area, subjects) are only safe if we can show they are normally assigned before t0.

How to read it. C11 is a requirement, not a pass/fail test. The leakage table compares each snapshot field with its value as of t0 = 7 days (where a timestamped table lets us rebuild it): share_changed is the share of law-capable bills whose snapshot value differs from the t0 value. Then: when are committee referrals and CRS summaries recorded relative to introduction, and when was each bill last updated relative to the end of its Congress?

Snapshot bill fields describe each bill's whole life, not its state at t0=7. They differ from the value at t0 for 48.5% of bills (n_cosponsors), 35.8% (n_actions and latest action), 11.9% (text versions) and 11.3% (more than one CRS summary). For 3.2% of bills the field encodes the outcome itself (became law). 93.2% of records were modified after their Congress ended. Every one of these fields must be rebuilt from timestamped events as of t0, or dropped. This is a requirement for every split. Feeding snapshot values is expected to inflate both tasks, likely most under a random split; the notebook does not measure the size of that inflation.

Caveats.

Fields without timestamps (n_summaries) cannot be rebuilt and must simply be excluded.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C24, C14. Are the labels of the most recent Congresses fully loaded?

Why it matters. 118 is the natural test Congress for task 1, and it looks different: lower positive density (A3), later non-original cosponsors (C3), and many records still being edited (C14). If cosponsor events or committee-report actions of 117/118 were still missing from the snapshot, those differences would be data latency, not behaviour, and 118 would understate task-1 and task-2 performance. Three tests: (1) internal consistency: the snapshot counts (bills.n_cosponsors, n_actions, latest_action_date) against the event tables; (2) staleness: events dated after the record's own update_date; (3) the end-of-Congress tail: if late events were missing, the share of a Congress's cosponsorships dated in its last 90 days (and of committee reports in its last 180 days) would be too low.

How to read it. Mismatch and stale shares should be 0; the tail shares of 117/118 are judged with rel_to_train (lower tail: only a deficit signals missing events). The last line compares, inside 118, how often bills with and without cosponsor rows were modified after the Congress ended (post-end edits driven by cosponsor loading would differ).

[PASS] C24: Labels of the most recent Congresses (cosponsor events, committee reports) are fully loaded | metric=1.211 (threshold consistency/stale shares = 0 in every Congress AND end-of-Congress tail shares not below the PI (outside 95% t prediction interval of ref 108-115 (lower tail; n=8)); metric = min t of the two tails over candidates)
Interpretation

These are label-completeness checks for 108-118. The snapshot cosponsor counts, action counts and latest-action dates match the event tables exactly (mismatch 0.000), and no event is dated after its record's update_date. The end-of-Congress tails of 117/118 are higher than training, not lower: 4.2-4.4% of cosponsorships fall in the last 90 days (0.5-3.9% in training), and 42-45% of committee reports fall in the last 180 days (24-35% in training). Missing late events would push these tails down, so C24 PASSES (min t = 1.21 on the deficit side). C24 therefore finds no evidence of missing labels, and 118's lower density and later timing (C3, C4) are most likely not caused by unloaded labels.

Caveats.

Internal consistency cannot detect events missing from both the counts and the event table (e.g. a cosponsor never recorded anywhere). The tail test is confounded: 116-118 have more late introductions (last-90-day share 0.058-0.061 vs at most 0.056 in training), which raises late-event tails and could hide a modest deficit. 118 also shows ongoing record maintenance: a withdrawn-row share of 0.34% (3-8x the 0.04-0.12% of earlier Congresses), and bills with cosponsor rows edited in the last year more often than bills without (31.7% vs 18.6%). None of this shows missing positives, but it means 'complete' cannot be asserted.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C15-C16. Data completeness and annotation latency

Why it matters. Policy areas, subjects, summaries and committee referrals are added by CRS and clerks after introduction. If the newest Congress (118, the natural test set) is less annotated than older ones, a model that uses those features is tested on degraded inputs, and the test score understates (or misstates) real performance. Congress 119, which is still in progress, lets us measure how fast annotations arrive: compare coverage for young versus old bills.

How to read it. The line chart shows per-Congress coverage of each annotation for law-capable bills. The second table shows, for Congress 119 only, coverage by bill age at the snapshot date.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C18. Is the policy area known at prediction time?

Why it matters. Sections B and D use the CRS policy area as a t0 feature (D's empirical-Bayes rate per policy area, B's bill attributes). In the snapshot almost every bill of 108-118 has one, but CRS assigns it after introduction, and the historical assignment date is not in the data. The in-progress Congress 119 is the only window onto that lag: if bills a few days old often lack a policy area, then a model trained on complete snapshots sees a feature at t0 that it would not have in deployment.

How to read it. Policy-area missingness of 119 bills by age at the snapshot, from the shared PA_MISSING_AT_T0 (so sections B, C and D quote the same numbers; 0-7 and 8-30 days matter for t0 = 0 and 7), and whether the youngest bills were introduced during a recess (floor actions per day from bill_actions). Proxy: CRS's current speed, not the speed in earlier Congresses.

Interpretation

Using the shared PA_MISSING_AT_T0 figures, policy area is missing for 85.7% of 119 bills aged 0-7 days and 14.0% aged 8-30 days, versus 0-0.8% for older bills. The rule binds: policy area must be masked, or replaced by a 'not yet assigned' state, for task 1 at t0 = 0 and 7, and for task 2 if it uses t0 <= 7 (C18 requirement). The youngest bucket was introduced during a low-activity week (5.6 floor actions/day vs a median of 15.6). So CRS may be slow partly because of the recess, but even 8-30-day-old bills miss it 14% of the time.

Caveats.

n=56 for the 0-7-day bucket, so its 95% binomial interval is roughly +/- 9 percentage points. That cannot move the conclusion that most week-old bills lack a policy area. The historical assignment lag is unobserved.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C25. Which prediction time t0 should task 2 use?

Why it matters. Task 2 (reported within 180 days) has no fixed prediction time. Whether the policy area, referral details and early cosponsors are legitimate features depends on it, and that decides whether the latency checks (C15b's policy-area part, C18, A13 with vs without policy area) constrain the split at all. A later t0 makes more features available but "spends" part of the label: bills already reported by t0 are no longer a prediction.

How to read it. For candidate t0 values: availability at that bill age of each feature. Timestamped features (referral, cosponsors, actions) use the worst Congress in 108-118; untimestamped ones (policy area, subjects) use 119 bills of about that age at the snapshot (small-sample proxy, n shown); summaries use the update_date lower bound. The last rows give the share of task-2 positives already reported by t0 (worst Congress), i.e. label lost by waiting.

Interpretation

The table shows the trade-off for task 2's prediction time. At t0 = 0 or 7, only timestamped features (early cosponsors and actions, referral at about 98%) are reliably available. Policy area is present for 12-26% (119 proxy, n = 41 / 27) and summaries for at most 1.2%. At t0 = 30, policy area reaches 96.9% (n=261), the smallest candidate t0 to clear 95% (C25 metric = 30). The 119-proxy columns use very small samples (n = 27-261). Subjects are non-monotonic in age (0.148 at t0=7 vs 0.027 at t0=30), which is likely small-sample noise. If t0 > 0, bills already reported by t0 should be dropped from the task-2 evaluation, not counted as easy positives.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C17, C22. Member turnover and the point-in-time candidate pool

Why it matters. The legacy pool per bill is "everyone who served in the chamber that Congress". Members who died, resigned or were seated mid-Congress are then candidates for bills introduced while they were out of office: guaranteed negatives that change the positive density and can take top-k slots from real candidates (a member who resigned in 118 still has a strong 117 history). This is a construction requirement for every split, not something that separates splits, but its size tells us whether D's backtest and the labels must switch to the shared point-in-time pool (window_targets(point_in_time=True) / ROSTER_ASOF).

How to read it. C17: share of the legacy pool not in office in the month of introduced_date + 7 (per Congress and chamber), and the share of task-1 positives who are outside the point-in-time pool (delegates and roster approximation errors: unrankable positives). C22: for S3 test folds, Recall@20 of a simple history ranker (sponsor-cosponsor affinity in the fit Congresses + recent activity) and the positive density, with the full-Congress roster vs the point-in-time pool.

Caveats.

Only two folds and one simple ranker. A stronger model that relies more on long member history could put more resigned members in its top K, so the effect may be larger for the GNN.

What this tests (from the notebook)

C19-C21. Companion and reintroduced bills across the split boundary

Why it matters. Many bills have a twin: an identical House/Senate companion in the same Congress, or a reintroduction of the same bill from an earlier Congress. Twins share sponsors, cosponsors and fate. A reintroduction in a training Congress is legitimate signal (it was known when the new bill was introduced). A same-Congress companion in the training portion is legitimate only if it was introduced earlier; if it was introduced after the evaluation bill (possible only under the random split S5), the model sees the future. Same-Congress companions also show what a by-Congress split forgoes: they are known at t0 only if the graph includes the evaluation Congress's own history up to t0.

How to read it. Twins = same-Congress bill_related links (any relationship) plus identical official titles as introduced (normalized; titles shared by > 30 bills are dropped as generic). For every evaluation unit: the share of eval bills with a same-Congress twin in the training portion (split into introduced before vs after the eval bill) and with an identical-title bill in a training Congress (earlier = reintroduction, later = future leak). Twins are themselves a CRS/clerk annotation assigned after introduction (proxy).

Interpretation

There are 250,731 directed twin links: same-Congress related or identical-title bills, plus reintroductions. Temporal splits (S1-S4) put no twin introduced after the evaluation bill into training (C19 PASS, 0%). The random split S5 does so through two routes: 20% of evaluation bills have a later same-Congress twin in training, and 25% a twin in a later Congress. C20's metric (0.45) is the sum of these two shares. Because a bill can have both, the share of affected bills is between 25% and 45% (C20 FAIL either way). S5 lets the model see the future copy of the bill it is predicting. Reintroductions from earlier Congresses, which are legitimate signal, link 32-36% of evaluation bills in the full-Congress splits. About 36% of evaluation bills have a same-Congress twin introduced before t0 (C21). A pure by-Congress split forgoes that signal unless the graph includes the evaluation Congress's own history up to t0 (the '+stream' variants).

Caveats.

Twins are themselves a CRS/clerk annotation, possibly added after introduction. Identical-title matching misses reworded reintroductions and may join unrelated bills with short titles (titles shared by more than 30 bills are dropped). The signal the 'twin known at t0' share describes is therefore partly unknowable in deployment.

Interpretation

The grouped bars summarise leakage by design. For S1a, S1b, S2 and S3, only the legitimate 'reintroduction (earlier Congress)' bar is non-zero (32-36%). S4 adds 17% legitimate earlier same-Congress twins and has a smaller reintroduction share (15%). S5 is the only split with non-zero 'LATER (leak)' bars (20% same-Congress, 25% later Congress; these can overlap). Any score from S5 is likely optimistic because of this leakage and should not be read as a baseline.

Caveats.

Means over each split's val and test units.
