Interpretation

Section tally: 12 pass, 4 fail, 8 info, 6 requirements. The four failures fall into two groups. Two are split-specific exclusions: C20, where S5 leaks twins, and C6b, where S4's test slice is mostly censored. The other two are drift findings about the newest Congresses: C3 (118's cosponsor timing) and C23b (S1pool tests only on post-break Congresses, a verdict sensitive to the assumed deployment break rate). None of the four argues against cutting at Congress boundaries. The C23 pass carries two qualifications: an unlocated Senate bend and a nominal House timing break inside 118. The six requirements apply to every split, which is why the summary table records them separately from the pass/fail verdicts.

Caveats.

Pass/fail counts are not a score: checks differ in importance and power, and they are not independent.

Open questions

  • Why do 118's late cosponsors arrive later (median lag 92 vs 62-75 days)? Candidates are a procedural change, more bills competing for attention (16.6k vs at most 11.4k in training), or a behavioural shift. Whether it starts inside 118 (House timing break at 2024-01, nominal only) is also open. The data cannot separate these, and the answer decides whether 119 will look like 118 or like earlier Congresses.

  • Are 118's labels truly complete? C24 finds no deficit, but its tail test is confounded by rising late introductions and cannot see events missing from both counts and event tables. 118 records are still being edited (29.2% in the past year).

  • Does the joint House x Senate regime matter? With only 4 divided Congresses, C8b cannot detect moderate effects (smallest verdict p = 0.245). 'Not required' rests on absence of evidence.

  • How fast was policy area assigned historically? The 85.7%-missing figure comes from 56 bills of the in-progress Congress at today's CRS speed. The historical lag, and therefore how much a t0 <= 7 mask is really needed for training-era bills, is unobserved.

D. Candidate splits and baseline backtest

When simple baselines are actually trained and scored, the rolling-origin by-Congress split (S3: train on 108..c-2, validate on c-1, refit on 108..c-1, test on c) does its job: validation picks near-best models and predicts Task 1 test levels. It works best with streaming same-Congress history, recency weighting, Task 2 selection averaged over several validation Congresses, and Congress 118 held back as a locked final test. A single test Congress (S1a/S1b) is too small to confirm real model differences, and the random split inflates Recall@20 by about 0.075.

Sections A-C checked the preconditions of a temporal split. This section checks the consequence. Each candidate split is used to train and score transparent baselines. Task 1 has count heuristics (popularity, party+pop, sponsor_hist), a 2-hop random-walk graph score (rw2hop, a fixed-weight version of SGC/LightGCN propagation) and a learned transductive embedding (svd). Task 2 has smoothed rates (chamber_maj, eb_rate, eb_rate_t0safe). The questions are whether validation picks the right model, whether test sets can resolve paired differences, whether validation predicts the test level, and which protocol choices cost or gain accuracy. All uncertainty comes from a 500-resample cluster bootstrap by sponsor (bills of the same sponsor are resampled together). The minimum detectable effect (MDE) is fixed at 0.01 Recall@20 / 0.01 AUROC. The tally is 15 PASS, 3 FAIL and 12 INFO.

What the data shows. (1) Under S3, validation choices transfer. Mean selection regret is 0.0028 Recall@20 for sponsor_hist, 0.0002 for rw2hop, 0.0007 for svd, and 0.0045 AUROC for the at-introduction Task 2 family (D11, D21, D23, D12b). Task 1 val-test gaps are within bootstrap noise (D1, D20, D22). (2) Paired model differences are stable on average but not in every single Congress. For the deployable Task 2 pair eb_rate_t0safe - chamber_maj (mean +0.020 AUROC), 3 of 7 single test Congresses (43%) fail to confirm the direction. That is why every single-test-Congress split fails D9. (3) Among valid temporal splits, protocol choices move scores more than the choice between S2 and S3 (the random split's +0.075 optimism is a split choice and is larger than every protocol effect except refitting). Streaming same-Congress history adds +0.037 Recall@20 in 7/7 folds. Refitting on train+val adds about +0.06. Recency weighting removes the advantage a 3-Congress sliding window has over the expanding window (-0.012 -> -0.0008). Upweighting regime-matched Congresses adds nothing beyond recency. (4) Two sources of optimism are large. The random split adds +0.075 Recall@20 (about 29% of the temporal level of 0.259). If Task 2 is scored at introduction, a policy area that usually does not exist yet adds +0.10 AUROC, about 45% of eb_rate's discrimination above chance (0.10 of 0.22).

What we infer. The defensible protocol is the notebook's D_FINAL_PROTOCOL. Develop on S3(+stream) rolling folds 112-117, report once on locked Congress 118, and treat 119 as the prospective test. Reserving 118 is affordable: the maximum paired miss risk rises from 0.033 to 0.115, still under the 0.20 bar (D27). One cost: on the 6 development folds, the at-introduction Task 2 family's selection regret rises to 0.0053 AUROC, just above the 0.005 tolerance (it passes only because no fold is significant), so Task 2 hyperparameters should be chosen on the mean of several validation Congresses (D17: regret 0.0019), not on c-1 alone. Report Task 2 levels per Congress with their spread, never as one number. They move by more than sampling noise from Congress to Congress (D3/D4, D2b), and a precise average level would need about 13 Congresses (D15).

Statistical caveats. The 7 rolling folds are not independent: consecutive folds share almost all training Congresses, and each test Congress is the next fold's validation Congress. Fold counts ("2 of 7 significant") and sign tests are therefore descriptive, not exact. 18 checks carry a verdict (15 PASS, 3 FAIL; the 12 INFO items are descriptive, not tests), each at the 5% level with no multiplicity correction, so one verdict could flip by chance. Borderline verdicts, such as D12's mean regret of 0.0078 resting on a single fold, deserve less weight than consistent 7/7 patterns. The baselines are stand-ins: the SVD is the only learned model, and its edge over unweighted sponsor_hist (+0.021) is confounded with recency weighting (recency alone adds +0.021 to sponsor_hist, D26), so the data do not show that low-rank learning beats recency-weighted counts. GNN-specific failure modes, such as overfitting via message passing, are also only approximated. The MDE of 0.01 is a stated convention, not something estimated from the data.

Implications for the split

  • Use the rolling-origin by-Congress split (S3) as the backbone: train 108..c-2, validate on c-1, refit on 108..c-1, test on c. Develop on folds 112-117, score locked Congress 118 once at the end, and treat 119 as prospective. Do not use a single test Congress (S1a/S1b) or pooled 117+118 to compare models: one Congress misses a real +0.02 AUROC Task 2 difference 43% of the time. Select Task 2 hyperparameters on the mean over several validation Congresses (D17: at-introduction regret 0.0019), not on c-1 alone: on the dev folds the c-1 rule's regret is 0.0053, above tolerance.

  • Evaluate the temporal GNN in streaming mode. Include the eval Congress's cosponsorship edges dated on or before introduced_date + t0 in the message-passing graph. This is leakage-free, matches deployment, and is worth about +0.037 Recall@20 for simple history models in every fold. Whether it also helps the 15.7% of positives from new members is a hypothesis to test (D24 strata under S3+stream); it was not measured, and popularity gains only +0.0035 from streaming.

  • Encode time or weight recent edges (recency half-life of about 1 Congress, or a time encoding or decay in the temporal GNN). Then keep the expanding window: unweighted history loses about 0.012 Recall@20 to a 3-Congress window, and weighted history does not. Regime-matched upweighting adds nothing beyond recency for these baselines. Compare the GNN against recency-weighted sponsor_hist (about 0.280), not the unweighted 0.259: the SVD's apparent +0.021 'learning' gain is roughly matched by recency weighting alone (additive estimate 0.259 + 0.021; the direct svd_hl1 vs sh_hl1 comparison was not run).

  • After choosing hyperparameters and the epoch budget on validation (c-1 for Task 1, the mean of several validation Congresses for Task 2), refit on train+val, or at minimum add Congress c-1's edges to the graph at test time. Leaving out the most recent Congress costs about 0.06 Recall@20.

  • For Task 2, fix the prediction time explicitly and build features as of that time. The policy area is usually missing at introduction and inflates AUROC by about 0.10 (about 45% of eb_rate's signal above chance). Report the at-introduction model as the primary result and policy-area models as a 'one month after introduction' variant.

  • Report Task 1 as per-fold scores plus the 7-fold mean, and Task 2 levels per Congress with their spread, never as one number (between-Congress std about 0.04 AUROC). Use sponsor-cluster bootstrap CIs (1.2-2.6 times wider than bill-level) and paired CIs for model comparisons.

  • Treat the random split only as a leaky upper bound. It inflates Recall@20 by +0.075 (about 29%), most strongly for the sponsor-history signal a GNN relies on. Give the GNN inductive node features (party/caucus, chamber, state, committee proxies) so it can handle new legislators that a pure embedding model cannot.

Detailed results

What this tests (from the notebook)

Sections A-C test the preconditions of a temporal split (similar distributions, node overlap, no leakage). This section tests the consequence: if we actually train simple, transparent baselines under each candidate split, does the split do its job? A split is useful for model selection if (1) validation picks the model that is best on test among close candidates (regret), (2) the test set is large enough to resolve paired model-vs-model differences, (3) the validation score level predicts the test level (for early stopping and reporting), and (4) its protocol choices (expanding vs sliding window, streaming same-Congress history, refit on train + val) do not cost accuracy. We also quantify how optimistic the leaky random split is and whether a within-Congress split behaves differently, and (D27) what it costs to keep Congress 118 as a locked final test that no model choice ever sees. One minimum detectable effect per task (D_MDE = 0.01 Recall@20 / 0.01 AUROC) is used by every selection, optimism and sizing check.

Protocol. Every split comes from SPLIT_DEFS / iter_eval_units() and SPLIT_VARIANTS (setup). Each validation unit is scored with baselines fit on its training Congresses; each test unit with baselines refit on train + validation ("select on val, refit, report test"; D19 checks that refit). The baselines are counts, smoothed rates, one graph-structural score (rw2hop, a 2-step walk on the time-masked cosponsorship graph) and one learned, transductive embedding model (svd: a truncated SVD of the sponsor x cosponsor training matrix, rank and recency chosen on validation), the closest cheap stand-in for a GNN with per-legislator embeddings (it can go stale and is cold for new members). The goal is to measure the split, not to win: conclusions that hold for count, graph and learned models are the robust ones.

Prediction times. Task 1 is scored at t0 = 0 and 7 days after introduction (task definition). Task 2 has no prediction time in the task definition; this section assumes prediction at introduction (same t0 as Task 1). At introduction the CRS policy area is usually missing, so the deployable Task 2 baseline is eb_rate_t0safe; eb_rate (policy area always present) is reported as the "predict about a month after introduction" variant. Task 2 selection (D12b) and test-set sizing (D9) are judged on the t0-safe variant; the policy-area variant is shown for reference.

D-c110-txt
Protocol variants (SPLIT_VARIANTS): S1a+stream: S1a + eval-Congress events dated <= introduced_date + t0 | S1b+stream: S1b + eval-Congress events dated <= introduced_date + t0 | S3+stream: S3 rolling folds + eval-Congress events dated <= introduced_date + t0 | S1pool: train 108-115 | val 116 | test 117+118 pooled (refit on 108-116 once)
What this tests (from the notebook)

Baselines, metrics and the backtest engine

Task 1 (cosponsor ranking). For each evaluable bill (law-capable, window not censored, at least one new cosponsor in (t0, t0+30]) we rank the eligible same-chamber legislators: voting members in office in the month of introduced_date + t0 (ROSTER_ASOF_ALL, the shared point-in-time pool, delegates and resident commissioners included as the task definition requires) minus the sponsor and anyone who already cosponsored by t0. popularity = legislator's number of cosponsorships in the training events; party+pop = same caucus as the sponsor first (as-of-Congress caucus, members.caucus), then popularity; sponsor_hist = times the legislator cosponsored this sponsor's bills in the training events (ties broken by popularity); rw2hop = a graph-structural score closer to what a GNN computes: a two-step random walk from the sponsor on the time-masked cosponsorship graph, h1 + 0.3 * h1 @ A, where h1 is the sponsor's row of the sponsor->cosponsor count matrix (row-normalised) and A the row-normalised symmetric graph (H + H^T). It rewards "cosponsors of my cosponsors" (multi-hop structure), not just direct history; it is a fixed-weight version of the propagation step of LightGCN / SGC-style GNNs. Streaming variants use the eval Congress's graph as of the first day of the month of introduced_date + t0. svd_r{rank}[_hl1] = learned embeddings: rank-r truncated SVD of log(1 + sponsor x cosponsor counts) in the training events (optionally recency-weighted, half-life 1 Congress), score = reconstructed affinity sponsor -> candidate. Legislators absent from training have a zero embedding (transductive cold start). Metrics: Recall@10, Recall@20, NDCG@20 per bill, averaged. Task 2 (advancement). prior = constant training rate (AUROC 0.5 by construction); chamber_maj = smoothed rate by chamber x sponsor-in-majority (majority_party(), sponsor caucus); eb_rate = empirical-Bayes rate by policy area x chamber x sponsor-in-majority, shrunk toward chamber_maj (20 pseudo-bills); eb_rate_t0safe = eb_rate, but bills whose policy area would not yet be assigned at introduction fall back to chamber_maj (rate measured on fresh 119th bills). Metrics: AUROC, average precision (AP) and AP lift = AP / positive rate (AP alone is not comparable across Congresses whose positive rate differs). Uncertainty. 95% percentile intervals from a cluster bootstrap by sponsor (500 resamples; bills of the same sponsor share coalitions, so they are resampled together). ci_low_bill / ci_high_bill give the naive bill-level bootstrap for comparison. The same resamples are used for every baseline of a unit, so paired differences (model A - model B on the same bills) get their own, much tighter, CIs. Near-tie families (for model selection, D11-D12, D21): Task 1 sponsor_hist with recency decay (half-life 1, 2, 4 Congresses or none) and a same-caucus tie-break variant; Task 1 rw2hop with second-hop weight in {0.1, 0.3, 1} and recency half-life 1 (weights 0.1, 0.3); Task 2 eb_rate with shrinkage m in {5, 20, 80} and a variant without sponsor-majority, and the same four members in their t0-safe form (*_t0s, policy area hidden for fresh bills); Task 1 svd with rank in {8, ..., 512} (powers of 2) x recency half-life {none, 1} (D22-D25).

Interpretation

This is the master table of mean test scores per split. It covers 60 units and 2,160 result rows, with no subsampling. On Task 1 Recall@20 at t0=0, the history-based scores (sponsor_hist, rw2hop) beat party+pop and popularity under every split. Plain by-Congress splits give 0.22-0.27 (S1pool 0.222, S1b 0.244, S3 0.259, S2 0.272). Streaming variants, which also add same-Congress history up to t0, are about 0.04-0.05 higher (S3+stream 0.296, S1b+stream 0.297). The two splits that train on same-Congress bills score higher still: S4 0.310 (Congresses 116-118, test = last 20% of bills) and the leaky random split S5 0.332. On Task 2, eb_rate AUROC is 0.69-0.72 on by-Congress splits but only 0.55-0.63 for the at-introduction version eb_rate_t0safe. Only 0.08% of Task 1 positives fall outside the point-in-time candidate pool (median pool size 434); the separate rerun in D18 confirms that the pool definition moves Recall@20 by only about +0.002.

Caveats.

Splits evaluate different Congresses and different numbers of folds, so columns are not paired comparisons; in particular S4 (3 Congresses, late bills only) is not paired with S3+stream (7 Congresses, all bills). Single-Congress columns (S1a = 117, S1b = 118) partly reflect how hard that Congress is. The S4 Task 2 AP lift of 3.89 rests on about 596 test bills per fold and should not be read as a real gain.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D1-D2, D20. Does the validation score predict the test score level?

The validation Congress stands in for the test Congress when we tune and early-stop. If val and test scores differ a lot (Congress c is systematically easier or harder than c-1), loss-based early stopping and score thresholds are tuned on a different target. We report the gap (test - val) per split and fold; a gap is significant when it exceeds the 95% half-width of the difference under the cluster bootstrap (sqrt(hw_val^2 + hw_test^2)). Calibration: instead of a fixed relative tolerance, a split FAILS when its gaps are larger than sampling noise explains: chi-square test of sum (gap / se_diff)^2 over its folds (df = number of folds; a single-fold split reduces to |z| > 1.96). Val and test share many sponsors, so se_diff is conservative. We also print the noise-expected mean |relative gap| (sqrt(2/pi) * se_diff / val) next to the observed one. Note that a pure level shift does not harm model selection as long as the ranking of candidates holds; rankings and selection regret are measured directly in D11-D12, D17 and D21, so the Task 2 level gap (D2) is informational. D20 repeats D1 for the graph-structural rw2hop baseline. In the chart each row is a split/fold, the two dots are val and test with 95% cluster-bootstrap CIs; long segments mean the validation Congress is a poor proxy.

Interpretation

On Task 1, validation predicts the test level. Under S3 the mean |test - val| for sponsor_hist is 0.011 Recall@20, and every per-fold gap (from -0.018 to +0.007) is inside its paired 95% half-width (0.024-0.029). D1 and D20 pass for every split except S1pool, whose val Congress 116 overstates its pooled 117+118 test by 0.032 (a 12% relative gap, 0.1196 in the calibration table, versus 0.038 expected from noise). On Task 2, eb_rate gaps are larger: 3 of 7 S3 folds (43%) are significant, for example +0.055 at c=112 and -0.055 at c=116. D2b fails for the at-introduction model under all multi-fold splits (S2, S3, S3+stream, S4) and under both single-fold splits tested on 118 (S1b, S1b+stream): its AUROC level moves between consecutive Congresses by more than noise.

Caveats.

D2b concerns calibration and level reporting, not model selection. Selection is tested directly in D12/D12b and passes. The chi-square treats folds as independent, but consecutive folds share Congresses. The single-fold splits pass D1 partly because a test with one degree of freedom has little power.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D3-D4. How much does the score level move from one Congress to the next?

The rolling-origin folds (S3) repeat the one-step-ahead protocol for every test Congress from 112 to 118. If a fixed baseline's score swings across folds more than sampling noise allows (between-fold std vs the cluster-bootstrap standard error, hw/1.96), then a single test Congress (as in S1) gives a Congress-specific number: report scores per Congress and their mean over rolling folds. This concerns the reported level; comparisons between models on the same test bills are paired and much more stable (D9). Lines are per baseline; shaded bands are 95% cluster-bootstrap CIs.

Interpretation

Task 2 AUROC drifts. The policy-area model eb_rate falls from 0.78 (112) to about 0.69-0.70 (116-118). The at-introduction model and chamber_maj dip sharply in 116-117 (eb_rate_t0safe 0.569 and 0.560; chamber_maj 0.535 and 0.545) and partly recover in 118 (0.619). Because the dip shows up in the sponsor-majority signal, part of it is linked to which party controls which chamber. 116 and 117 both had a Democratic House.

Caveats.

The regime explanation is an inference. D26 finds that regime-matched training weights do not recover the loss for these count models, and the 95% bands in 116-118 are wide (about ±0.04).

What this tests (from the notebook)

D5-D6, D11-D12, D17, D21. Does validation pick the model that is best on test?

The real job of a validation set is choosing among close candidates (hyperparameters, decay rates, regularization). D11, D12 and D21 use near-tie families and measure, per rolling fold, whether the validation-best candidate is also test-best (hit rate), how much test score is lost by trusting validation (regret = test score of the test-best minus test score of the val-chosen candidate) and the Kendall tau between the val and test orderings. Family members are often statistically indistinguishable on one Congress, so a regret only counts as significant when the paired cluster-bootstrap CI of (test-best minus val pick) on that test Congress excludes 0 (this is liberal: the test-best is itself chosen on test). A check FAILs only if mean regret > D_TOL = MDE / 2 (0.005) and at least 2 of 7 folds have significant regret (2+ false alarms out of 7 at the 5% level has probability ~4%). D17 repeats the selection using the mean val score of the last three rolling folds. D5-D6 compare the main baselines (informational: most pairs are far apart). D12b repeats D12 for the t0-safe Task 2 family (the deployable one if Task 2 predicts at introduction). Single-fold splits (S1a, S1b) cannot meet a "2 of 7 folds" rule, so their by_split entry is the regret measured on their own fold (a metric, not a verdict), and the detail says where it falls in the S3 distribution of per-fold regret.

Interpretation

Validation picks good models from near-tie families. Task 1 regrets are tiny: sponsor_hist family mean 0.0028, rw2hop 0.0002, with Kendall tau 0.86-0.94 between val and test orderings. Val consistently picks the recency-weighted members (sh_hl1 in 6/7 folds, rw_b0.1_hl1 in 6/7). The Task 2 families have low hit rates (0.14-0.29) and low tau (0.24-0.43), because members differ by less than noise: the median val margin is 0.0005 AUROC. D12 passes with a mean regret of 0.0078 AUROC, above the 0.005 tolerance, because only 1 of 7 folds is significant; D12b (at-introduction family) passes with 0.0045. Selecting on the mean of the last three val folds (D17) cuts regrets further: 0.0015 for eb_rate, 0.0019 for eb_rate_t0safe. D5 (Task 1 main baselines keep their val-to-test order in only 57% of folds) is not a selection failure: it reflects the near-exact tie between rw2hop and sponsor_hist (paired mean difference -0.0002), whose order flips by chance; D6 (Task 2, candidates far apart) keeps its order in 100% of folds.

Caveats.

D12's pass rests on the two-part rule. Its mean regret exceeds tolerance and is driven by one fold (118). The 'test-best' is chosen on test, so regret is biased upward. That makes these passes conservative, but it also means the significance counts are liberal.

Interpretation

Per-fold regret is zero or almost zero in most folds for every family. The exceptions: sponsor_hist at c=113 (0.014); the at-introduction Task 2 family at c=116-117 (0.013, 0.017); and above all eb_rate at c=118 (0.044 AUROC). The 116-117 values match the sign flip in the value of the sponsor-majority feature (dev-fold differences eb_m20_t0s - eb_nomaj_m20_t0s of -0.012 in 116 and +0.017 in 117). Validation on 116 favoured the variant without that feature, which then lost on 117.

Caveats.

The 0.044 regret at c=118 belongs to the policy-area eb_rate family: tuning that variant on the 117 validation Congress alone can cost several AUROC points on the locked test. The deployable at-introduction family has almost no regret at 118 (0.0001); its losses happen at 116-117 (0.013, 0.017). Both patterns support averaging selection over several val folds (D17).

What this tests (from the notebook)

D22-D25. A learned, transductive embedding model: selection, staleness and cold start

Count heuristics cannot overfit and have no per-legislator parameters, so they cannot show the two failure modes that matter most for a GNN under a by-Congress split: (1) a high-capacity model's validation choice may not carry over to test (it can fit Congress-specific structure), and (2) learned per-legislator embeddings go stale across an election (a member's role changes: chamber or party switch, majority status flip, new committee portfolio), which a count heuristic hides. We fit a truncated SVD of log(1 + sponsor x cosponsor counts) on each fold's training Congresses (ranks 8-128, typical GNN sizes, plus 256 / 512, close to memorised history; each with or without recency weighting: 14 candidates; rank = capacity), choose the candidate on the validation Congress and refit on train + val for test, exactly as the S3 protocol prescribes. D22 is the val-test level check (as D1), D23 the selection regret (as D11), D24 reports Recall@20 separately for positives from new legislators (zero embedding) and returning ones, and D25 tests staleness: among returning legislators, is the learned model's recall loss on members whose role changed larger than the count heuristic's loss on the same positives (difference in differences, cluster-bootstrap CI)? The member-committee roster is not in the data, so "committee shift" is a proxy: cosine similarity < 0.5 between the committee-referral profiles of the member's sponsored bills in their last training Congress and in the eval Congress (both with >= 5 referred bills); it is used only to stratify the evaluation, never as a feature.

Interpretation

Mean test Recall@20 rises steadily with SVD rank: from 0.241 (rank 8) to 0.280 (rank 512) with recency weighting, and from 0.194 to 0.260 without it. Recency weighting adds 0.02-0.05 at every rank. Recency-weighted ranks of 32 or more (0.263 and up) and unweighted rank 512 (0.2603) exceed the unweighted sponsor_hist reference (0.259). Lower rank (more compression) monotonically hurts, so higher capacity does not overfit across Congresses here. The two levers are capacity and weighting recent edges more; the top recency-weighted SVD (0.280) only matches what recency-weighted counts reach (about 0.280, see D26).

Caveats.

If gains keep rising up to rank 512, the model may simply be memorising pairwise history. Small GNN embeddings (32-128 dimensions) may need other inputs (features, multi-hop structure) to match it.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D7. How optimistic is the random bill split?

A random split mixes bills of the same Congress (and of future Congresses) across train and test, so the baselines see the very legislators, coalitions and sponsor relationships they are tested on. We compare the random split's test bills of each Congress with the temporal (S3) test score of that same Congress, on the same bills (the S3 model scores the S5 test bills of Congress c too), so the optimism has a paired cluster-bootstrap CI. Calibration: optimism counts when its mean exceeds the section-wide minimum detectable effect D_MDE (0.01 Recall@20 / 0.01 AUROC, the smallest difference worth acting on; the cell first compares it with the data) and it is significant in at least 2 of 7 Congresses.

Why one fixed MDE. Earlier rounds used the median validation margin between the two best near-tie candidates as the MDE. That margin measures the spacing of our candidate grid (e.g. shrinkage 5 vs 20 pseudo-bills), not what matters in practice, and made almost every Task-2 pair "relevant". The cell prints that margin next to the MDE: when the grid margin is far below the MDE, validation is choosing among ties, which is harmless and is exactly what the regret tolerance (MDE / 2) allows. A positive gap confirms the random split overstates performance and must only be used as a leaky upper-bound reference.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D8, D13-D14. Same-Congress history: within-Congress split (S4) and the streaming protocol

A temporal GNN deployed during a Congress can see that Congress's cosponsorships up to the prediction time. S4 tests this on the last 20% of each Congress's bills. The streaming variants (S1a+stream, S1b+stream, S3+stream) keep the by-Congress pools but let the baselines also count every eval-Congress cosponsorship dated on or before introduced_date + t0 of the bill being scored (Task 2: eval-Congress bills whose 180-day label had resolved by the scored bill's introduction). This is leakage-free by construction and is how a temporal model would be used. If streaming adds a lot, the by-Congress split should be evaluated in streaming mode (and the cold-start problem from section B is largely an artefact of forbidding same-Congress history).

What this tests (from the notebook)

D9, D15. Are the test sets large enough for what the split is used for?

A split is used to compare models and protocols on the same test bills, so the relevant noise is that of the paired difference: Congress-level difficulty shifts move both models together and cancel. For each decision-relevant pair we compute, on every rolling test Congress, the paired difference and its cluster-bootstrap CI. Two different questions follow: (a) single-Congress risk: how often would ONE test Congress (S1a / S1b) fail to confirm the direction of a real difference? p_miss_1C = share of the 7 test Congresses whose paired CI does not exclude 0 in the direction of the mean (wrong sign or not significant); p_flip_1C = share with the opposite sign. More test Congresses do not reduce the Congress-to-Congress heterogeneity of an effect, so the deployment Congress can still differ: pi_next = 95% prediction half-width of the effect in a new Congress (t, 6 df). (b) average effect: the CI half-width of the mean effect over k = 1, 2, 7 test Congresses, 1.96 * max(sd_between, se_1C) / sqrt(k). A pair is relevant if |mean difference| >= D_MDE (0.01, the same MDE as every other check here); smaller differences are not worth acting on. The by_split verdict: a split holds if, for every relevant model / near-tie pair, its miss risk is <= 20% (80% power): empirical p_miss_1C for one test Congress, the normal approximation Phi(|mean| / (sd / sqrt(k)) - 1.96) for k = 2 (S1pool) and k = 7 (S2 / S3). Caveat: these are different quantities. The one-Congress risk includes Congress-to-Congress heterogeneity of the effect; the k-Congress risk is about the average effect, so multi-fold splits pass more easily by construction. The deployment-relevant risk, pi_next relative to the MDE (how far the effect can move in the next Congress), does not shrink with k; D9b records it for every by-Congress split, also from the recent folds 115-118 only (the early folds 112-115 are least like 119). Most of the gain from k = 7 reflects a narrower target (the average effect), not more certainty about any particular future Congress. Compare D9b.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D10. Do older Congresses help (expanding) or hurt (sliding window)?

If the process drifts, old Congresses can teach stale patterns and a sliding window (only the last 3 Congresses) can match or beat the expanding window. Both windows are scored on the same test bills, so the per-fold difference has a paired cluster-bootstrap CI. We run it for plain count baselines, for their recency-weighted versions (half-life 1 Congress), and for the graph-structural rw2hop (with and without recency weighting), and for the learned SVD embeddings (val-picked member, same hyperparameters in both windows). If only the unweighted models prefer the sliding window, the right conclusion is "weight recent edges", not "drop old Congresses". Folds share most training Congresses, so the sign test is descriptive. Positive values = expanding window is better.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D26. Regime-matched vs recency training weights

Section A finds the deployment Congress (119, unified Republican control) closest to the last Congresses with the same House / Senate majorities, and the majority-sponsor effect depends on which party controls the chamber. If that matters for prediction, "train on the most recent Congresses" (recency weighting, sliding windows) is the wrong remedy and training should upweight Congresses with the same regime as the target. The regime of a Congress is known when it starts (election results), so this is leakage-free. On every S3 test fold we refit on 108..c-1 with four weightings and score the same test bills: unweighted, recency (half-life 1 Congress), regime-matched (x2 for training Congresses with Congress c's House and Senate majorities, from majority_party()), and regime x recency. Task 1 uses sponsor_hist; Task 2 uses eb_rate_t0safe (prediction at introduction) and eb_rate. Positive paired differences = regime weighting helps. Folds with no regime-matched training Congress give 0.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D16. Task 2 sensitivity to information not available at prediction time

CRS assigns the policy area some days after introduction, so a Task 2 model scored at introduction often does not have it. eb_rate_t0safe hides the policy area for the share of bills that lack it when fresh (measured on the in-progress 119th Congress). If the score drops noticeably, the Task 2 feature set must be built "as of" the prediction time, otherwise every split overstates performance.

Interpretation

Hiding the policy area when it would not yet be assigned at introduction costs eb_rate 0.05-0.15 AUROC per Congress (mean 0.10). The largest drops are in 112 (0.155) and 116-117 (0.119, 0.133). Measured as discrimination above chance, eb_rate has 0.724 - 0.5 = 0.224 and eb_rate_t0safe keeps 0.624 - 0.5 = 0.124, so about 45% of eb_rate's signal (0.10 of 0.22) depends on the policy area, ranging from about 24% (114) to 69% (117) per Congress. This counts as leakage only if Task 2 is scored at introduction, which the notebook adopts as an assumption; the task definition (reported within 180 days) does not fix the prediction time. Under that assumption a policy-area feature would leak future information under every split.

Caveats.

The share of bills without a policy area comes from 56 recent bills and is applied uniformly. A model that predicts the policy area from bill text would recover some of the gap.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D18. Does the candidate pool definition matter?

Task 1 ranks the point-in-time pool (members in office in the month of introduction + t0). The legacy pool (everyone who served in the chamber at any time that Congress) also contains departed and not-yet-seated members, which inflates the negatives. We rerun the S3 test folds with the legacy pool to see whether scores or the ordering of baselines depend on that choice.

Switching from the legacy pool (everyone who served that Congress) to the point-in-time pool raises Recall@20 by only about +0.002 for all baselines, and their ordering does not change. The candidate-pool definition is not a material source of evaluation bias.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D19. Refit on train + validation, or keep the validation-selected model?

Test units "select on val, refit on train + val". A GNN chooses its epoch count by early stopping on val, and the refit has no val left to stop on, so the refit must reuse a fixed budget (the epoch or hyperparameter value chosen on val). For each S3 fold we compare the test score of the val-selected family member without refit (fit on 108..c-2) and with refit (same member, fit on 108..c-1). If refitting does not help, keeping the val-selected checkpoint (and its early-stopping signal) loses nothing; if it helps, refit with the val-chosen budget.

What this tests (from the notebook)

D27. A locked final test: develop on folds 112-117, report once on 118

In S3 / S2 every test Congress 112-117 is also the validation Congress of the next fold, and D9 recommends comparing models on the mean over rolling test folds. If the team compares GNN architectures or feature sets on that mean and then reports it, the reported number was chosen on test data. The fix is a locked test: develop, tune and compare on the rolling folds 112-117 only (hyperparameters on each fold's val Congress, architectures on the mean over the 6 development folds or on the mean of their val Congresses, D17), then freeze the pipeline (features, model, val-chosen epochs), refit on 108-117 and score Congress 118 once. Congress 119 is the prospective test once its windows close. This cell measures what reserving 118 costs: whether the selection checks still pass on 6 folds, how much the miss risk (D9) and the level CI (D15) grow from k = 7 to k = 6, and whether the development folds predict the locked fold (118 inside the development prediction interval). In the chart each row is a relevant model pair: grey dots = development folds, band = 95% prediction interval for a new Congress from those folds, orange dot = the locked fold 118 with its paired CI.

Interpretation

Reserving 118 as a locked test costs little overall, with one Task 2 exception. Every selection check still passes on the 6 development folds 112-117. Task 1 regrets stay small, and the policy-area eb_rate regret drops from 0.0078 to 0.0017 once fold 118 is left out. But the deployable at-introduction family eb_rate_t0safe (the one D12b judges) rises from 0.0045 to 0.0053, above the 0.005 tolerance; it passes only because no fold is individually significant, and with hit rate 0.29 and tau 0.24 validation is weak at choosing among t0-safe variants. The maximum paired miss risk rises from 0.033 to 0.115, under the 0.20 bar, and the median CI half-width of mean differences grows only from 0.0076 to 0.0080. The development folds predict 118 reasonably well: 8 of 9 relevant paired differences fall inside the development prediction interval. sponsor_hist's absolute level on 118 (0.2439) falls just below its interval (mean 0.2617 ± 0.0172), so 118 is marginally harder than the development Congresses. D27 passes, and the notebook's final protocol is: develop on S3(+stream) folds 112-117, lock 118, treat 119 as prospective.

Caveats.

The 118 levels for the SVD and both Task 2 models fall inside their prediction intervals. Those intervals are wide (Task 2 at-introduction ±0.135), so 'inside' is a weak test. The 0.0053 vs 0.005 exceedance is small and the selection regret is biased upward (test-best is chosen on test), but it is the quantity the protocol will actually face.

Each row shows a relevant pair's 6 development-fold differences, the 95% prediction interval for a new Congress, and the locked 118 value with its paired CI. Task 1 pairs are tight and 118 lands within their bands: svd - sponsor_hist +0.024, sponsor_hist - party+pop +0.067, svd_r32 - svd_r128 -0.014. Streaming's gain on 118 (+0.053) lies just above its interval (upper bound 0.0525), so same-Congress history mattered more in 118. The Task 2 pair eb_rate_t0safe - chamber_maj averages +0.023 on the development folds but only +0.004 on 118, with a CI that crosses zero (-0.009 to +0.015). One locked Congress cannot confirm that small Task 2 advantage, as D9 predicted.

Caveats.

The majority-feature pair's prediction interval (-0.094 to +0.256) is wide enough that almost any 118 value would 'fit'. Coverage is informative only for the tight Task 1 pairs.

One line per check. FAIL does not automatically rule out a split: read the detail for the implication (e.g. report the mean over rolling folds instead of a single test Congress).

Interpretation

The summary has 3 FAILs, and none of them rules out the recommended protocol. D7 condemns only the random split S5. D9 fails every split with a single test Congress or 2 pooled ones (S1a, S1b, their streaming versions, S1pool), not S2 or S3. D2b says the at-introduction Task 2 AUROC level shifts between consecutive Congresses, which is a reporting constraint, not a selection problem. All selection, calibration (Task 1), refit, window, regime and locked-test checks pass.

Caveats.

With 18 verdict checks and no multiplicity correction, individual borderline verdicts (D12, D12b on dev folds, S1a+stream calibration) are fragile. The consistent patterns across 7 folds are the robust evidence.

Open questions

  • Will a GNN's validation choices (epochs, depth, embedding size) transfer as well as the SVD's? The SVD has no training dynamics, so D22/D23 are only a lower bar for a model with message passing and early stopping. Does any learned model beat recency-weighted counts at all? The notebook never runs svd_hl1 vs sh_hl1 directly.

  • How much of the Task 2 drop in 116-117 is regime-driven? The value of the sponsor-majority feature flips sign there, and its prediction interval for a new Congress is 15 times the MDE. Count-based regime weighting does not fix it, so whether a GNN with majority-status features can is untested.

  • Is Congress 118 representative of 119? 118 is marginally harder than the development folds for sponsor_hist, and the Task 2 at-introduction advantage almost vanishes there. One locked Congress cannot separate a real trend from noise.

  • The at-introduction policy-area missingness (86%) comes from 56 bills of an unfinished Congress. Historical CRS lag may differ, which would change the size of the Task 2 leakage correction.

Decision: which split to use

Use rolling-origin, by-Congress folds with an expanding training window (S3): validate on c-1, test on c, develop GNNs on test Congresses 112-117, keep 118 as a test you score once, and for Task 1 give the model the evaluation Congress's own edges dated up to introduction + t0 ('+stream'). For Task 1 every non-rolling split fails a validity check and the stream gain is large and consistent. For Task 2 the non-rolling splits are rejected on weaker grounds, and whether to stream and whether S3 beats the 3-Congress sliding window (S2) are unresolved: both differences sit on the minimum detectable effect and flip depending on whether 118 is included.

This section combines the 100 de-duplicated checks from Sections A-D and turns them into a split choice with explicit rules. The key design choice is how each kind of check is used. Only validity checks (leakage, whether validation predicts test, test-set size, censoring) can rule a split out. Drift checks (later Congresses differ from earlier ones) select remedies instead. Requirements are construction rules that every split must follow. At the registry level there are 19 validity checks: 15 PASS, 2 FAIL, 2 INFO. The two failures are D7 (a random bill split inflates Task-1 Recall@20 by 0.0745) and D9 (one test Congress is too small to settle model comparisons near the minimum detectable effect, MDE = 0.01). Three checks pass overall but fail for particular splits: C5 fails for the within-Congress split S4, and D1 and D20 fail for the pooled-test split S1pool. The scorecard uses these per-split verdicts.

What gets rejected, by task. Task 1: every non-rolling split has at least one validity FAIL. S1a and S1b (and their +stream variants) fail D9, S4 fails C5, S5 fails D7, and S1pool fails D1, D20 and D9. The notebook labels this rule (R1-T1) robust. Task 2: the evidence is weaker. The single-Congress splits and S1pool are dropped only through D9, and R1-T2 is labelled borderline. S4 and S5 have zero Task-2 validity failures. They are excluded because too few checks judged them (1 and 0) and because of unclassified failures: C6b for S4 (80.8% of its test bills are censored for Task 2) and C19/C20 for S5 (45.2% of evaluation bills have a later twin bill in training).

What the data shows (sponsor_hist and eb_rate_t0safe baselines, not GNNs). Under S3, the validation Congress tracks the test Congress for Task 1: the mean |val-test| gap is 0.61x the test 95% CI half-width, and validation picks the test-best model within families of close candidates (D11, D17, D21, D23 pass). Adding the evaluation Congress's edges dated up to introduction + t0 (+stream) raises Task-1 Recall@20 from 0.259 to 0.296. The direction is consistent in 7/7 paired folds (+0.026 to +0.053, mean +0.037, 3.7x the MDE), and the two largest gains are in the two most recent Congresses (+0.046 at 117, +0.053 at 118). An exact sign test would give p ~ 0.016, but the expanding windows share almost all of their training data, so the notebook treats sign tests across these folds as descriptive (D10 text). For Task 2, validation picks the right model (D12, D12b, D17 pass) but not the right level. Test AUROC falls from a mean of 0.655 (Congresses 112-115) to 0.583 (116-118), and the gap/half-width ratio is 1.28 (D2b FAIL).

Disclosure: 118 has already been looked at. Every backtest number quoted here (0.296, 0.259, 0.61x, 1.28x, the 7/7 folds, 0.583) comes from 7 folds that include 118. So 118's labels were used, at the baseline level, to choose the protocol, and 118 is not untouched for that decision. 'Locked' therefore applies to GNN development from now on. The partial mitigation is D27: on the 6 folds 112-117, within-family selection regret stays within tolerance for every family (e.g. T1 sponsor_hist 0.0032, T2 eb_rate_t0safe 0.0053; tolerance MDE/2). D27 does not re-run the split ranking or the stream and window comparisons. Recomputing those from the per-fold chart data on 112-117: the Task-1 conclusions hold (stream gain +0.034, 6/6 folds positive; S3 minus S2 = -0.012, 0/6 folds favour S3). The Task-2 conclusions do not: the stream gain moves from +0.008 (7 folds) to +0.011 (6 folds), and S3 minus S2 from -0.009 to -0.011, so both cross the 0.01 MDE that R3-T2 and R5-T2 use. The level is about the same (S3 Task 1 0.2617 on 6 folds vs 0.2591 on 7; Task 2 0.6244 vs 0.6236), and the largest miss risk for a relevant model pair rises from 0.033 to 0.115, still below the 0.20 limit. One warning sign: for sponsor_hist, 118 (0.2439) falls outside the prediction interval derived from the development folds (D27 in_pi = False), and it is the lowest plain-S3 Task-1 fold. It is a level outlier for this one baseline only: the 118 levels of the other three models (svd, eb_rate_t0safe, eb_rate) fall inside the development interval, and so do 8/9 relevant paired differences.

What is inferred, not tested. (1) The model-selection checks were never run on S3+stream for either task, so 'validation picks the best model under streaming' is carried over from plain S3. (2) S3 beats S2 only through R4b, a regime-coverage tie-break. Without recency weighting S2 is better on Task 1 (S3 minus S2 = -0.0124; sliding is significantly better in 6 of 7 folds). With a one-Congress half-life the two are equal (-0.0008). On Task 2 the notebook calls them equivalent (-0.0087, within the MDE), but on 112-117 the difference is -0.0106. Either way it is driven by one fold (c=112: -0.058; the other folds lie between -0.008 and +0.002), so 'equivalent' is better read as 'unresolved'. (3) The robust/borderline labels count checks that reuse the same 7 folds, so treat 'robust' as 'consistent', not 'replicated'.

Bottom line. - Task 1: S3 folds (train 108..c-2, validate c-1, refit on 108..c-1, test c) with +stream time-filtered neighbour sampling. Compare GNNs on the paired mean over 112-117, and score 118 once at the end. - Task 2: use the same S3 folds. The notebook's rule-based pick is plain S3, but the data do not clearly favour plain S3 over +stream. The stream gain is +0.0077 on 7 folds and +0.0114 on 112-117, i.e. on the MDE boundary. Its sign is mixed (4 of 7 folds positive, per-fold SD 0.022), and one fold dominates (+0.051 at 112; without it the 6-fold mean is about +0.001). Selection reliability under streaming is untested, and level transfer is worse (gap ratio 1.64x vs 1.28x). Report plain-S3 and +stream Task-2 AUROC side by side, and treat the S3-vs-S2 choice for Task 2 as open too. - Use the expanding window only with a recency weight tuned on validation. Without one, S2 is equally defensible. Report per-Congress scores and the fold mean, never a single Congress.

Implications for the split

  • Development protocol (both tasks): rolling-origin by-Congress folds (S3). For each test Congress c in 112-117, train on 108..c-2, tune and early-stop on c-1, refit on 108..c-1, and score c. Then freeze the pipeline, refit on 108-117 and score 118 once. 118 was already used for the baseline-level protocol choice. D27 shows within-family selection regret stays within tolerance without it, but it does not re-run the split ranking; recomputed on 112-117, the Task-1 choices hold while the Task-2 stream and window verdicts become borderline. So 'locked' means locked against GNN tuning from now on. Use 119 only as a prospective check.

  • Task 1: give the GNN the evaluation Congress's own edges dated up to introduction + t0 (+stream; time-filtered neighbour sampling in PyG), never the final graph. On a count baseline this adds +0.037 Recall@20 (7/7 folds; +0.034 over 112-117), and it cuts cold-start positives from up to about 20% to at most 0.7%.

  • Task 2: use the same S3 folds, but do not treat plain S3 as clearly better than +stream. The stream gain is +0.0077 on 7 folds and +0.0114 on 112-117 (on the MDE boundary, 4/7 folds positive, driven by +0.051 at 112), selection is untested under streaming, and the val-test gap ratio is 1.64x vs 1.28x. Report plain-S3 and +stream Task-2 AUROC in parallel, and also keep S2 as a Task-2 comparison (S3 minus S2 = -0.0087 on 7 folds, -0.0106 on 6, driven by c=112).

  • Use an expanding window only with a recency weight or edge-time decay whose half-life is tuned on validation. Unweighted, the sliding window S2 is 0.0124 Recall@20 better, significantly in 6 of 7 folds (popularity loses 0.0202). The recommended combination (S3 + stream + recency weighting) has never been evaluated, so check it on the development folds before committing. Without decay, S2 (+stream) is equally defensible.

  • Build legislator nodes inductively (party as of the Congress, chamber, state, committees, tenure, majority and sponsor-in-majority flags). Do not rely on per-node ID embeddings learned only from training Congresses.

  • Compare architectures on the paired mean over the 6 development folds 112-117 (same bills), not on one Congress. D9 shows a single test Congress cannot settle differences near the MDE (0.01), and D27 shows 6 folds keep the largest miss risk at 0.115.

  • Reject random bill splits (D7: +0.0745 optimism; C20: 45.2% of evaluation bills have a later twin in training) and within-Congress splits (C5 for Task 1; C6b: 80.8% of Task-2 test bills censored). Use single-Congress splits such as S1a/S1b for debugging only.

Detailed results

What this tests (from the notebook)

Sections A-D each tested one family of conditions a split relies on and recorded every result in the shared check registry (CHECKS) and, for D, in the backtest table SPLIT_RESULTS. This section reads only those two objects: nothing below is hardcoded, so if you change a threshold or rerun on new data, the tables, scores and the recommendation update with it.

How checks are used. Every check has a kind. Validity checks ask whether a split gives an honest, usable estimate (leakage, val predicts test, enough test Congresses, censoring): a FAIL is a reason to prefer a different split, and only these rank the splits. Drift checks ask whether later Congresses differ from earlier ones: every forward split fails them by design (that is the split doing its job), so a drift FAIL selects a remedy (recalibration, recency weighting, per-Congress reporting), not a different split. Requirements are construction rules every split must follow (time-filter edges, rebuild features as of t0); they never count as split failures. A few split-dependent checks have no kind ("unclassified"); they are not used for the main ranking, but the recommendation is re-run with them included as a robustness test.

Interpretation

The registry has 102 checks, which become 100 after removing duplicates (C4 duplicates A3, and B5b duplicates another check). The non-requirement checks break down into 10 drift FAILs (A: 7, B: 1, C: 1, D: 1), 19 validity checks (15 PASS, 2 FAIL, 2 INFO; 17 of them in D), 3 unclassified FAILs (C6b, C20, C23b) and 11 construction requirements. The registry-level validity FAILs are only D7 and D9. C5, D1 and D20 are PASS in the registry but carry split-specific FAILs (C5 for S4, D1 and D20 for S1pool), and the scorecard uses those per-split verdicts. Section A contains only drift checks. 7 of its 26 FAIL (A1b, A2, A3, A4, A8, A13, A17), so base rates and bill volume really do move: A3 (cosponsor density) has a standardized deviation of -5.2 relative to the training spread (well beyond the 95% t prediction bound), and A8 (bill volume) has one of +4.5 (also well beyond it). Sections A, B and C mainly supply remedies and construction rules: time-filter edges (B10: for evaluation bills of 116-118, on average 52% of the evaluation Congress's final cosponsor graph does not exist yet at t0=0), filter related-bill links (B6b: 42.7% point to later bills), and build training inputs as of t0 (B12, binding).

Caveats.

The A-section prediction-interval checks (e.g. A1, A3, A8) FAIL only if at least one test survives a Holm correction within the check. Other drift checks use different rules: A17 uses a Poisson-binomial test on the number of failing clusters, B2 a fixed bound, D2b a cluster-bootstrap gap. So 'corrected for multiplicity' holds only for the A-section interval checks, and even there only within a check, not across the registry. Across 100 checks a few false FAILs/PASSes are expected. Many checks reuse the same 11 Congresses (108-118), so verdicts are correlated and the counts are not independent votes. The 'metric' column mixes units (z-scores, shares, regret).

decision-c145-o0
Interpretation

The stacked bars show the counts from the table above, by section and kind. Validity evidence sits almost entirely in Section D: 17 of the 19 validity checks (13 PASS, 2 FAIL, 2 INFO), against 1 each in B (B1b) and C (C5). Drift FAILs come mostly from Section A (7 of 10). So the split choice rests on backtests of simple baselines, while the distribution audits mainly show that the data is non-stationary and needs remedies. Unclassified INFO checks are common in C and D (7 and 8). They describe the data but decide nothing.

Caveats.

Bar length counts checks, not evidence weight. A single check such as D9 can involve many paired comparisons across folds, while others are a single threshold test. Requirement 'FAIL' (B6b, B12) means a construction rule is binding, not that any split is invalid.

What this tests (from the notebook)

Split scorecard: what supports and what undermines each candidate

For every candidate split (the five base splits plus D's protocol variants) the scorecard combines (1) the validity checks that judged it (passes support the split, fails undermine it), (2) the unclassified split-dependent checks (shown separately), (3) how many drift checks it exposes, and (4) the backtest in SPLIT_RESULTS: for each task the baseline that validation would pick (best mean val score, as a modeler would choose), its mean val and test score, the mean |val - test| gap per fold relative to the test score's own 95% CI half-width (ratio < 1 = the gap is within sampling noise), the fold-to-fold standard deviation of the test score, and the number of test bills. Task 2 uses only baselines available at introduction (no policy area, per requirement C18 and the D16 drop). The SPLIT_RESULTS baselines are all unweighted (every training Congress counts the same). Section D also scored recency-weighted family members (e.g. sh_hl1, half-life 1 Congress) in D_FAMILY_RESULTS, but only for S2 and S3. The *_rw columns repeat the val pick with those members added, so S2 and S3 can be compared on a model that is allowed to down-weight old Congresses; - means "not evaluated". How to read it: a usable split has 0 validity fails with many checks judged; a split judged by few checks has not "passed", it was simply not tested. Splits with 1 test fold have no fold variability.

Interpretation

The scorecard shows that only the rolling families S2, S3 and S3+stream combine zero validity failures with 7 folds and 30,203 Task-1 test bills. For Task 1, S1a and S1b fail D9, S4 fails C5, S5 fails D7, and S1pool fails D1, D20 and D9. Task-1 val-test gaps stay within sampling noise on every rolling split (gap/half-width 0.66 for S2, 0.61 for S3, 0.51 for S3+stream; fold SDs 0.010, 0.009, 0.006). For Task 2 the ratio is above 1 on every rolling split (1.28 for S2 and S3, 1.64 for S3+stream). Under forward by-Congress evaluation with the at-introduction baseline, validation therefore does not predict the next Congress's AUROC level. That conclusion does not extend to S4 (0.865) or S5 (0.615), whose ratios are below 1 but which are rejected on other grounds. S5's higher Task-1 score (0.332) is consistent with leakage: D7 measures +0.0745 optimism over S3, and C20 finds 45.2% of evaluation bills have a later twin in training (C19/C20 fail for S5 only). Neither check isolates how much of the optimism the twins cause. With recency weighting (sh_hl1, one-Congress half-life) S2 and S3 score 0.283 and 0.282 on Task 1, against 0.272 and 0.259 unweighted.

Caveats.

15 split-dependent checks are unclassified and left out of the main ranking (the robustness re-run includes them and the picks do not change). 'val_judged' partly measures effort: D11, D12, D17, D21 and D27 were run only on S2/S3 (D27 also covers S3+stream), and D22/D23 only on S3, so S3's 13 vs S2's 11 judged checks is not a quality gap. S4's Task-1 score (0.311, 2,331 bills) comes from a later slice of each Congress that is heavily censored for Task 2 (C6b: 80.8%). S1pool (0.222) is below both of its components scored separately (0.2615 for 117 under S1a; 0.2439 for 118 with sponsor_hist refit on 108-117, which is the S3 c=118 fold; S1b's own validation pick, rw2hop, scores 0.2450). If S1pool scores 118 with the same 108-116 model that S1a uses for 117, and the pooled value is a bill-weighted mean (5,101 + 5,138 = 10,239 bills), then 118 under the stale model scores about 0.18, against 0.244 after refitting on 108-117. That is a sizable one-Congress staleness penalty, and it argues for refitting every Congress, as S3 does. This is an inference from the table, not a separately reported number.

Caveats.

decision-c149-o0
Interpretation

For Task 1 the rolling-family points sit in a narrow band. S3 test Recall@20 is 0.244-0.272 across Congresses 112-118, S3+stream is 0.288-0.307, and each validation point is close to its test point (S3 per-fold |val-test| 0.002-0.018). The +stream band lies entirely above the plain band. Per-fold gains are +0.026 to +0.053 (mean 0.037 over 7 folds, 0.034 over 112-117), and the largest gains are at 117 and 118. For Task 2, S3 test AUROC for eb_rate_t0safe falls from 0.628-0.668 (112-115) to 0.560-0.619 (116-118), and per-fold |val-test| gaps reach 0.09 (c=116). So validation is a poor guide to the AUROC level, even though D12/D12b show it still ranks models correctly. Under S3 the validation score of fold c equals the test score of fold c-1 (same Congress, same training window), so D1 is in effect a lag-1 stability test of per-Congress scores. Under +stream, Task-2 per-fold differences are mixed in sign: lower at 113, 117 (0.548 vs 0.560) and 118, higher at the other folds. The mean is +0.0077 over 7 folds and +0.0114 over 112-117 (my per-fold computation on the chart data). The 6-fold value crosses the 0.01 MDE, but almost all of it comes from +0.051 at 112. Without that fold the mean is about +0.001, and the per-fold SD is 0.022, so the Task-2 stream question is unresolved rather than 'no gain'. The same holds for S3 minus S2 on Task 2 (-0.0087 on 7 folds, -0.0106 on 6): it is driven by -0.058 at 112, and the other folds lie between -0.008 and +0.002.

Caveats.

The 7 folds are not independent: the expanding windows overlap almost completely, and adjacent Congresses share members and political context. Fold SDs (0.009 for T1 and 0.045 for T2 under S3) probably understate uncertainty about a future Congress. The Task-2 downturn starting at 116 has two candidate explanations, neither tested: the limits of a weak at-introduction baseline (AUROC around 0.62), and the regime flip at 116 (to DH/RS). Policy-area masking (D16: 0.10 AUROC drop) lowers the overall Task-2 level, but it applies to every fold, so it cannot explain the timing of the drop. All per-fold numbers include 118, which has already informed this analysis.

What this tests (from the notebook)

Recommendation: explicit rules applied to the recorded checks

The recommendation is a short chain of rules. Each rule names the checks it reads, prints the values it used and its verdict, and says what it implies. A conclusion is labelled robust when at least two independent checks support it and none contradicts it (and no section disagrees on that quantity); otherwise it is borderline and the printout says what to watch. The split ranking is computed per task (checks are assigned to Task 1, Task 2 or both from their wording) and is re-run with the unclassified checks included. A pick is labelled ROBUST only if (a) both runs pick the same split, (b) the criterion that separates it from the runner-up comes from rules that are all robust, and (c) its model-selection checks were run on that split itself rather than inherited from its base split.

Rule Question If it fails
R1 Any validity FAIL for the split (leakage, val does not predict test, too few test Congresses, censoring)? drop the split for model selection
R2 Cold start: share of eval positives from legislators unseen in train (B1) vs with in-Congress history (B1b/B1c) inductive features and/or the +stream protocol
R3 Does streaming eval-Congress history up to t0 change scores (D13, SPLIT_RESULTS) and keep val honest (D14)? evaluate a temporal GNN with +stream
R4 Party regimes: do they change the effects (A5b, D26, C23b)? evaluate per regime
R4b Does the split drop the eval Congress's regime from training (C8), and does that matter given R4? prefer a window that keeps every regime
R5 Expanding vs sliding window, with and without recency weighting (D10, SPLIT_RESULTS, D_FAMILY_RESULTS, A14) sliding window, or expanding + recency weights
R6 Val predicts test level and model choice (D1, D20, D14, D2b, D11/D12/D12b/D21/D23/D17), per split actually tested report per-Congress scores; flag inferred evidence
R7 Fold stability and test size (D3, D4, D9, D27) use several rolling test folds; lock the last Congress
R8 Drift FAILs exposed by the chosen split remedies (below), not a different split

Interpretation

The rule chain is the core of the decision. R1-T1 removes S1a, S1b, S4, S5, S1pool and the S1 +stream variants for Task 1 (robust). R1-T2 removes only the single-Congress splits and S1pool, via D9 alone (borderline). S4 and S5 are not removed by R1 for Task 2. R2/R3-T1 are robust: without in-Congress history, up to 18-20% of positives in the forward splits (maximum over evaluation Congresses) come from legislators unseen in training (31.4% for S1pool). With +stream this is at most 0.7% (B1b), and Task-1 Recall@20 rises by +0.037, 3.7x the MDE, so the model must be inductive and time-aware. R3-T2 finds no material streaming gain for Task 2 (+0.0077 < MDE; borderline), and its 'keep it for consistency' is a convenience suggestion. That verdict depends on 118: over 112-117 the gain is +0.0114, above the MDE, so by the notebook's own rule it would reverse. R4 finds regime effects stable given chamber-majority features (A5b, D26 pass), which is why R4b's penalty on S2 is only a tie-break. R5 is the key conditional result: unweighted, the expanding window loses 0.0124 Recall@20 to the sliding window (beyond the MDE/2 = 0.005 tolerance; -0.0117 on 112-117), and with recency weighting only 0.0008. R5-T2's 'equivalent within the MDE' (-0.0087) also depends on 118: on 112-117 it is -0.0106. R6-T2 and R7 settle reporting: select on validation, report per-Congress results and the fold mean, and lock 118.

Caveats.

'Robust' requires at least two supporting checks and none contradicting. Several supporting checks (D1, D20, D22, D11, D21, D23) share the same S3 folds and baselines, so they corroborate rather than replicate. R5's A14 proxy (0.643 favours sliding) is distributional, not a score comparison. R3-T1 sizes the stream gain for a count baseline (sponsor_hist). A GNN may gain more or less. R7's 'lock 118' was decided with statistics that already include 118 (see the overview). D27 shows only that within-family selection regret stays within tolerance on 112-117. It does not re-run the split ranking, R3 or R5. Recomputed on 112-117, the Task-1 rules hold, but the Task-2 stream and window verdicts sit on the MDE boundary, with mixed signs and single-fold dominance, so they are unresolved rather than settled.

Interpretation

For Task 1, three splits are usable under both the main and the robustness ranking: S3+stream, S3 and S2. S3+stream ranks first only because it matches the deployment protocol (protocol_mismatch 0 vs 1). That criterion is legitimate, because at prediction time the evaluation Congress's earlier edges are known. But it is a choice about information availability, not about score, and its sel_checks count is 0 (inferred = 1). For Task 2 the notebook's pick is plain S3. S3 and S2 tie on failures (0) and judged checks (6), S3 wins only on the R4b penalty, and S2's test AUROC is numerically higher (0.632 vs 0.624 on 7 folds; 0.635 vs 0.624 on 112-117, which is just beyond the MDE). S3+stream ranks third for Task 2 with 4 judged checks and protocol 'stream (not needed)'. S4 and S5 have 0 failures but are 'too little evidence' (1 and 0 judged checks), with unclassified fails C6b and C19/C20. The final printout's 'one pipeline' line extends S3+stream to Task 2 for consistency and notes that Task-2 selection checks (D12/D12b/D17) were not run on S3+stream.

Caveats.

The ranking is lexicographic (failures, evidence, protocol, penalties), so small changes in how checks are classified could reorder S2 and S3. The 'test' column is not a ranking criterion, and rightly so: ranking by test score would reward the most optimistic protocol (S5). Task 2's 74,609 test bills give tight per-fold estimates, but the between-fold SD (0.045) dominates. D15 implies about 13 test Congresses would be needed for a precise absolute Task-2 level.

What this tests (from the notebook)

Practical guidance for the GNN

Read this together with the RECOMMENDATION printout above; the guidance assumes its rules came out the way they do in the current run (re-check if a rerun flips a verdict).

  • Folds. Develop on rolling-origin folds: for each development test Congress c, train on 108..c-2, tune and early-stop on c-1, refit on 108..c-1 with the tuned hyperparameters, and score c. Compare architectures on the mean over the development folds (paired, same bills), never on one Congress. Keep the last complete Congress (D_FINAL_PROTOCOL['locked_test']) as a locked test you score once, and treat the in-progress 119th as a prospective check only. A single by-Congress split (train 108-115 / val 116 / test 117 or 118) is fine for quick debugging, but R7/D9 show one test Congress cannot settle close model comparisons.
  • Inductive, not purely transductive. Many eval positives come from legislators absent from the training Congresses (R2). Give legislator nodes inductive features (party as of the Congress, chamber, state, committee seats, tenure, majority status) and do not depend on per-node ID embeddings learned only from the training Congresses. GraphSAGE-style aggregation or a heterogeneous GNN with feature encoders fits; a lookup-table embedding model does not.
  • Time-filtered neighbor sampling (the +stream protocol). For a bill scored at t0, the graph may contain every edge dated <= introduced_date + t0: earlier Congresses plus the eval Congress's own sponsorships and cosponsorships so far. Never use the eval Congress's final graph (B10), committee edges recorded after t0 (B7), related-bill links not yet known (B6b), or snapshot count fields (C11). Build training examples the same way, from as-of-t0 snapshots (B12), so train and eval inputs match.
  • Window and weighting (conditional). The expanding window is only as good as the sliding one if the model down-weights old Congresses (R5/D10). With unweighted count or graph features, the last-3- Congress sliding window (S2) scores as well or better. So: if you use an expanding window, add a recency weight or edge-time decay and choose its half-life on validation. If you do not, S2 is a legitimate choice. The remaining arguments for the expanding window are weak (R4b: S2 leaves the eval Congress's party regime out of training, but regime effects look stable, A5b/D26) or about evidence (more checks were run on S3). Add chamber-majority / sponsor-in-majority features rather than regime-specific weighting (R4/D26).
  • Model selection under streaming. The selection checks (D11/D17/D21/D23) were run on plain S3 folds, not on S3+stream. Until they are rerun under streaming, treat "val picks the test-best model" for the streaming protocol as inferred, not tested. D14 only shows that the score level carries over.
  • Task 2. Pick models on validation (rankings transfer, D12/D12b). The AUROC level does not carry over from one Congress to the next (D2b), so report per-Congress AUROC plus the fold mean, and never quote a val AUROC as the expected test level. AUROC does not change under monotone recalibration, so recalibrating cannot fix this. If you need calibrated probabilities, recalibrate on the eval Congress's already-resolved bills (labels are known 180 days after introduction), not on Congress c-1. Hide the policy area for bills younger than its availability lag (C18/C25). Task 2 can share Task 1's folds.
  • Monitor. Every quantity in the "Monitor" line drifts between Congresses. Rerun this notebook when a Congress completes. If a validity check the choice relies on flips, the ranking changes automatically.

Open questions

  • Does validation still pick the test-best model under streaming? Neither the Task-1 checks (D11/D17/D21/D23) nor the Task-2 checks (D12/D12b/D17) were run on S3+stream folds, so this is inferred from plain S3 for both tasks.

  • How do S2+stream and recency-weighted +stream baselines compare with S3+stream? Neither was evaluated, so it is unknown whether the stream gain and the recency gain add up or overlap.

  • Is the Task-2 AUROC drop after Congress 115 (0.655 to 0.583 in fold means) real drift, a regime effect, or a limitation of the weak at-introduction baseline? With 7 dependent folds, and D15 implying about 13 Congresses for a precise level, the data cannot separate these.

  • Is 118 an unusual Congress? For sponsor_hist its level falls outside the development prediction interval (D27), but it is a level outlier for one baseline only: the other three models' 118 levels, and 8/9 relevant paired differences, fall inside the interval. Its labels already informed this analysis, and including or excluding it flips the Task-2 stream and S3-vs-S2 verdicts across the MDE. A clean, fully held-out confirmation must wait for 119.

Recommended train / validation / test split

Use rolling-origin, by-Congress folds with an expanding training window and graphs built strictly as of each bill's prediction time. The window is recency-weighted: validated for Task 1, and a tuned choice still to be checked for Task 2. Develop and compare models on test Congresses 112-117 (train 108..c-2, validate c-1, refit 108..c-1, test c), score Congress 118 once as the locked final test, and check on 119 prospectively.

Think of it as replaying history one Congress at a time. To test on, say, the 115th Congress, the model learns from Congresses 108-113, has its settings tuned on 114, is retrained on 108-114 with those settings, and is then scored on 115. Repeating this for every Congress from 112 to 117 gives six honest 'next Congress' forecasts. When predicting who will cosponsor a bill, the model may use everything that had happened by that moment, including earlier cosponsorships in the same Congress. For the committee-report task, the main version uses only earlier Congresses plus the bill's own sponsor, committees and early cosponsors. Nothing dated later is ever used. Older Congresses are kept but down-weighted, so recent behaviour counts more. For the GNN, the oldest Congress (108) serves only as background history, never as a training example, because a bill from 108 has no earlier Congresses to learn from. The simple baselines stay as in the notebook (fit on 108..c-1), so the bars the GNN must beat do not change.

Models are compared on all six forecasts together, because one Congress is too noisy: for a real Task-2 difference, a single Congress failed to confirm it in 3 of the 7 Congresses tried. Even six Congresses only resolve fairly large differences: roughly 0.012-0.015 for Task 1, and 0.017-0.036 AUROC for Task 2 (more for pairs whose gap swings a lot), because Task-2 results swing more between Congresses. So a model 'wins' only if its advantage holds up consistently across the six Congresses under a formal test. Otherwise it is a tie and the simpler model is kept. Each Congress's result is shown, not just the average. When the design is final, the frozen recipe is run once on Congress 118 and that is the headline number. Congress 119, still in progress, is a true out-of-sample check, compared like-for-like on bills introduced early in a Congress. The alternatives fail in concrete ways. The random split peeks at the future. The within-Congress split loses most Task-2 labels to censoring. A single test Congress is too imprecise. A short sliding window is no better for Task 1 once old data is down-weighted.
