Per task

Cosponsor prediction (Task 1)

Rolling-origin S3 folds with +stream (the evaluation Congress's edges dated <= introduced_date + t0 in message passing, via temporal neighbour sampling) and a recency half-life tuned on validation. Tune and early-stop on c-1, refit on 108..c-1, test on c for c = 112..117, then score 118 once. Single-Congress splits do not fail a validity check for Task 1 (D9 passes on Task-1 pairs, worst miss 1 of 7). The case for rolling folds is precision and representativeness: one Congress cannot resolve near-MDE choices, and 118 is off-distribution in density and timing. The stream gain is +0.037 Recall@20 in 7/7 folds (+0.034 on 112-117). Validation predicts the score level under streaming (D14) and picks near-best models on plain S3 (D11, D21, D23); selection under streaming still has to be checked. The legislator encoder must be inductive. The target bill's sponsor and cosponsors with lag in [0, t0] are inputs at both t0 = 0 and t0 = 7, and they are removed from the ranked candidates. Labels are cosponsors with lag in (t0, t0+30].

Reporting:

Recall@K (K = 20 primary, plus other K) and NDCG, for t0 = 0 and t0 = 7 separately. Give per-Congress scores for 112-117, their paired mean with a t(5) or two-stage-bootstrap interval, and the locked 118 score separately. Compare against random, popularity, party+popularity, and count baselines run under the same S3+stream protocol: at least sponsor_hist 0.296 (t0 = 0) / 0.275 (t0 = 7) and rw2hop 0.295, plus recency-weighted sponsor history and the learned SVD once run with streaming. 118 has about 40% lower positive density, and in 117-118 a larger share of cosponsors are original (A4), so less remains to predict after day 0 at t0 = 0. Do not read raw recall drops across Congresses as model failure (A3, A4). Decide comparisons with the t(5) test on per-fold differences (Holm-adjusted across several candidates); for a single pairwise comparison, about 0.012-0.015 Recall@20 is the smallest difference six folds reliably detect. Stratify by new vs returning legislators (D24) and by number of positives.

Bill advancement (Task 2)

The same S3 folds, with the prediction time fixed at introduction and policy area masked. The primary result is plain S3, as the notebook's split-ranking rules pick. For a GNN, plain S3 means every example, in training and evaluation alike, sees all earlier Congresses' edges cut at its own cutoff plus its own bill's edges dated <= intro + t0 (sponsor, referral committees, cosponsors in [0, t0]), and no other same-Congress bills or edges; related-bill edges are dropped because they are same-Congress by construction (B6a). +stream is a sensitivity row. For Task 2, +stream means label feedback as the notebook ran it: same-Congress bills whose 180-day label is fully resolved by the cutoff (intro + 180 <= scored bill's intro + t0) contribute their labels, as extra supervised examples, label-bearing nodes (only bills with intro + 180 <= cutoff, label as a node feature, edges time-filtered at the scored bill's cutoff) or rate features; the notebook tested the extra-examples and rate-feature forms. Label-feedback +stream is statistically indistinguishable from plain (+0.008 AUROC, 4 of 7 folds positive, driven by c = 112) and less well supported for selection and level calibration. Never use open-window bills' report status or non-referral committee edges (B7). Streaming same-Congress edges into Task 2 (Task 1's mechanism) was never tested and would be a separate, labelled variant. The notebook also suggests one shared S3+stream pipeline for both tasks (decision-c152-txt); we keep plain S3 primary because selection and level calibration were verified only there. Choose hyperparameters on the mean of validation Congresses c-3..c-1 (D17), because single-validation regret reaches 0.0053-0.0078 and validation does not rank near-ties (hit rate 14-29%). Recency weighting is a tuned choice here (+0.0096, D26), not yet covered by the window or selection checks. The evidence is weaker than for Task 1: non-rolling splits are excluded through D9 (R1-T2 borderline), and expanding vs sliding (-0.009 / -0.011, one fold) is unresolved and untested with recency weighting. Six folds detect only Task-2 differences of about 0.017-0.036 AUROC (more for highly heterogeneous pairs), so expect many ties.

Reporting:

AUROC and average precision, with each Congress's prevalence (or AP / prevalence), per Congress and per chamber, plus the fold mean with a t(5) interval and the spread. Never quote one AUROC level or a validation AUROC as the expected test level (D2b; about 13 Congresses would be needed for a precise level, D15). Baseline to beat: recency-weighted eb_rate_t0safe under plain S3 (about 0.63; 0.624 unweighted + 0.0096, D26), with unweighted 0.624, S2 0.632 and label-feedback S3+stream 0.631 as references. The at-introduction model is the primary result. The t0 = 30 policy-area model is a labelled variant, because policy area at introduction inflates AUROC by about 0.10 (D16). Report label_alt (reported OR passed origin chamber within 180 days) as a sensitivity analysis for 116-117 (A1b).

Evaluation protocol

  1. Fix the prediction times. Task 1: t0 = 0 and t0 = 7 days after introduction, label window (t0, t0+30]. Task 2: primary at introduction (t0 = 0, policy area masked), with a 'one month after introduction' variant (t0 = 30, policy area allowed, bills already reported by t0 removed from training, validation and evaluation alike) (C25, D16).

  2. Time-mask at evaluation (required, B10). The cutoff is inclusive at day resolution: an edge or feature is visible if and only if its date is <= introduced_date + t0. This matches the notebook's lag_days <= t0; using '<' would silently drop day-0 original cosponsors. Each example's input is built from up to three parts: (i) all edges from Congresses before the example's own, cut at the cutoff; (ii) the example's own bill's edges dated <= cutoff: sponsor, referral committees, and cosponsors with lag in [0, t0]; (iii) task-specific same-Congress information, used only under +stream. Plain S3 = (i) + (ii), with no other bill, edge or label from the example's own Congress; this includes related-bill edges, which are same-Congress by construction (B6a) and are dropped under plain S3 (step 5). +stream = (i) + (ii) + (iii), where (iii) differs by task, matching what the notebook tested: Task 1 +stream adds the other same-Congress bills' sponsorships and cosponsorships dated <= cutoff (the notebook's _stream_mats / _rw_stream, D13). Task 2 +stream (label feedback) adds the outcomes of same-Congress bills whose 180-day window is fully resolved by the cutoff (their intro + 180 <= the scored bill's intro + t0; the notebook's _grp(..., stream=True), D-c125-md), either as extra supervised examples, as label-bearing nodes, or as updated rate features. If used as nodes, attach only bills with intro + 180 <= cutoff, carry the label as a node feature, and time-filter their edges at the scored bill's cutoff (none of their post-cutoff cosponsor or committee edges, and no label of an unresolved bill). The extra-examples and rate-feature options are the ones the notebook actually tested. Never use the report status or non-referral committee edges of same-Congress bills whose window is still open: those encode the label (B7) and are biased by censoring. Task 1's mechanism applied to Task 2 (same-Congress edge streaming) is a separate variant that the notebook never tested; if run, label it as such. The +0.008 AUROC Task-2 stream figure refers only to label feedback. Part (ii) is the graph analogue of the bill attributes the plain-S3 rate baselines used, so plain S3 does not remove the bill's own signal. Never use the evaluation Congress's final graph. Training examples are built exactly like evaluation examples: under plain S3, a training bill in Congress j sees nothing else from Congress j; under +stream it sees only the part (iii) information available at its own cutoff. Task 1 uses +stream. The Task-2 primary uses plain S3, with label-feedback +stream as a sensitivity row.

  3. Mask in training too. Excluding the target bill's own future cosponsor edges from message passing is required (-1.8 Recall@20 points if kept, B12). Building every training example from a full as-of-(intro + t0) snapshot is recommended so training and evaluation inputs match, but it is not shown to be necessary (+0.007, CI -0.005 to +0.017, on only 2 folds).

  4. PyG implementation. A per-seed cutoff rules out full-batch R-GCN/HGT on one static HeteroData graph, even per Congress, because later bills' edges would be visible to earlier bills. Use temporal mini-batch sampling: NeighborLoader / LinkNeighborLoader with edge-level timestamps (time_attr) on every relation type including reverse edges, per-seed input_time (edge_label_time for link loaders) = intro + t0, and a temporal_strategy, so the cutoff applies at every hop. PyG keeps edges with time <= seed time, which is the inclusive convention of step 2. Plain S3 cannot be expressed by time filtering alone: a Congress-start mask would also delete the seed's own in-Congress edges (part ii), PyG's temporal sampler has only an upper time bound per seed, and with reverse relations the path seed bill -> sponsor -> another earlier same-Congress bill would reach part (iii) at two hops. A construction that works: for supervision or evaluation Congress j, build a graph G_j that holds all edges from Congresses < j (with reverse relations), and attach each Congress-j target bill only through one-directional incoming relations (legislator -> bill sponsor/cosponsor, committee -> bill referral) with no reverse relation, so no other Congress-j bill is reachable; temporal sampling with the seed's cutoff then trims the seed's own edges to lag <= t0. Training bills from Congress j use G_j in the same way. Because a Congress j-1 bill is an incoming-only target in G_{j-1} but a bidirectional history node in G_j, one HeteroData graph cannot serve a mini-batch mixing supervision Congresses: implement as one loader per supervision Congress j (batches drawn per j, gradients accumulated across j), or as a disjoint union with Congress-tagged copies of current-Congress bill nodes, and cache G_j across configurations. This per-Congress graph construction is the main memory and engineering cost of the recipe, and it is needed only for the Task-2 plain-S3 rows: Task 1 under +stream is pure time filtering, so it uses one global temporal graph with per-seed cutoffs. Under +stream (Task 1), Congress-j edges get reverse relations and are time-filtered at the cutoff. The alternative is snapshot bucketing (for example weekly) with the bucket boundary at or before each seed's t0. Node features follow the same split: under plain S3, compute legislator, committee and normaliser features (activity, degree, per-Congress normalisers (A8), a committee-referral profile built from the legislator's own sponsored bills, tenure) as of the start of the example's Congress; only under +stream compute them as of the cutoff. A PyG node feature tensor is static per node, so under +stream derive time-varying legislator features inside the model from the time-filtered sampled edges (e.g. degree counts in the sampled subgraph) or look them up from per-day snapshot tables keyed by the seed's cutoff; never use one static per-Congress tensor. Normalising with full-Congress statistics is a leak in either case. Add a unit test written on edges and bill nodes (legislator and committee nodes carry no timestamps): under plain S3, every sampled edge dated inside the seed's Congress is incident to the seed bill, and no sampled bill node other than the seed belongs to the seed's Congress. For Task 1, the target bill's sponsor edge and its cosponsors with lag in [0, t0] are input (message-passing) edges at both t0 = 0 (the original cosponsors, 33-47% of all cosponsorships, A4) and t0 = 7. Labels are cosponsors with lag in (t0, t0+30], and they are never message-passing edges. Remove the sponsor and the already-seen cosponsors from the candidate and negative pool (the notebook's Excl mask), draw negatives from the remaining members eligible at intro + t0, and evaluate only bills with at least one remaining positive, as the notebook does. Supply training negatives explicitly (a custom sampler restricted to the same-chamber pool eligible at the cutoff, minus Excl); do not use LinkNeighborLoader's default neg_sampling, which draws uniformly from all legislators. At evaluation, score and rank every eligible candidate for each bill, not a sampled subset; the notebook's Recall@K and NDCG, and so the 0.296 bar, rank the full pool. To keep this affordable (about 435 candidates per House bill), encode the bill and the legislators separately, both at the bill's cutoff, score pairs with a decoder, and cache legislator embeddings per introduction day (bills introduced the same day share a cutoff), instead of one LinkNeighborLoader subgraph per pair. Add unit tests asserting that every sampled edge and feature timestamp is <= its seed's cutoff, that the seed bill's day-0 cosponsors are present in its input, and that no label edge appears in message passing.

  5. Filter leaky relations. Keep only referral committee edges dated <= t0 (B7). Related-bill links (bill_related): the source stores essentially only same-Congress links (cross-Congress 0.014%, B6a), so under plain S3 drop bill_related edges entirely (otherwise the seed reaches earlier same-Congress bills and, through their sponsors and cosponsors, part (iii)). Under +stream (Task 1, and any labelled same-Congress edge-streaming variant for Task 2), keep only links to bills introduced <= intro + t0, with the edge time set to the later bill's introduction date so the temporal sampler enforces it (B6b). Companion and twin bills (C20) are a strong same-Congress signal, so the Task-2 plain-S3 primary deliberately forgoes it, matching the plain-S3 rate baselines, which used no related-bill information. Never use legislative subjects or CRS summaries (B5b, C13, C15a). Mask policy area at t0 <= 7 with an explicit 'not yet assigned' state, applied identically in training (C18). Rebuild count and outcome fields as of t0 (C11).

  6. Use point-in-time entities. Use the as-of-Congress party (party_code_asof, C10). The Task-1 candidate pool is the members in office at intro + t0, including delegates (C17). Legislator nodes get inductive features (party, chamber, state, a committee-referral profile from the legislator's sponsored bills cut at the start of the Congress under plain S3 and at the cutoff under +stream, tenure, majority and sponsor-in-majority flags; a dated member-committee roster is not in the data, D25) rather than ID-only embeddings, because about 20% of positives come from legislators unseen in training (B1, R2).

  7. Weight recency. Weight training examples by Congress (per-example loss weights with a half-life) on the expanding window, and tune the half-life on validation; this is the direct analogue of what D10/D26 validated. Edge-time decay (a relative-time edge encoding or a custom weighted convolution; RGCNConv/HGTConv/SAGEConv take no edge weights) is an optional architectural variant whose half-life is not the same object (start at 1 Congress; D10, D26). For Task 1 this is validated and subsumes the sliding-window question (D10). For Task 2 recency weighting helps the rate baseline (+0.0096 AUROC, better in 2 folds, worse in 0, D26), but it is a tuned choice: the window comparison and the selection-regret checks were not run with it. Run recency-weighted S3 vs S2 as a sensitivity row, and include the half-life in the step-12 selection checks.

  8. Burn-in for history depth. With per-seed cutoffs, a training example from Congress 108 sees no earlier Congress and one from 109 sees only one, while test bills in 112 see at least four. The count and rate baselines never faced this, because they aggregated 108..c-1 and scored only Congress c. So use Congress 108 as message-passing history only: supervise on 109..c-2 (training) and 109..c-1 (refit), keeping 108's edges in the temporal graph. Optionally also drop 109 from supervision if validation favours it. Add history-depth features (number of earlier Congresses visible, days since the Congress started), which also cover thin in-Congress history for early-session bills under +stream. Report fold 112 separately, because it has the least supervision (109-110) and also drives the Task-2 streaming and window results.

  9. Run the six development folds. For each c in 112..117: train on 108..c-2, tune on c-1, refit on 108..c-1 and score c (supervision subject to the burn-in step). For the GNN refit, fix the number of gradient steps (or epochs scaled to data size) from the validation run, and check the no-refit checkpoint on one fold, because the refit gain (+0.025 under streaming) was measured on parameter-free baselines (D19). For Task 2, pick hyperparameters on the mean of validation Congresses c-3..c-1 (D17; c-1-only regret on the development folds is 0.0053, above tolerance, D27). This reuses earlier folds' validation scores, at no extra training cost, only if each shortlisted candidate has also been run on the two preceding folds. Otherwise run it there first, or fall back to c-1-only selection and disclose the D12b caveat. The 3-validation rule's regret on the 6 development folds was not separately verified.

  10. Compare models with one inference rule. Use the same test bills for all models. Per fold, compute the paired difference with a sponsor-cluster bootstrap CI (1.2-2.6x wider than a bill-level bootstrap, D-c128-txt). Across folds there is one decision rule. Candidate A beats B only if their 6-fold mean paired difference favours A and an interval excluding 0 confirms it. Use a t interval on the six per-fold differences (df = 5), or a two-stage bootstrap that resamples Congresses and then sponsors, whichever is wider. When more than two candidates compete, apply Holm to the t(5) p-values of the pairwise differences (or report Bonferroni-adjusted intervals if intervals are shown). If the adjusted test does not confirm the difference, the candidates are tied. Call a resolved difference practically relevant only if it is also at least the 0.01 MDE. Report the number of configurations compared. Planning guide, not a threshold: with six folds, the smallest difference detectable with 80% power depends on the pair's between-Congress spread. For one Task-1 comparison (sd 0.008-0.010) it is about 0.0115-0.0145; for Task 2 (sd 0.012-0.025) it is about 0.017-0.036 AUROC. With Holm over 3-5 comparisons (for example each candidate against the incumbent), the first-step critical t rises from 2.57 to about 3.5-4.0 (3.53 for m = 3, 4.03 for m = 5), and these grow to about 0.015-0.021 (Task 1) and 0.022-0.054 (Task 2). Holm's m is the number of comparisons, not candidates: all-pairwise comparison among 5 candidates is m = 10, which raises the first-step critical t to about 4.8 and the detectable differences above these ranges. Expect most GNN architecture comparisons to end as ties. Pre-register the tie-break: among statistically tied candidates, pick the simplest or cheapest (fewest parameters, lowest training cost), not the nominal best. Report per-fold values and the next-Congress prediction interval (D9b) next to the mean.

  11. Beat the right baselines, under the same protocol. Task 1 under S3+stream: at least unweighted sponsor_hist 0.296 Recall@20 at t0 = 0 (0.275 at t0 = 7) and rw2hop 0.295 (7-fold means, D13). Run recency-weighted sponsor history and the learned SVD under S3+stream first; that higher number becomes the bar. Non-streaming references (sh_hl1 0.282, SVD 0.280 under plain S3) are not the bar. Task 2: recency-weighted (half-life 1) eb_rate_t0safe under plain S3, about 0.63 AUROC (0.624 unweighted + 0.0096 from D26; compute the exact value on the development folds). Keep 0.624 as the unweighted reference, and list S2 (0.632) and label-feedback S3+stream (0.631) as sensitivity references (7-fold means, decision-c152-txt). Report baselines for 112-117 and for 118 separately, as for the GNN.

  12. Close the untested gaps before GNN work. Re-run the selection checks (D11/D17 for Task 1, D12b/D17 for Task 2) on the streaming folds with the GNN's own hyperparameter grid, including the recency half-life for Task 2 (and, for Task 2, under the label-feedback +stream definition of step 2). Back-test the full expanding + streaming + recency recipe, with burn-in, on the development folds.

  13. Freeze and score 118 once. Freeze features, architecture, half-life and tuning rule. Run the identical recipe on the 118 fold (train 108-116, tune on 117, refit 108-117) and report it as the headline result next to the development fold mean.

  14. Check prospectively and redeploy. Score closed-window 119 bills with a model refit on 108-118, against a prediction interval from development folds truncated to the same introduction-date window. Re-run the notebook's validity and drift checks when a Congress completes.

Why this split

  • It is the only family with no validity failure for either task and enough test data (25,065 Task-1 and 60,765 Task-2 development test bills). Random (D7), within-Congress (C5, C6b) and pooled 117+118 (D1, D20) splits fail validity checks. Single-Congress splits fail D9 only through Task-2 pairs. For Task 1 they pass D9 (worst miss 1 of 7) but are still rejected for precision and representativeness (next reason and alternatives).

    D7 C5 C6b D1 D20 D9 D-c128-txt decision-c147-txt decision-c151-txt

  • Several test Congresses give a usable estimate of the average effect: the median 95% half-width of a paired mean difference is about 0.008 at k = 6 under the notebook's normal approximation (about 0.010 with a t(5) interval). One Congress cannot resolve near-MDE Task-1 choices (sh_hl1 vs sh_none+caucus flips sign in 1 of 7 Congresses; expanding vs sliding misses in 1 of 7), and its level would be specific to that Congress, which is off-distribution for 117 (Task 2) or 118 (Task-1 density). Averaging does not reduce next-Congress variability (D9b), so per-fold results are reported too.

    D9 D9b D27 D-c128-txt D-c140-txt A3 A1b C3

  • On plain S3 folds, validation on the next Congress picks near-best Task-1 models (regret at most 0.0032, tau 0.86-0.94) and costs little for Task 2 when the mean of three validation Congresses is used (regret at most 0.0019). Refitting on train + validation adds +0.025 Recall@20 under streaming without hurting Task 2. So 'tune on c-1, refit, test on c' is honest and efficient for baselines; the GNN refit is checked separately.

    D11 D21 D23 D17 D12 D12b D19 D-c119-txt D-c138-txt D-c140-txt

  • Streaming is leakage-free under the time-masking rules, matches what is known when a prediction is made, adds +0.037 Recall@20 in 7/7 folds for Task 1, and nearly removes cold start. For Task 2 the notebook's split-ranking rules pick plain S3, and its Task-2 streaming variant is label feedback from resolved same-Congress bills, not edge streaming. Plain and label-feedback +stream are statistically indistinguishable there, and selection and level calibration are less well supported under streaming (val-test gap 1.64x vs 1.28x the CI half-width; selection checks not run). The notebook also suggests one shared S3+stream pipeline for both tasks (decision-c152-txt). We keep plain S3 as the Task-2 primary because selection and level calibration were verified only there, and report +stream as a sensitivity row.

    D13 D14 B1b R3-T1 R3-T2 decision-c147-txt decision-c152-txt D-c125-md

  • For Task 1, an expanding window with recency weighting matches the sliding window (-0.0008 Recall@20), so recency weighting is validated there (D10). It gives a data-hungry GNN more examples, and the tuned half-life lets validation decide how much old data matters. For Task 2, recency weighting helps the rate baseline (+0.0096 AUROC, D26), but it is a tuned choice that the window comparison and the selection-regret checks have not yet covered, so it is checked on the development folds. As a tie-breaker only: the expanding window keeps every chamber majority in training (the sliding window covers both majorities for only 57% of units, C8), though regime-matched weighting adds nothing measurable (D26, +0.0011).

    D10 D26 C8 R4b R5 D-c130-txt C-c85-txt

  • A locked final Congress protects the headline number from the selection bias of comparing architectures on the development folds. That is the main reason to reserve 118. The cost: the D27 sizing pass is fragile. Under t(5), the worst relevant pair misses with probability about 0.28 (0.115 under the normal approximation). The cause is not a small effect. That pair is a large difference (about +0.08 AUROC) whose size and direction vary between Congresses (sd about 0.06). Six folds also detect only about 0.012-0.015 for Task 1 and 0.017-0.036 AUROC for Task 2 (more for heterogeneous pairs). So comparisons are judged with the t(5) test (Holm-adjusted across candidates), unresolved ones are ties, and 118 is kept locked anyway.

    D27 R7 D-c140-txt D-c140-o1

Alternatives considered and rejected

OptionWhy not

Single expanding split: train 108-115 / val 116 / test 117 (S1a), or train 108-116 / val 117 / test 118 (S1b)

For Task 2, one test Congress fails to confirm a real +0.020 AUROC difference in 3 of 7 Congresses (43%; very imprecise with n = 7, never reversed): D9 FAIL. For Task 1 it passes D9 (worst Task-1 miss 1 of 7) but cannot resolve near-MDE choices, and each candidate test Congress is off-distribution (117 for the Task-2 label, 118 for Task-1 density and timing), so a single number would mostly reflect that Congress. Acceptable for debugging only.

D9 D-c128-txt A-c17-txt A-c13-txt C3 decision-c147-txt

Pooled test: train 108-115 / val 116 / test 117+118 with one refit on 108-116 (S1pool)

Fails D1, D20 and D9. It scores 118 with a model one Congress stale: 21.7% of 118 bills have a sponsor with no training history (bound 14.4%), 31.4% of positives are cold, and the pooled score (0.222) is below both of its components scored separately.

D1 D20 D9 B2 B-c49-txt decision-c147-txt

Within-Congress temporal split (S4: first 60% / next 20% / last 20% of each Congress)

Fails the Task-1 censoring check (C5) and loses 80.8% of Task-2 test bills to censoring (C6b). Its higher Task-1 score (0.311) comes from a small, late slice (about 777 bills per fold). No break lies inside a Congress, so nothing justifies cutting inside one.

C5 C6b C-c82-txt C23 D8 decision-c147-txt

Random bill split 70/15/15 (S5)

Direct future leakage: +0.0745 Recall@20 optimism (D7), and 45.2% of evaluation bills have a later twin in training (C20). It also hides all drift between history and deployment. Use only as a labelled leaky upper bound.

D7 C20 C19 D-c124-txt C-c106-txt

3-Congress sliding window (S2) as the main protocol

Not invalid, and kept as a sensitivity analysis. For Task 1 with recency weighting it is no better than the expanding window (-0.0008) and gives the GNN less data. The Task-2 S3-vs-S2 gap (-0.009 / -0.011) comes almost entirely from one fold (c = 112: -0.058) and was not tested with recency weighting; for the unweighted day-30 eb_rate reference the sign reverses (expanding +0.0027, 5 of 7 folds, D10). Missing chamber majorities in 43% of its units is a tie-breaker, not a demonstrated loss.

D10 C8 D26 R4b R5 decision-c149-o0 decision-c152-txt D-c130-txt

Plain by-Congress graph for Task 1 (S3 without +stream), or a static full-graph transductive GNN

Without streaming, Task 1 loses 0.037 Recall@20 and about 20% of positives come from legislators unseen in training. A full-graph setup evaluates on the evaluation Congress's final graph, about 52% of which does not exist at t0 (B10), and full-batch training on a static graph lets each bill see its own future edges, which costs 1.8 Recall@20 points (B12).

D13 B1 B1b B10 B12 R2

Risks and mitigations

RiskMitigation

Congress 118 already informed the protocol choice at the baseline level, so the 'locked' test is not pristine.

Lock 118 against all GNN tuning from now on, disclose its prior use, and treat 119 (closed windows, like-for-like comparison) as the clean prospective confirmation.

Model selection was never tested under streaming (D11/D12b/D17 ran on plain S3 only), and the full expanding + streaming + recency recipe was never run as a whole.

Re-run the selection-regret checks on the streaming folds with the GNN's own grid, and back-test recency-weighted sponsor history under S3+stream, before GNN work. If regret exceeds tolerance, select on plain-S3 validation or the 3-validation mean.

Six dependent folds give little power. Under t(5) the worst relevant pair's miss risk is about 0.28, driven by between-Congress heterogeneity of a large effect. Overlapping training windows and correlated adjacent Congresses make the effective k smaller than 6.

Use the t(5) test on per-fold differences (Holm-adjusted across candidates) or the two-stage bootstrap as the only decision rule (protocol step 10). Treat 'k of 6' patterns as descriptive, report per-fold values and next-Congress prediction intervals, and pick the simplest candidate among statistical ties.

The development fold mean becomes optimistic as more architectures are compared on it, because each test Congress is also a later fold's validation Congress.

Report it as a development number and report the number of configurations compared. Apply Holm correction across more than two candidates. If no candidate wins after correction, pick the simplest or cheapest of the tied candidates (a pre-registered rule), not the nominal best. Make the single 118 score the headline.

Task-2 validation does not rank near-tie models (hit rate 14-29%), and a GNN grid may be more spread out than the baseline families.

Select on the mean of three validation Congresses (D17). Treat Task-2 differences that the (Holm-adjusted) t(5) test does not confirm as ties; for Task 2 this typically means differences below about 0.017-0.036 AUROC, more for heterogeneous pairs.

The Task-2 AUROC level shifts between Congresses (fold means 0.655 to 0.583), and in 116-117 the label misses many chamber-passed bills.

Report Task-2 AUROC and AP (with prevalence) per Congress and per chamber, never one pooled level. Report the label_alt sensitivity. If calibrated probabilities are needed, recalibrate on the evaluation Congress's already-resolved bills, not on c-1.

A naive PyG implementation leaks future edges or features (static full-batch graphs, per-Congress normalisers, legislator features computed over the whole Congress).

Temporal neighbour sampling with inclusive per-seed cutoffs on all relations, identical example construction in training and evaluation, as-of-Congress-start features under plain S3 and as-of-cutoff features under +stream, one-directional attachment of current-Congress target bills under plain S3, explicit eligible-pool negatives, the target's seen cosponsors as inputs and excluded from candidates, disjoint supervision and message-passing edges, and unit tests on sampled timestamps (protocol step 4).

Refitting a GNN reuses an epoch budget chosen on less data, with no early-stopping signal; the refit gain was measured only on parameter-free baselines.

Fix gradient steps (or scale epochs to data size) and compare against the no-refit checkpoint on one fold.

Running six folds per configuration is expensive for a GNN.

Use the single debug split for early iterations. Run all six folds only for shortlisted configurations, and run each shortlisted candidate on every fold so the 3-validation rule can reuse earlier folds' scores; otherwise fall back to c-1 selection with the D12b caveat. Reuse per-fold time-filtered loaders across configurations.

With per-seed cutoffs, GNN training examples from the earliest Congresses have almost no history, unlike test bills, a shift the baselines never faced. It is largest in fold 112.

Burn-in (protocol step 8): use 108 as message-passing history only, add history-depth features, and report fold 112 separately for both the GNN and the baselines.

Cold start remains for bills introduced in the first weeks of a new Congress, when freshmen have little in-Congress history even with streaming.

Rely on inductive legislator features. Stratify Task-1 results by legislator novelty (D24) and by introduction date within the Congress.

What would change this recommendation

  • If selection checks re-run on streaming folds show validation regret above tolerance, select models on plain-S3 validation (or the mean of several validation Congresses) and use streaming only at test time.

  • If a GNN without recency weighting is used, switch the main window to the 3-Congress sliding window (S2). Also switch if S2+stream beats S3+stream with decay on the 6-fold mean with a t(5) test (Holm-adjusted if several candidates) that confirms the difference. For Task 2, the same rule applies to the recency-weighted S3 vs S2 sensitivity row.

  • If a recency-weighted Task-2 model with label-feedback +stream (step 2: labels of same-Congress bills whose 180-day window is fully resolved) beats plain S3 on the 6-fold mean with a t(5) test (Holm-adjusted if several candidates) that confirms the difference, and the selection checks pass under it, make label-feedback +stream the Task-2 primary. A raw mean gain is not enough: a +0.015 AUROC gain with a between-Congress sd of 0.022 gives a t(5) p-value of about 0.16. Same-Congress edge streaming for Task 2 is untested; it needs the same test before it can be adopted, and it must never include open-window bills' report status.

  • If 119 falls outside the prediction interval built from development folds truncated to the same introduction-date window, treat recent drift as structural: add 118 to every final fit and shorten the recency half-life.

  • If Task 2 is redefined (for example t0 = 30 with policy area, or label_alt as the primary label), re-run Section D's Task-2 checks, because the streaming and window verdicts were borderline for the current definition.

  • If compute allows only one split, use train 108-116 / val 117 / test 118 (S1b) and report it as a single-Congress estimate with explicitly wide uncertainty, not as a model comparison.

Method and glossary

The evidence comes from the executed notebook notebooks/split_analysis.ipynb on Congresses 108-118 (173,437 bills, 145,738 law-capable; 2.1M cosponsorship events; snapshot 2026-10-17). Sections A-C ran distribution, graph-structure, boundary and leakage checks against 95% prediction intervals built from 6-8 training Congresses, with Holm correction within some checks. Section D trained transparent baselines under nine candidate splits and scored them with 500-resample sponsor-cluster bootstraps and paired CIs. The Task-1 baselines were popularity, party+popularity, sponsor history, a 2-hop random walk and a truncated-SVD embedding; the Task-2 baselines were smoothed rates. The final section de-duplicated 102 checks to 100 and applied explicit rules (R1-R8) to rank splits per task. This synthesis weighs those results independently. It re-attributes the D9 single-Congress verdict by task, and recomputes the 6-fold miss risk with a noncentral t distribution (df = 5) from the notebook's per-fold chart data (D-c140-o1); it also computes 80%-power detectable differences under t(5), with and without Holm, from the notebook's between-Congress spreads (D-c128-txt). These recomputations are ours, not notebook outputs. Multiplicity: many checks use the 5% level without family-wise control, so a few FAILs and PASSes are expected by chance, and many PASSes with n = 6-8 mean 'not detected' rather than 'stable'. The recommendation rests on a few large-effect results (D7, C6b, C20, D13, D19) that survive any reasonable correction. Borderline verdicts (D9 at k = 6, D12, D12b, R3-T2, R5 for Task 2) should be read as inconclusive. Main limitations: (1) all backtests use simple baselines, not GNNs, so GNN-specific behaviour (early stopping, refit, message-passing overfitting) is untested; (2) the 7 rolling folds share most training data and adjacent Congresses are correlated, so the effective number of folds is below 7 and fold counts are descriptive; (3) the 0.01 MDE is a convention; (4) Congress 118 informed the protocol choice, and its records are still being maintained; (5) several figures are proxies, notably policy-area availability at t0 (n = 56 bills of the in-progress 119th); (6) the notebook's Task-2 streaming variant is label feedback from resolved same-Congress bills, so same-Congress edge streaming for Task 2 is untested; model selection under streaming, the recency-weighted Task-2 window comparison, and the full expanding + streaming + recency combination were never directly evaluated; (7) the B12 training-consistency test covers only 2 folds with a logistic count ranker.

Glossary

Rolling-origin (forward-chaining) evaluation

Repeatedly train on everything before a cut point, test on the next period, then move the cut point forward. Here, each Congress 112-117 is one test fold.

Expanding vs sliding window

Expanding: training always starts at Congress 108 and grows (S3). Sliding: training uses only the last 3 Congresses (S2).

Refit

After choosing hyperparameters on validation Congress c-1, retrain on 108..c-1 (training plus validation) with those settings before testing on c.

+stream (streaming protocol)

Adding same-Congress information that was known at prediction time, defined per task as the notebook tested it. Task 1: the other same-Congress bills' sponsorship and cosponsorship edges dated up to the bill's introduction date + t0. Task 2 (label feedback): the outcomes of same-Congress bills whose 180-day window had fully closed by the cutoff; open-window bills are never used. Streaming same-Congress edges into Task 2 is a separate, untested variant. 'Plain' (plain S3) gives each example only earlier Congresses plus its own bill's edges up to the cutoff. Training examples are built the same way as evaluation examples in both variants.

Time-masking

Removing every node, edge or feature value dated after the prediction time from the model's input.

Temporal neighbour sampling

Mini-batch message passing in which each seed node only samples neighbours through edges whose timestamp is at or before that seed's prediction time, at every hop.

t0

Prediction time, measured in days after a bill's introduction (0 or 7 for Task 1).

Locked test

A held-back Congress (118) that is scored exactly once after all design decisions are frozen.

Prospective test

Evaluation on data that did not exist when the protocol was chosen (Congress 119).

MDE (minimum detectable effect)

The smallest difference treated as worth acting on, fixed by convention at 0.01 Recall@20 or 0.01 AUROC. It is not the same as the smallest difference six folds can detect (see next entry).

Detectable difference (80% power)

The smallest true difference that a test on six per-fold values would confirm 80% of the time. It grows with the between-Congress spread of the difference and with Holm correction: about 0.012-0.015 for a single Task-1 comparison and 0.017-0.036 AUROC for a Task-2 comparison, and more for highly heterogeneous pairs or with Holm correction.

Miss risk

The probability that a test set fails to confirm the direction of a real model difference. For one Congress the notebook measures it as an empirical share of Congresses; for k folds it is a power calculation for the mean. The two are not directly comparable.

Next-Congress prediction interval (D9b)

The range in which one new Congress's paired difference should fall, from the spread across past Congresses. It does not shrink as more folds are averaged.

t interval (df = 5)

A confidence interval for the mean of six per-fold values that accounts for estimating their spread from only six numbers; it is about 31% wider than the normal-approximation interval.

Holm correction

A step-down adjustment of p-values that keeps the chance of any false 'winner' at 5% when several comparisons are made. It acts on p-values; when intervals are reported for several comparisons, Bonferroni-adjusted intervals are the matching choice.

Selection regret

How much test score is lost by picking the model that is best on validation instead of the one that is best on test.

Hit rate / Kendall tau

Hit rate: share of folds where the validation-best candidate is also test-best. Kendall tau: rank agreement between validation and test orderings (1 = identical).

Sponsor-cluster bootstrap

Resampling bills in groups by sponsor to estimate uncertainty, which respects the correlation between bills from the same legislator.

Paired comparison

Comparing two models on the same test bills, so Congress-level difficulty cancels out of the difference.

Recall@K

The share of a bill's true future cosponsors that appear among the model's top K ranked legislators.

NDCG

Normalized discounted cumulative gain: a ranking score that rewards placing true cosponsors near the top.

AUROC

The probability that a randomly chosen advancing bill is scored above a randomly chosen non-advancing bill. 0.5 is chance level.

Average precision (AP)

The area under the precision-recall curve. It depends on prevalence, so report it together with the base rate.

Cold start

A legislator (node) that has no history in the training graph, so an ID-based embedding cannot score it.

Inductive vs transductive

An inductive model computes node representations from features and neighbours, so it handles unseen nodes. A transductive model learns a fixed embedding per training node.

Censoring

A label that cannot be observed yet because its outcome window (30 or 180 days) has not closed by the data snapshot.

Regime

Which party controls the House and the Senate in a given Congress.

Burn-in

Keeping the earliest Congress (108) in the graph as history while excluding its bills from supervision, so every training example has at least one earlier Congress of history.

Original cosponsor

A cosponsor who joins on the day the bill is introduced (lag 0). Original cosponsors are known at t0 = 0, so they are inputs, not labels.

Conclusion: the split we will use

The short answer

Yes: start with a simple split, then move to a better one. Choose the simple split so that the better split is just "more of the same". The simple split below is the last fold of the better split (fold 117), as long as we also retrain on 108–116 before testing on 117. The code carries over unchanged. Numbers from the single split are for building and debugging. Model comparisons are made only on the full set of folds.

Step 1: a simple split for building the pipeline and the first baselines

Test (after retraining on 108–116) 117 2021–2022 15,242
Locked final test (never used for tuning) 118 2023–2024 16,565
Excluded 119 2025–now (in progress) n/a

Not every bill is scored. Bills whose label window runs past the end of the Congress are dropped, and for cosponsor prediction so are bills that gain no new cosponsor in the 30-day label window. That leaves about 4,000–5,000 scored bills per Congress for cosponsor prediction and about 10,000–14,000 for advancement (more in recent Congresses).

Rules that come with it. These apply to every split we use, now and later:

  1. Split by Congress, in time order. Never split randomly.
  2. Build each example's graph as it looked at prediction time. Use only edges and features dated on or before the bill's introduction date plus t0 (0 or 7 days for cosponsor prediction, 0 for advancement). About half (52%) of a Congress's final cosponsor graph does not exist yet at that moment (B10). - For cosponsor prediction, this includes earlier cosponsorships from the current Congress. - For advancement, the main version uses only earlier Congresses plus the bill's own sponsor, referral committees and day-0 cosponsors.
  3. Drop bills whose label window runs past the end of their Congress. Bills die at adjournment, so for these bills a "no" can never be confirmed.
  4. Use point-in-time facts. Use each legislator's party as of that Congress, and draw candidates only from members in office at prediction time (C10, C17).
  5. Never use fields written later. That means legislative subjects, CRS summaries, later text versions, and final counts such as a bill's total number of cosponsors (C11). For advancement, also hide policy area at introduction, and in the main version drop related-bill links, which almost only connect bills of the same Congress.

Why this split. The reasons use only the data, not any model results:

  • Time order is required. In a random split, 45% of evaluation bills have a related or identically titled bill introduced later that sits in the training set (C20). A time-ordered split has none (C19). Knowledge-graph benchmarks show the same problem: Schlichtkrull et al. (2018), the R-GCN paper, following Toutanova and Chen (2015), note that FB15k and WN18 put a fact in training and its reverse in test, so much of the task becomes memorisation. FB15k-237 was built to remove those pairs.
  • Use whole Congresses, not slices of one Congress. The closest prior work on cosponsorship (Russo et al., ACL 2023) splits inside each Congress: the first 60% of the period trains, the next 20% validates, and the last 20% tests. Applied to our advancement label, a within-Congress split fails. Among the last 20% of each Congress's bills, 81% have a 180-day window that runs past adjournment, so their outcome is incomplete and they must be dropped (C6b). Cutting by time, as Russo et al. do, would be even worse, because the last 20% of a Congress is shorter than 180 days. Their label, active vs passive cosponsorship, has no future window, so they don't face this problem. A Congress boundary is a natural cut: every Congress starts with a fresh set of bills.
  • Test on 117 and lock 118.
  • Both 117 and 118 differ from the training years in ways every forward-in-time split shares: more bills, a lower committee-report rate in the House (the Senate stays within its historical range), and more cosponsors signing on the first day (A8, A2, A4).
  • 118 also has fewer cosponsors per bill after day 0, and they sign later (A3, C3). So report it separately.
  • Its records are still being maintained: 29% were edited in the past year (C14). No labels are missing (C24), but we treat 118's labels as provisional.
  • We therefore test on 117 and keep the most recent complete Congress, 118, as a locked final test. One caveat: 118 already appeared once in this split analysis, as one of the baseline folds. It has never been used to tune a model, and it must stay that way.
  • Exclude 119. It is still in session, so its labels are not final.
  • Enough data, and each chamber's majority party is represented.
  • There are 82,644 training bills and about 15,000 each for validation and test.
  • In 116 and 117, the House majority party and the Senate majority party each also hold that chamber in at least one training Congress (C8).
  • The exact combination in 116 (Democratic House, Republican Senate) never appears in training. We found no sign that the combination matters beyond each chamber's majority (C8b).

What the simple split cannot do. Congresses differ from one another by more than random noise (A2, A4, A8). A single test Congress is one draw, so on its own it cannot show whether a small improvement is real. This is the reason to move on once the pipeline works.

Step 2: a better split for comparing models, based on the baseline results

Rolling "next Congress" folds. Repeat the simple split once for each Congress c from 112 to 117:

  1. Train on 108 to c−2.
  2. Tune on c−1. For advancement, tune on the mean of the three preceding validation Congresses (D17).
  3. Retrain on 108 to c−1 with the chosen settings.
  4. Test on c.

Fold 117 is the simple split. Report every fold together with the average. At the very end, run the frozen final model once on 118, and later check it on the finished part of 119.

Each row is one honest "next Congress" forecast. Tune on the validate Congress, then refit on train + validate before scoring the test Congress. 108 is message-passing history only (GNN burn-in). Prospective: refit on 108-118, score 119 bills whose label windows have closed.

Why. This is what the baseline runs showed:

  • One test Congress is too noisy for advancement and imprecise for cosponsor prediction. A real 0.02 AUROC difference in advancement prediction went unconfirmed in 3 of 7 Congresses when it was judged on a single Congress (D9). Six folds help, but by our power calculation they still resolve only fairly large differences in a single comparison: about 0.012–0.015 in Recall@20 and 0.017–0.036 in AUROC (more when several models are compared). So we decide each comparison with a paired t-test on the six per-fold differences, and treat differences the test does not resolve as ties.
  • The previous Congress is a good tuning set for cosponsor prediction. It picks near-best models (D11, D21, D23) and predicts the test score level (D1). Model selection was tested only without the current-Congress history (next bullet), so it still has to be confirmed with it; the score-level check also passes with it (D14). For advancement it does not rank close models well, which is why tuning uses the mean of the three previous validation Congresses (D17).
  • The random split really does inflate scores. On the same bills it adds +0.075 to Recall@20 (D7), which confirms that rejecting it was right.
  • For cosponsor prediction, let the model see the current Congress up to the prediction time. Earlier cosponsorships in the same Congress raise Recall@20 from 0.259 to 0.296, higher in all 7 folds (D13). These figures use test Congresses 112–118; on the six development folds 112–117 the gain is +0.034. This also fixes the "new legislator" problem. Without it, about 18–20% of the correct answers are legislators the model never saw in training; with it, under 1% are (B1, R2).
  • Keep old Congresses, but down-weight them. For cosponsor prediction, recency weighting makes the growing window as good as a short sliding window (D10). For advancement this is still open, so we run the sliding window as a side check.
  • For advancement, report each Congress separately. The AUROC level shifts from one Congress to the next (D2b), so a single averaged number hides real differences.

When to switch

  1. Build and debug the whole pipeline on the simple split: data loading, time-masked graphs, baselines and metrics.
  2. Once the baselines reproduce, run the same code on all six folds. That costs only more training runs, not new code.
  3. From then on, make every model comparison with a paired test on the six per-fold differences, reporting each fold and the average. Treat unresolved differences as ties. The simple-split numbers become the "fold 117" row.
  4. Run 118 once, at the end, with everything frozen.

One paragraph for the paper

We split the data by Congress in time order. For model development we use rolling-origin evaluation: for each Congress c from 112 to 117, we train on Congresses 108 to c−2, tune hyperparameters on c−1 (for bill advancement, on the mean of the three preceding validation Congresses), retrain on 108 to c−1 and test on c. We report every fold and decide model comparisons with a paired t-test on the six per-fold differences. Congress 118, which informed only our baseline protocol analysis, is scored once with the frozen configuration, and the ongoing 119th Congress is excluded. Each example's graph contains only information dated on or before its prediction time. For cosponsor prediction this includes earlier cosponsorships in the same Congress; for advancement it is limited to earlier Congresses and the bill's own edges. We use whole Congresses rather than a random or within-Congress split for two reasons. In a random split, 45% of evaluation bills have a related or identically titled bill introduced later that sits in the training set. In a within-Congress split, 81% of the last fifth of each Congress's bills have a 180-day advancement window that runs past adjournment. Our first pipeline runs use a single fold (train 108–115, validate 116, retrain on 108–116, test 117), the last of the six development folds.
